prisma-calibration/getting-started/insta.title: Installing the Calibration App
prisma-calibration/getting-started/insta.content:
Prisma Calibration is included in the Windows and Linux Prisma Suite downloads. The Generator-only package cannot create calibration data or publish personal models.
This wiki describes the current app. The downloadable packages may be older, and Windows and Linux releases may differ. Check Installing Prisma and the release notes for the version you download.

Download the Suite archive for your platform from Prisma’s GitHub Releases page: ZIP on Windows or .tar.gz on Linux x86-64.
Extract the entire archive. On Windows, use File Explorer’s Extract All; on Linux, use your archive manager or run tar -xzf followed by the downloaded archive’s path. Do not run either application from inside an archive preview.
Put the extracted Suite folder in a normal writable location, not a protected system folder (such as Program Files on Windows), a cloud-synchronized folder, or a network share.
Keep the entire Suite folder together. Generator and Calibration share packaged software, but each owns a separate visible data tree and Workspace.

No Python, PyCharm, VS Code, OpenSCAD, CAD kernel, or manual package installation is required. See Installing Prisma for platform status, the Windows unsigned-app warning, and general portable-install guidance.
Bring an existing Calibration library into a blank Suite
Do not copy individual database, model, or asset files into the new Workspace. In the existing Calibration app, create an All Data and Artifacts backup and include raw images if you want the new copy to retain them. Start the blank Suite’s Calibration app, open Backup / Restore, and restore that package. Verify the Logbook, Images, Filaments, Geometries, and model status before retiring the older copy.
Keep the original installation and backup until the restored Suite has been checked. A backup stored only inside the live Prisma folder will be lost if that whole folder or drive is lost.

prisma-calibration/getting-started/launc.title: Launching the Calibration App
prisma-calibration/getting-started/launc.content:
Open the extracted Prisma Suite folder. On Windows, double-click Prisma Calibration.exe. On Linux, open a terminal in that folder and run:
./"Prisma Calibration"
A console/terminal remains attached, Calibration starts a local server, and it asks the operating system to open the interface in your default browser. Keep the console or terminal open while you use Calibration; closing it stops Calibration without stopping a separately running Generator. If the browser does not open, use the local address printed after Address:.
The launcher normally uses http://127.0.0.1:8016. If that port is busy, it chooses another local port and prints the actual address after Address:. Starting Calibration a second time reopens the already-running app instead of allowing two processes to write the same Workspace.
On a blank first launch, Prisma creates an empty SQLite database and these folders inside the Suite:





























FolderOwnership and purposeCalibration/InboxUser-facing incoming calibration photographs. Removed Images is beneath it.Calibration/Output/StepsUser-facing STEP/STL geometry exports.Calibration/Output/BackupsBackup and RAW-archive packages created by Calibration. Copy important packages somewhere independent.Calibration/Output/Published ModelsPortable model-library ZIPs created by Export Library Package.Calibration/WorkspaceCalibration’s authoritative SQLite database, managed image copies, measurements, current working models, recovery state, and internal files. Do not rearrange individual files here.
Calibration owns this entire tree; Generator neither reads nor edits its Workspace. Likewise, Calibration does not edit Generator’s installed libraries. Publish to Generator creates a new library copy for Generator.
Prisma keeps normal state inside the extracted Suite folder, not in a separate per-user application-data location such as %LOCALAPPDATA%. You may move or copy the entire Suite folder while both applications are closed. For normal Calibration backup or migration, use Backup / Restore rather than manually moving Workspace contents.

prisma-calibration/getting-started/index.title: Getting Started
prisma-calibration/getting-started/index.content:
The calibration app turns 3D-printed filament swatches into the color models the generator prints from. This page walks through the workflow from an empty library to publishing models. Start with one sample to learn the steps, then build up the evidence you need: a complete library requires more than one strip. For the reasoning behind each step see How It Works; for the details of each screen, How To Use.
What you need

The three things the app can’t do for you: a multi-color 3D printer, the filaments you want to characterize, and a lightbox with a camera that shoots RAW (Prisma also uses the camera-rendered JPEG embedded in the RAW).
The app itself — see Installing and Launching. The Suite starts Calibration with Prisma Calibration.exe on Windows or Prisma Calibration on Linux; neither packaged platform requires Python, an IDE, or manual dependency installation.

It opens on a single page titled Calibration Logbook, with an empty database created automatically inside Calibration/Workspace on a blank first launch. It is a single-user tool: browser tabs share the same running app and data. If one operation would interfere with another, the app asks you to wait.
The shape of the work
A sample is one printed strip — a geometry filled with specific filaments — that you photograph and measure. You build up a library of samples, then fit models from the measurements you trust. The first run touches every stage once.

1 — Add your filaments
On the Filaments tab, use + New Filament for each filament: color name, manufacturer, material, and a hex color for the UI. Set its policy while you’re there — mark your white diffusers White-cap eligible, and leave Exclude from model fits off for anything you want the models to learn or a newly published Generator library to offer for new work. See Filaments.
2 — Choose a geometry
A geometry is the strip layout: a row of swatches with exactly one variable material role stepping through a range of thicknesses, plus any constant-thickness roles the design needs above or below it. On the Geometries tab, + New Sample Geometry opens the step builder, or reuse an existing geometry. See Geometries.
3 — Create the sample
On the Logbook tab, + New Samples fills a geometry with your filaments — one sample per filament you’re characterizing (the Multi mode spawns a batch at once). The sample now exists, waiting for photographs. See Creating New Samples.
4 — Print and photograph (outside the app)
Export the geometry’s print files with Export Geometry Files (Geometries tab), print the strip in the chosen filaments, and photograph it on the lightbox as RAW. Take one empty-lightbox RAW too — that’s the blank used for flatfield correction.
5 — Assign the photos
On Images → Assign Images, place the photos in the Calibration Inbox, use Import from Inbox, then assign each sample its strip image and a blank. For many samples at once, CSV Bulk Assignment does it from a spreadsheet. See Images.
6 — Extract the colors
On Images → Processing Queue, your sample sits under Ready to Process. Process All runs strip detection, deskew, flatfield correction, and per-swatch color extraction. If it lands in Failed or Flagged for Manual Processing, Manual Process lets you click the four corners by hand. Then Accept the result — only accepted extractions feed the models. See Processing Queue.
7 — Fit the working models
On the Modeling tab, the Overview shows your evidence and flags gaps; Fit Models builds Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and The Camera Transform from the samples you’ve included. This does not change Generator. The Camera Transform needs at least five eligible samples with both transmission and camera-rendered appearance measurements; with fewer, that stage is skipped. Five samples are a minimum for fitting, not a promise of good coverage. See Modeling and Fit Models.
8 — Publish a Generator library
When all three working models are current, press Publish Models in the top bar. Give the library a name, version, and publisher, then either:

Publish to Generator to install a new inactive library into the Generator in this Suite; or
Export Library Package to create a portable ZIP in Calibration/Output/Published Models for another Prisma installation or a release download.

Publishing leaves Calibration’s working models in place, and later fitting cannot change the published copy. Select the new library through Config → Model Library in Generator when you are ready to use it. See Publish Models for the library details and how to publish an update to an existing library.
From here

How To Use — the reference for every screen, plus Maintenance and Backups.
How It Works — what a measurement is, how the models work, and why the app keeps transmission and appearance apart (Transmission vs Appearance).
Prisma Lithophane Generator — the app that prints lithophanes from the models you just fit.

prisma-calibration/how-it-works/color-mo.title: Color Model v1
prisma-calibration/how-it-works/color-mo.content:
Color Model v1 — the transmission model — describes each filament with one measured curve per color channel: transmission as a function of printed thickness. Stacks are predicted by multiplying curves. It is the system’s original color model; Color Model v2 models whole stacks jointly instead.
The profile
A profile is not a fitted formula. A single exponential (Beer-Lambert) does not follow real measurements across thickness — each RGB channel averages a band of wavelengths, which bends the curve, as does scattering in the more opaque filaments — so the model stores the cleaned measurements themselves as knots and interpolates between them with a monotone cubic spline, one per channel. The curve passes exactly through every knot.
Three constraints shape it: transmission is exactly 1 at zero thickness; values clip to [0, 1]; and each channel is forced non-increasing — more material never transmits more light. Beyond the last measured knot the curve continues exponentially, with the decay rate taken from the last two knots.
Composition
A stack’s predicted transmission is the product of its layers’ curves, per channel — order-free, since multiplication commutes. The product law is exact only for narrow bands and pure absorbers (Transmission vs Appearance); the measured residual on real stacks is handled by the pair corrections below.
Where the knots come from
Two kinds of samples feed a filament’s profile:

Solo strips — the filament printed alone; each swatch is a direct thickness-and-transmission measurement.
White-base strips — the filament printed over a white base. The base is peeled off by dividing every swatch by the strip’s own zero-thickness swatch: a local control from the same print and photograph, canceling the base’s transmission and any exposure difference in one stroke. Below 0.3 mm these win over solo measurements, because ultra-thin solo prints are structurally unreliable.

Strips printed over a colored base are deliberately excluded: the light reaching the filament there is already filtered, so dividing out the base measures absorption of pre-filtered light rather than the broadband response — historically an error near twenty percent for complementary pairs. The app shows these as diagnostics; they never enter a profile.
The merged points are then cleaned: duplicates at the same thickness collapse; interior points deviating more than 35% from the local exponential trend drop as outliers; the zero-thickness anchor is prepended; monotonicity is enforced; values floor at 0.003 so compositions never hard-clip; and the curve truncates one knot past where it sinks under the measurement noise floor (average transmission 0.008).
Which samples count
A filament’s fit uses every accepted processed sample that survives the exclusions above, where it is the variable layer and physically on top; stacks with fixed layers above the variable are skipped rather than reinterpreted. Results waiting for review do not count. Exclusion controls are honored throughout — individual swatches, whole samples, or a filament excluded from modeling entirely.
Refitting and use
Fit Models attempts every target profile and then regenerates the corrections when at least one profile succeeded. If one profile fails while another succeeds, the successful profiles can become current before the workflow reports failure and stops. Modeling fits the profiles together; it does not offer a one-filament refit. Changes to a sample — its images, geometry, or filament assignments — mark models that used it stale. Generator reads the profiles from its active published library and composes stacks with the same product law. Run Publish Models after fitting to make the new models available to Generator.
Pair corrections
Multiplying per-filament curves is an approximation: each RGB channel spans a band of wavelengths, and band-averaged transmissions do not multiply exactly (Transmission vs Appearance). Print a real two-filament stack and its measured transmission disagrees with the predicted product. Pair corrections patch that residual empirically, measured pair by measured pair.
What a correction is
For an overlay filament printed on a specific base stack, the correction is the measured-to-predicted ratio per channel, tabulated against overlay thickness:
C_c(d) = \frac{T_{\text{measured},c}(d)}{T_{\text{predicted},c}(d)}
Values clamp to [0.3, 3], anchor at exactly 1 at zero thickness, and interpolate linearly between knots, holding constant beyond the last. Channels too dark to trust — predicted transmission under 0.02, or nothing measured — record no correction (a ratio of 1). At prediction time the plain composed product is multiplied once by the correction at the overlay’s thickness, looked up by the exact overlay-and-base combination.
Derivation
Corrections regenerate at the tail of a multi-profile fit, from every accepted processed stacked sample — the variable filament over its fixed base layers. Predicted transmission comes from the freshly fitted profiles; each swatch contributes one ratio; duplicate observations at the same thickness average. Single-base and two-base stacks are both measured, and the base’s identity and thickness are part of the correction’s key.
Where they apply — and where they don’t
The table is directional and exact-match: a pair never printed and measured gets no correction, silently. The consumers differ:

The calibration app’s Modeling review applies the pair corrections to its Color Model v1 predictions by default, and can also show the uncorrected series for comparison.
Generator always applies them to matching two-filament combinations while building its color lookup table.
In that path the two-base measurements are not used, curves measured at different base thicknesses are averaged into one, and when both orderings of a pair exist their factors are averaged too.

The photo stack model replaces this mechanism with a fitted correction layer of its own (Color Model v2).

prisma-calibration/how-it-works/color-mo.title: Color Model v2
prisma-calibration/how-it-works/color-mo.content:
Color Model v2 — the photo stack model — is fitted on whole measured stacks rather than one filament at a time the way Color Model v1 is. It is now the generator’s default appearance model.
Density, not transmission
The model works in optical density, because density adds where transmission multiplies. Each filament carries a fitted density-versus-thickness curve per color channel; a stack’s core prediction sums its layers’ densities and converts back to transmission through
T_c = f_c + (1 - f_c)\,e^{-D_c}
where D is the summed density and f a small fitted floor below which transmission never falls.
If density added cleanly, this would be — floor aside — the same arithmetic as Color Model v1’s multiplication. It does not add cleanly — broadband channels and scattering see to that (Transmission vs Appearance) — so the sum carries fitted context terms: how white bases and caps shift density in the presence of color, and an interaction term that engages when two or more distinct colors stack.
Perceptual refinements
The density core’s output then passes through fitted adjustments in perceptual coordinates, each anchored to measurements and gated to the stack shapes it was fitted on: a tint-retention pull that keeps stacked color layers’ tints from washing out in the density sum; a cap-transfer adjustment for single-color stacks under white; measured single-color response profiles that can override the prediction where a closely matching stack was actually photographed; and, for stacks of exactly two colors, a corridor between the two colors’ solo endpoints — measured where available, modeled otherwise — that pulls the result toward it. Bare two-color stacks with no white anywhere are a special case: where that exact pair was printed and measured, a multiplicative transmission correction is applied to the density core directly, bypassing the perceptual refinements entirely. A learned residual layer sits on top of everything else — the correction layer, below.
Evidence and fit
Training evidence is every included swatch from an accepted processed extraction, represented by its realized stack — what is physically present once zero-thickness layers drop out. Results waiting for review do not count. Samples that reference a filament flagged exclude from model are held out of the fit entirely. The remaining evidence is classified by shape: white only, a bare color, color over white, several colors over white, and two sandwich forms. Targets are the measured transmissions of Extraction, compared in OKLab. The fit is staged: white curves from white-only swatches; color curves as the residual density above the white they were printed on; then each context term in sequence, grid-searched to minimize class-balanced perceptual error. The fit uses all included measurements rather than reserving some for a separate check, and records its errors per stack shape.
Runs and use
Fit Models fits both color models and rebuilds the camera transform when its inputs changed. Each successful v2 stage saves the curves, fitted adjustments, error summaries, and per-sample predictions as the current working model. Keep Calibration open until fitting finishes. A separate Publish Models action copies the models, correction layer, and filament list into a new Generator library. Generator uses v2 from its active library when Appearance Model is set to Color Model v2 (the default); its predictions remain in the model domain (Transmission vs Appearance).
The correction layer
However carefully the stages above are fitted, structured residuals remain. The correction layer removes the predictable part of them by memory rather than formula: it stores the fit’s own residuals and, for each new prediction, asks what the model got wrong on the measured stacks most like this one.
The mechanism
Every training stack contributes one stored residual — measured minus predicted, in OKLab. At prediction time the layer considers only residuals from the same context: the same set of colors, the same whites, the same stack shape. Within that context, residuals are weighted by similarity to the query — a Gaussian kernel over the prediction and the stack’s thicknesses — and averaged:
\hat{r} = \frac{\sum_i w_i\, r_i}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad w_i = e^{-\frac{1}{2} d_i^2}
The estimate is capped in magnitude and scaled by an authority factor that grows with the number of contributing measurements — few witnesses, small correction. The corrected prediction is the base prediction plus the estimate. A stack whose context was never measured gets no correction at all.
Fitting and scope
The layer is fitted in the same run as the model, on the same measurements, restricted to the supported stack shapes; diagnostic-only stacks contribute nothing and receive nothing. How much it improves a prediction depends on the available measurements.
Contrast with v1
Color Model v1’s pair corrections are fixed ratio tables: multiplicative, in transmission, keyed to exactly the printed pair at its printed base thickness. This layer is additive in perceptual coordinates, generalizes across the whole stack description — thicknesses and predicted color — within a measured context, and weighs its own confidence explicitly. Both share the same honesty about extrapolation: no measurement, no correction.
Where it applies
Generator always applies this correction layer with Color Model v2, or the pair corrections with Color Model v1. In Calibration’s Sample Comparison, Color Corrections: On/Off lets you judge the predictions with and without corrections.
Limits
A filament with no fitted curve silently uses a generic fallback. Stack shapes outside the supported classes are still predicted by the density core; the correction layer never fires for them, and the refinements engage only where their structural gates happen to match. There is no automatic fall-back to Color Model v1 — the two are alternatives selected in settings.

prisma-calibration/how-it-works/extracti.title: Extraction
prisma-calibration/how-it-works/extracti.content:
Extraction turns one photograph into color measurements. It uses a source photo of a printed strip on a lightbox, the matching blank photo (same lightbox, no strip), and the strip’s known geometry. Capture RAW photographs for calibration; the Image Inbox accepts .cr2, .dng, .tif, and .tiff files. The result is per-swatch transmission — the fraction of the lightbox’s light each thickness step passes, per color channel.
Two image domains
Extraction uses a display version — for RAW input, an auto-brightened rendering — to locate the strip and show it on screen. A linear version, with no tone curve or brightness adjustment, keeps pixel values proportional to light and is used for measurement. Automatic detection first tries the embedded preview, then uses full-resolution images for measurement. Transmission is only meaningful in the linear domain; see Transmission vs Appearance.
Locating the strip
The detector first looks for the lightbox — the large bright region of the photo — and searches inside it when found. If no lightbox is detected, it searches the full frame; the final pure-geometry fallback is available only when a lightbox rectangle exists. Detection strategies run in fixed order, each proposing candidate outlines that are screened against the strip’s expected proportions, computed from its geometry:

difference from the blank (per-channel ratio, then absolute difference);
dark-shape-on-bright thresholding, then the reverse;
edge detection;
color saturation, for translucent tinted filaments the grayscale strategies miss;
a pure-geometry fallback that places the expected rectangle at the lightbox center.

First success wins.
Alignment
Three corrections put both images in the same aligned view. The photo is oriented upright (a per-photo rotation plus the sample’s recorded open-side direction). The detected strip is rotated to horizontal and cropped. It is then flipped, if needed, so the thinnest step sits on the left. On the automatic path that flip is decided by brightness, since thin steps transmit more light; on the manual path (below) the hand-clicked corner order and the sample’s recorded open-side orientation fix the direction, so no brightness flip is applied. The blank is warped onto the sample photo by matching the lightbox positions in each, then carried through the same rotation, crop, and flip, so strip and blank align pixel for pixel.
The measurement
Per channel, each pixel’s transmission is the ratio of the light that arrived through the strip to the light the lightbox delivered at that same spot:
T_c(x,y) = \operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{S_c(x,y)}{B_c(x,y)},\ 0,\ 1\right)
where S is the linear strip photo and B the registered linear blank. This division is the flatfield correction: it cancels the lightbox’s spatial unevenness.
Swatch regions come from geometry alone: the strip’s known millimeter dimensions place the border, the equal-width steps, and a small inset at the open edge, where over-extrusion distorts the print. No image signal adjusts the dividers. Within each step, a central patch spanning half the cell’s width and height is sampled, and the swatch’s per-channel value is the median of its pixels’ transmissions — a median of ratios, robust to dust and local defects. The display-domain median is stored alongside for on-screen swatches, and the blank’s own median brightness is recorded for traceability; it is never divided again.
Appearance capture
When embedded-JPEG appearance extraction succeeds, the result also records how the camera rendered each swatch. Rather than re-detect the strip inside that preview, it reuses the location the transmission extraction already settled on: the embedded JPEG is rotated and scaled into that same coordinate frame, and the swatch patches are sampled at the matching positions. (An independent detection of the strip within the JPEG remains as a fallback for when that recorded location is unavailable.) Failure is recorded in diagnostics and leaves appearance absent without invalidating transmission. These camera-rendered colors are not light measurements; they are the fitting target for The Camera Transform.
Manual fallback
When automatic detection fails, the strip’s four corners are clicked by hand (Manual Processing). The quad is rectified with a full perspective warp — the automatic path uses rotation only — its direction is fixed by the hand-clicked corner order and the recorded open-side orientation rather than by the brightness flip, and blank registration must succeed exactly rather than fall back to an approximation. From the flatfield division onward, the measurement is identical.
Outcomes
A successful extraction saves one current result per sample: every swatch’s transmission and display colors, any available appearance colors, and information about how the strip was located. A failed extraction is shown as Failed so it cannot be mistaken for a new measurement. If saving the replacement fails, the app keeps the previous result. A manual preview does not replace the saved measurement. Whether a saved result feeds model fits is decided later, when you Accept it in the Processing Queue.
Illustration

The linear RAW sample and registered blank produce transmission measurements. Matching patches from the embedded JPEG provide appearance colors, giving the Camera Transform paired evidence across the two domains.

prisma-calibration/how-it-works/maintena.title: Maintenance Operations
prisma-calibration/how-it-works/maintena.content:
The Maintenance dialog gathers the app’s housekeeping: audits, preview rebuilds, quarantine, geometry exports, and model fitting.
The discipline
Start with Run Preflight to see what will be affected, any warnings, and what is blocked. Only one maintenance job runs at a time, and it cannot run alongside a backup, restore, or another model fit. Operations that can stop safely offer Cancel and remain Cancelling… until the current item finishes. Others are labeled Runs to completion.
Completed standard operations save an Activity Log report. An operation blocked before it starts, or interrupted by an error before it produces a report, may have no log entry. Re-extraction keeps its reports with the results you are reviewing instead.
Audits only read. Rebuilds replace files the app can generate again. Cleanup moves eligible unused files to quarantine rather than deleting them. Overwriting exported geometry files requires a typed confirmation phrase.
The operations
Health Checks — five read-only audits. Audit Library Integrity checks database health and every semantic reference: samples pointing at missing filaments, geometries, images, or blanks; processed samples without measurements; extraction records that disagree with review state. Audit Missing Artifacts finds previews, thumbnails, source files, and geometry artifacts that should exist but don’t. Audit Orphaned Artifacts finds the reverse — files no current record claims. Audit Source Image Custody verifies each photo’s active/archived/missing state and its checksum against the database. SQLite Integrity Check runs the database’s own integrity scan. Library Integrity and SQLite Integrity run to completion once started; the other audits can stop between inspected items.
Cleanup — Quarantine Orphaned Artifacts moves orphans into a timestamped quarantine folder for review. It never deletes, and never touches raw photos or the database.
Repair / Rebuild — regeneration of derived data, in Missing Only or Force Rebuild mode. Rebuild Image Previews re-renders the JPEG previews of source and blank photos. Rebuild Extraction Images Only re-renders extraction thumbnails by replaying the accepted extraction’s recorded strip location — display only; it never re-extracts or changes measurements. Regenerate STEPs/STLs rebuilds internal managed geometry artifacts, never user-facing exports.
Geometry Exports — Export Geometry Files writes STEP/STL print files, either for geometries used by samples or for all geometries. Overwriting existing exports requires typing a confirmation phrase. If the data changes after preflight, the app asks you to check again before exporting.
Calibration Models — Fit Models fits Color Model v1 and Color Model v2 and rebuilds The Camera Transform when its measurements or fitting choices have changed. It runs to completion once started. See Fit Models for the evidence requirements.
Images — Re-extract Sample Images re-runs extraction on accepted samples, refreshing transmission and/or appearance measurements when a batch needs redoing. The old measurements stay in place while you review the new results. Choose Save or Skip for each sample, then Save Results to apply only the ones you kept. See Re-extract Sample Images.
The safety nets around it
Three separate mechanisms cover what maintenance deliberately doesn’t. Restore points are automatic database-only snapshots taken at server startup, at most one per six hours, pruned by age and count; restoring one replaces only the database — after preserving the current file — behind a typed phrase, and is offered only when startup finds the database broken. Backup / Restore is user-initiated packaging: database only, or all data and artifacts with or without raw photos; every restore first creates an automatic safety backup. The RAW image archive covers source photos alone. Maintenance itself never touches backups or raw sources.

prisma-calibration/how-it-works/model-fi.title: Model Fitting
prisma-calibration/how-it-works/model-fi.content:
Fitting is the step that turns your measurements into Calibration’s current working models. Fit Models, available on Modeling and in Maintenance, fits Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and The Camera Transform in a fixed order. This page explains which measurements count and how a fit replaces the previous models. Publishing a library for Generator is a separate step. The mathematics of each fit lives on its model’s own page.
One run, three fits
Each model uses the measurements it needs and replaces its own current result. The run orders them — Color Model v1, then Color Model v2, then the Camera Transform — and stops at the first failure. A model completed before the failure may already have become current. V1 can also save the filament profiles that succeeded before stopping because another profile failed. The two color models refit every run. The Camera Transform refits when its measurements or fitting choices have changed, or when explicitly forced; otherwise it is skipped as up to date. It needs at least five eligible samples, so with fewer it is skipped even when forced.
What counts as evidence
Every fit draws on accepted processed results and honors the same rules. Results waiting for review do not count for any of the three models.

The sample record defines the stack. Each swatch’s bottom-to-top layers come from its geometry and filament assignments — exactly one variable layer, with whites classified as base or cap by their physical position. A white sandwiched between colors is rejected as ambiguous rather than guessed at.
Measured color comes from extraction results (Extraction). Missing or malformed measurements are reported as errors.
Exclusions apply to every model. A filament flagged exclude from model removes every sample it appears in — in any role, base or overlay — from every fit. Per-sample and per-swatch exclusions made in Modeling are honored too. Each model also has its own limits: v1 skips geometries with fixed layers above the variable layer, while v2 classifies each swatch’s stack by shape.

Changing which filaments count as white or which are excluded changes how the models are fitted. After changing these choices, check the model status and run Fit Models again.
Check before fitting
Run Preflight shows which models will be fitted and why. If the data changes between that check and the fit, the app asks you to check again. Progress is reported for each stage. Once Fit Models starts, it runs to completion and offers no Cancel action.
One current fit per model
Each successful stage saves its files — profiles and pair corrections for v1, the stack model for v2, and the camera transform — as Calibration’s current result. The app keeps one current fit per model; it does not offer a history of old working fits. Changing a measurement used by that fit marks it stale until Fit Models replaces it. Adding new measurements does not automatically include them in an existing model: run the fit again to use them.
Keep Calibration open until fitting finishes. If the app is force-closed while saving a model, its saved files and model status may disagree after restarting. Check all three statuses and Publish Models readiness before using the working set; the publication checks verify the model files as well as their status.
Publishing to Generator is a separate copy
Once all three working models are current, Publish Models checks them together with the filament list. Publish to Generator installs a new library without activating it; Export Library Package writes the equivalent ZIP. Later changes in Calibration cannot change that copy. The new library affects lithophane generation only after it is selected through Config → Model Library in Generator and Generator restarts.
Judging the result
The Modeling page reads Calibration’s current working models back and lays measured color beside every model’s prediction — in both the transmission and appearance domains (Transmission vs Appearance), with corrections on or off — which is how a fresh fit is judged and how untrustworthy samples get excluded before the next one.

prisma-calibration/how-it-works/sample-g.title: Sample Geometry
prisma-calibration/how-it-works/sample-g.content:
A sample geometry is the design of a printable calibration strip: which layers it has, how thick each swatch is, and its physical footprint. Geometries are designed in the app, printed, and referenced by every sample measured from them.
Anatomy
A strip is a grid of swatches — in practice a single row — wrapped by a spine: a solid border wall along the left, right, and back edges, at least as tall as the tallest swatch stack, open on the fourth side. Each swatch is a small rectangle, 12 × 20 mm by default, with a 3 mm spine. Prints distort slightly at the open edge, so measurement insets away from it (Extraction).
Layers and the staircase
A geometry’s thickness structure is a stack of layer roles, ordered bottom to top. Exactly one role is variable: its thickness changes per swatch, forming the staircase that sweeps the thickness axis — 0.20 mm to 0.76 mm in 0.08 mm steps by default. Every other role is fixed, one thickness across the whole strip, used for known layers beneath or above the material under test.
Roles are slots, not materials. The geometry says “a fixed 0.20 mm layer under a variable layer”; each sample decides which filament fills each slot, so one geometry serves any number of filaments.
Layer height is deliberately not part of a geometry — it is a slicing decision, not a shape.
Identity
A geometry’s shape cannot change once created; only its alias and bundle membership can be edited in the app. Two geometries with the same layout, roles, and thicknesses cannot coexist, even under different names. Samples refer to their geometry, so every measurement traces to the exact printed shape. A geometry used by a sample or bundle cannot be deleted.
From design to print
Export produces a STEP model, and per-layer STL files, with one solid body per layer role, named so the slicer shows which body is which layer. Geometries can be grouped into bundles — sets designed to print together, with shared filament slots mapped once and applied to every member when creating samples in bulk.
What geometry drives
Extraction takes everything spatial from the geometry: the expected proportions used to locate the strip in a photograph, and the swatch grid that divides the rectified strip into measurement regions. Fitting realizes each swatch as a physical stack — the roles in bottom-to-top order, with the variable role at that swatch’s thickness — which is the exact input Color Model v1 and Color Model v2 are fitted against.
Figures for review

The geometry fixes the strip’s spatial layout and bottom-to-top layer roles. Exactly one variable role changes thickness from swatch to swatch; each sample assigns the filaments that fill those roles.

Layer roles are ordered bottom to top. The variable role may stand alone or sit between fixed roles; only its thickness changes from swatch to swatch.

prisma-calibration/how-it-works/the-came.filePath: Prisma Calibration/How It Works/The Camera Transform.md
prisma-calibration/how-it-works/the-came.title: The Camera Transform
prisma-calibration/how-it-works/the-came.content:
Models predict physical transmission; every photograph, and every source image handed to the generator, lives in camera-rendered color. The camera transform is the fitted map between them: given a stack’s transmission, it predicts the color the camera would render for that stack on the lightbox. Transmission vs Appearance explains the domains; this page explains the map.
Form
The forward transform has two stages. A linear map acts on six features of the transmission triple — the three channels and the square roots of their pairwise products — capturing channel crosstalk; every feature scales linearly with the input, so this stage treats overall brightness changes uniformly. Per-channel monotone tone curves then bend each output channel to match the camera’s tone rendering, and outputs clip to the displayable range.
Data
Each accepted swatch can contribute one data pair: its measured transmission, and the camera’s own rendering of that same swatch read from the JPEG embedded in the raw photo (Extraction). Several filters thin the corpus. Any sample that references a filament flagged exclude from model in the registry — in any layer role — is dropped whole, so an untrusted filament never influences the fit. Samples whose measured swatch order fails to track transmission (weak appearance-order correlation) are dropped whole as well, and physically implausible rows — a bright rendering against low measured transmission — are discarded. Then per-row hygiene: swatches with any channel at or near clipping (250 of 255 and above) are censored from the fitting loss — a clipped channel says only “bright,” not how bright — but remain in evaluation.
Fit
Both stages are fitted jointly in the forward direction: initialized coarsely, then refined by comparing errors in CIELAB, so errors are weighted perceptually rather than by raw channel difference. The fit needs at least five eligible samples. Quality is checked by dividing samples into five groups and, in turn, fitting on four groups and predicting the fifth. All swatches from a sample stay together. The groups are balanced across measured transmission behavior and do not depend on filament names or categories. If the mean color error on those checks exceeds 6 dE76, the fit is rejected and the previous transform stays in place. After the checks pass, the final transform is fitted on all clean evidence.
Inverse
The generator needs the opposite direction — given a source-image color, what transmission must a stack achieve? The forward map is inverted numerically and stored as a lookup table across the display color range. Generator uses that table to convert source colors into the transmission values it must match. The inverse is never fitted separately, so the two directions share a single model; small differences after converting a color there and back come from numerical approximation. The forward direction converts the generator’s predictions into camera-rendered color for previews.
Publication
Each successful build saves a new camera transform as Calibration’s current result. Keep the app open until fitting finishes. After an abnormal stop, Publish Models checks that the saved files still match the recorded fit; missing or damaged files block publication. Generator uses the transform copied into its active model library.
The transform is anchored to one camera and one photographic setup. A new camera means re-photographing samples and refitting (Transmission vs Appearance).

prisma-calibration/how-it-works/transmis.title: Transmission vs Appearance
prisma-calibration/how-it-works/transmis.content:
Calibration keeps two representations of color and never confuses them.
Transmission is physical. Each measurement is the fraction of the lightbox’s light a swatch passes, per RGB channel, taken from linearly decoded raw photos: 1.0 means as bright as the bare lightbox, and values scale in proportion to light. This is the model domain — Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and every stack prediction live here. Extraction covers how it is measured.
Appearance is what the camera says the scene looked like: the colors of the JPEG the camera itself rendered — white-balanced, tone-curved, saturated by its picture pipeline. It is not proportional to light, but it is the ground truth for how a backlit print reads.
A third render exists only outside the measurement path: an auto-brightened preview decode, used to locate the strip and shown behind on-screen swatches. Its brightness adapts to each photo, so it is comparable to nothing and no model consumes it.
Why models live in transmission
Stacked translucent layers filter light multiplicatively: the light emerging from a stack is the product of the layers’ transmissions. That law holds only for linear measurements, and exactly only for purely absorptive layers and narrow spectral bands — an RGB channel averages a band of wavelengths, so the product is a close approximation rather than an identity, and the residual is what pair corrections absorb (Color Model v1). Rendered color breaks products outright — tone curves with offsets, channel crosstalk, saturation boosts — so a model fitted on appearance could not compose stacks by multiplying layers. Every model is therefore fitted on, and predicts, linear transmission.
Why judgments live in appearance
The source image a user hands the generator, and every judgment a human makes of a print or preview, live in rendered color. A transmission value shown directly on screen misrepresents the color it stands for. Comparisons must therefore happen within a single domain: the generator carries source-image colors inward to the model domain before solving, and carries predictions outward to appearance before showing them.
The bridge
One fitted map connects the domains — from transmission to that camera’s rendered color, numerically inverted for the inward direction. See The Camera Transform.
Both domains are anchored to a single camera: transmission carries its color response; appearance is its rendering. Changing cameras invalidates both sides — samples must be re-photographed and the transform refitted.
Illustration

The color models fit and predict physical transmission. The Camera Transform carries those predictions into camera-rendered appearance and is numerically inverted when the generator must travel inward.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/backups/ar.content:

Raw camera files are by far the biggest thing in your library, and once a sample is measured they’re rarely needed day to day. The Archive RAW Images panel of  Restore moves them out of the working library to reclaim space — without losing them.
It’s two separate steps, deliberately: you never delete originals you haven’t safely stored first.


Step 1 — Create RAW Image Archive
Packages your current raw photos into a standalone archive ZIP, written to Calibration\Output\Backups. This only copies — nothing is deleted. Verify the archive exists, then move it somewhere safe (another drive, cloud storage), just like a backup.
Step 2 — Remove Archived Images From Active Library
The destructive step, gated accordingly. Point its Archive or Backup File control at the archive you just stored (or an All Data and Artifacts backup that includes raw images). A window opens to validate the file and preview exactly which files it covers. To proceed you must type the confirmation phrase — then it removes only the files the archive actually contains. Anything not in the archive is untouched.

Run step 2 only after the archive from step 1 is stored somewhere safe.
To bring the originals back later, see Restore Archived Images.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/backups/cr.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}Backup /RestoreCreateBackupRestore FromBackup


The Create Backup panel of  Restore packages your work into a single ZIP. Pick a backup type, then click Create Backup.

Essential Data Only
A small package of just the database — your filaments, geometries, samples, image assignments, measurements, and model-fit records. No images, print files, or current model files are included. Use All Data and Artifacts to include those files, or run Fit Models after restoring the database. This backup never contains the Generator model libraries you published separately. Restoring Essential Data Only replaces only the database and leaves managed files in place.
All Data and Artifacts
The working database plus generated model and image files and exported geometry files. When this type is selected, an Include raw image files checkbox appears:

On — the original camera files go in too. Raw photos are big — expect a large ZIP.
Off — everything except those originals. Much smaller; your current raw files simply stay where they are.

Calibration backups do not include Generator’s installed model libraries or other backup and library-package ZIPs. Keep independent copies of any published packages you want to retain.
Where it goes
The backup is written as a timestamped .zip in Calibration\Output\Backups; the finished job reports the exact path. Making the package is the app’s job; keeping it safe is yours. Copy it to another drive or your cloud storage — a backup that lives only inside the live Prisma folder protects you from very little.

The inverse of Archive RAW Images: pull raw camera files back into the working library after you archived and removed them.

Point the Archive or Backup File control at a raw-image archive ZIP (or an All Data and Artifacts backup that includes raw images) and click Restore Archived Images.
A window opens to validate the file and preview how many of its images are missing from your library; it restores only the matching missing images. It never overwrites photos you already have. Images that conflict with the current records or do not belong to this library are skipped and reported.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/backups/re.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}CreateBackupRestore FromBackupArchive RAWImages


The Restore From Backup panel of  Restore brings a backup package back. Point the Backup File control at a Prisma backup .zip, then click Restore Backup.
This is also the supported way to bring an existing Calibration library into a new blank Prisma Suite. Create an All Data and Artifacts backup in the old app (including raw images if the new copy should retain them), then restore that ZIP in the blank Suite. Do not copy individual SQLite, asset, or model files into Calibration\Workspace.

It never restores blind
First the app validates the ZIP — checking that it is a Prisma package with an intact database — and previews what it contains and what restoring will replace. It then asks you to type the displayed confirmation phrase. Before replacing the database, the app creates a pre-restore Essential Data Only safety backup. The completed restore reports that backup’s path; it can be selected later through Restore From Backup if you need to return to the previous database state.
What gets replaced
Depends on the package (see Create Backup for the types):

Essential Data Only — replaces the database only. Managed images and geometry files stay in place.
All Data and Artifacts, with raw images — replaces everything, raw photos included.
All Data and Artifacts, without raw images — replaces everything else but keeps your current raw photos in place; the package has none to supply.

When it finishes, the app refreshes itself and the restored data is live. For migration, verify the Logbook, Images, Filaments, Geometries, and Modeling status before deleting or retiring the previous installation. Keep the source installation and backup until that review is complete.

The top bar’s Backup / Restore button opens one dialog with four panels. Use these workflows to create supported, portable packages of the app’s managed database, geometry files, images, measurements, and model files.


Create Backup — package your work into a ZIP you can move somewhere safe.
Restore From Backup — bring a package back, after the app checks it and you confirm.
Archive RAW Images — move the bulky raw camera files out of the working library, safely.
Restore Archived Images — pull archived raw files back in when you need them.

Only one of these runs at a time, and none while a Maintenance job is running. Each is start-then-report: kick it off, watch the progress panel, and the dialog refreshes when it’s done.
The app also creates automatic SQLite restore points at startup when enough time has elapsed and prunes old restore points automatically. They contain only the database and are surfaced through the recovery screen if the database fails its startup checks. They are not portable backups and contain no images; the packages you create here remain the supported way to protect and move your work.

Your first calibration strip
Goal: carry one simple, single-geometry sample from an empty library to an accepted measurement, then explain what additional samples are needed before fitting a complete model set.

Register the filament and explain each policy setting used.
Create or select a one-variable-role sample geometry.
Create the sample and label the physical strip with its sample ID.
Export, slice, and print the geometry without changing its dimensions or role assignments.
Capture a blank image and sample image in one fixed session.
Assign the images and open-side direction, process the sample, and review the extraction.
Inspect the sample under Modeling. Build up the included measurements before running Fit Models; the Camera Transform requires at least five eligible samples.


A Geometry Bundle with Multi

Show the bundle’s shared-slot mapping.
Select Geometry Bundle, set one shared slot to Multi, and preview the resulting sample count.

A transparent strip that needs Manual Processing

Process the ready sample and identify its Failed or Flagged state.
Open Manual Process and place corners in the required order.
Accept the manual extraction candidate.

Curate evidence and refit
Goal: investigate a suspect model comparison without automatically discarding useful evidence.

Compare measured and predicted Transmission and Appearance domains.
Check the source assignment and extraction before changing fit inclusion.
Demonstrate one justified swatch exclusion and one justified whole-sample exclusion.
Review Filament Coverage and run Fit Models again.


Back up, archive RAW images, and recover

Create Essential Data Only and All Data and Artifacts backups.

Restore missing RAW images from the archive.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/filaments/.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}FilamentsGeometries


The Filaments tab is the app’s filament library. Add a filament here before assigning it to a calibration sample.

Read the library
The line above the table shows the number of filaments and how many have a fitted profile. One row represents one filament:

Filament — the color name, with its color chip.
Manufacturer — the brand.
ID — the filament’s permanent identifier.
Samples — how many samples use it.
Processed — how many of those are measured.
Profile — pending (no data yet), strips only (measured but not yet fitted), or profiled.

Only Filament, Manufacturer, and Profile are sortable. A profiled filament may still be unavailable for new generation if it is excluded from model fits.
Add a filament
Click + New Filament, then fill in:

Filament — the color name. Required.
Manufacturer — the brand. Required.
Material — the material type, such as PLA.
Hex Color — the color chip shown in the app. It does not describe the filament’s measured optical behavior.
Notes — optional information you want to keep with the filament.

The drawer builds a permanent Generated ID from the manufacturer and color name. Review it before clicking Create — the drawer refuses to save if the ID already exists in the library, and the ID does not change if you rename the filament later.
Policy settings

White-cap eligible — allows the filament to serve as a white base or cap and identifies it as white during model fitting. Use this only for suitable white or near-white filaments.
Special role: Transparent and Special role: Black — descriptive tags. They do not exclude the filament from fitting.
Exclude from model fits — removes every sample containing this filament from model fitting and makes the filament unavailable for new generator runs. It does not delete the filament or its existing data.

Use Exclude from model fits to retire a filament without breaking samples that already reference it. To exclude one questionable sample instead, use the controls under Modeling.


                  
                  Camera Transform classification 
                  
                

White-cap eligible is also the filament classification used by The Camera Transform. There is no separate camera-classification control.


View, edit, or delete
Click a row to open its drawer. Used By lists every sample containing the filament. Click Edit to change its name, manufacturer, material, displayed color, policy, or notes.
Delete works only when the filament has no samples or fitted profile. Otherwise, exclude it instead.

This dialog writes a geometry’s printable 3D files. Reach it from Create + Export in the builder, or from Export in Geometry Details.

Give the export a name, then choose one or both formats:

Export STEP — one model containing a labeled solid body for each material role.
Export STLs — one file for each material role.

The bodies and files are labeled LR_01, LR_02, and so on. These are material roles, not individual printer layers. Match each label to the filament assigned to the same role in New Samples. LR_01 is the bottom material role.

Exports are written under Calibration\Output\Steps. STL sets use a named subfolder. If an export with the same name already exists, the app asks before overwriting it.
Once an export request starts, the dialog remains open and its name, close, and export controls stay disabled until the request succeeds or fails. Closing the window, pressing Escape, or clicking outside cannot hide a still-running export.
Print it faithfully
The physical strip must match its sample record:

Import the STEP as separate bodies, or import the complete set of role-specific STLs.
Confirm the slicer did not scale the geometry or change its units.
Assign each LR body exactly the filament recorded for that role in New Samples.
Inspect the sliced layer preview. Every role must remain present, and the variable swatches must retain their intended thickness progression.
Keep the printed strip associated with its sample ID.

Export several geometries

Click any row on the Geometries tab to open that geometry’s details.

The drawer shows the geometry’s Alias, ID, Bundle membership, Last Modified, and a Used By list of every sample created from it. Two sections cover its files:

Exported Files — the print files written for you, in Prisma’s output folder. These are the ones you open in your slicer; each entry has a Copy Path button — click it, then paste straight into your slicer’s open dialog.
Managed Artifacts — a summary of the app’s internal copies. Leave these alone; the app maintains them itself.

Header actions

Export — write fresh print files for this geometry. See Export Sample Geometry.
Edit — switches to edit mode, with Save, Discard, and Delete.

Only the alias and bundle membership are editable — a geometry’s material roles and thicknesses never change after creation. Bundle membership can also be changed directly in the drawer; adding or removing it applies immediately. Delete is refused while any sample or bundle still uses the geometry.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/geometries.content:

A bundle groups geometries and maps their material roles to shared filament slots. It lets one set of filament choices create coordinated samples across several geometries.
A bundle does not combine its geometries into one print file or arrange them on a print plate. Export and arrange each geometry separately.
Manage Bundles on the Geometries tab opens the bundle drawer: bundles on the left and the selected bundle on the right.

Create the bundle

Enter a name in the new-bundle row and click Create.
Select the bundle.
Under Bundle Geometries, click Add Geometries… and choose its members.
Under Bundle Filament Mapping, click Edit Mapping.

Map shared filament slots
Each geometry has its own roles, such as LR_01 and LR_02. The mapping editor adds shared slots named Shared Filament A, Shared Filament B, and so on. Map every geometry role to one of these slots.
A shared slot means “use the same filament in every role mapped here.” The roles do not need the same LR number or role type.




















Shared slotGeometry 1Geometry 2Shared Filament ALR_01, FixedLR_02, VariableShared Filament BLR_02, VariableLR_01, Fixed
Selecting one filament for Shared Filament A during sample creation fills both mapped roles. A shared slot may also feed several roles in the same geometry.
Drag a shared-filament token onto a role, or select the token and then click the role. Add slots with + Add Shared Filament Slot. When every role is assigned, click Save Mapping.

The bundle status reports its readiness:

Unmapped — no complete mapping has been saved.
Incomplete — one or more roles are not assigned.
Mapped — every role is assigned and the bundle can create samples.
Invalid — the saved mapping no longer matches the bundle’s current records.

Adding a geometry makes the bundle incomplete until its roles are mapped. You may save an incomplete mapping, but New Samples will not allow that bundle to be selected.
During sample creation, assigning one filament to every shared slot creates one sample per member geometry. Setting one shared slot to Multi creates one sample per geometry for every selected filament. See Creating New Samples for the count rules.
Rename, remove, or delete
Use a member’s remove control to take it out of the bundle. Select a bundle to Rename or Delete it. Deleting a bundle does not delete its geometries.
Illustration

A shared filament slot follows the mapping, not a layer’s LR number or vertical position. Here one filament identity fills the only variable role in one geometry, a fixed bottom role in another, and a fixed top role in a third.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/geometries.title: New Sample Geometry
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/geometries.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}GeometriesNew SampleGeometryGeometryDetails


+ New Sample Geometry on the Geometries tab opens the strip builder.

Before you build
Plan the material stack from bottom to top. LR_01 is the bottom material role. Higher numbers sit above it. These are material roles, not individual printer layers; each role may span many printer layers using one filament.
Every geometry requires exactly one Variable role. Add Fixed roles where the calibration design needs constant-thickness material above or below it.
If you need the sample to support Color Model v1, keep all fixed roles below the variable role. Color Model v1 does not use geometries with a fixed role above the variable role.
Build the strip

Under Strip Layout, set Swatch Width (mm), Swatch Height (mm), Number of Swatches, Spine Width (mm), and Spine Thickness (mm).
Under Variable Layer Increment, enter First Swatch Thickness (mm) and Swatch-to-Swatch Increment (mm), then click Fill Values to populate an even sequence. You can also edit the individual swatch values directly.
Click + Add Layer Role for each fixed role and enter its thickness.
Drag roles into the physical order shown in the preview. The builder displays the top of the stack first; LR_01 remains the bottom role.
Give the geometry an Alias. Bundle membership is optional.

The role types mean:

Variable — thickness changes across the swatches.
Fixed — one thickness continues across every swatch.

Fixed does not mean backing, support, white, or color. Those properties come from the filament assigned when a sample is created.
Spine Total
Spine Total is the spine’s total height, not the swatch stack’s height. The builder starts it at the tallest swatch stack plus 0.08 mm and will not allow a lower value. Any spine material above the swatches belongs to the topmost role, so review this value after reordering roles.

The Visual Preview updates as you work. The Top View shows the strip footprint and swatch divisions proportionally; the Side View uses the same horizontal scale and exaggerates thickness vertically so the layer structure remains visible. The Strip Diagram Preview retains the compact role/thickness summary. Confirm the role order and thicknesses there before saving.
Save the geometry

Create — save the geometry into the library.
Create + Export — save it, then open Export Sample Geometry.

The role order and thicknesses cannot be edited after creation. If they are wrong, create another geometry. Only the alias and bundle membership can change later.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/geometries.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}FilamentsGeometriesSampleLogbookNew SampleGeometryGeometryDetailsManageBundlesExport SampleGeometry


The Geometries tab contains reusable calibration-strip designs. A geometry defines the strip’s swatches, material roles, and thicknesses. It does not specify which filaments fill those roles. Filaments are assigned when you create a sample in the Sample Logbook.

Understand the role stack
Each material role becomes a separate body in the exported model. Roles are labeled from the bottom of the printed stack upward: LR_01 is the bottom role, LR_02 is above it, and so on.
A geometry has exactly one Variable role. Its thickness changes from swatch to swatch so one strip measures several thicknesses. Every Fixed role keeps one thickness across the strip. Fixed describes thickness, not purpose: a fixed role may sit above or below the variable role and may contain any filament.
The builder displays the physical stack from top to bottom. Moving a role changes its position and updates its LR label. For a fuller explanation, see Sample Geometry.
Read the library
Each row shows the strip diagram, Alias, Bundle, # Layers (the number of material roles), Used by, and Last modified. Click a row to inspect its ID, bundle membership, exports, and samples.
What you do here

+ New Sample Geometry — design a new sample geometry. See New Sample Geometry.
Click a row — inspect its details, export it, rename it, or change its bundle membership. See Geometry Details.
Manage Bundles — map roles across several geometries for coordinated sample creation. See Manage Bundles.
Export Geometry Files — export STEP or STL files for geometries used by samples or for the whole library.

Geometry files
The geometry definition is the permanent record. Printable STEP and STL files are generated from it and may not exist until you export them. See Export Sample Geometry for the required role-to-filament matching.
Export Geometry Files opens a batch workflow. Missing Only creates absent files. Force Export can replace existing exports after confirmation. You may export Only Geometries Used By Samples or All Geometries, in STEP, STL, or both formats.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/images/ass.title: CSV Bulk Assignment
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/images/ass.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}AssignImagesCSV BulkAssignmentProcessingQueue


When you have many samples to set up, CSV Bulk Assignment assigns each sample’s image, blank image, and orientation from a spreadsheet. You will find it in the Image Inbox on Assign Images. Place every referenced image in the Calibration Inbox, click Import from Inbox, and import the images before opening this dialog; the spreadsheet refers to the imported filenames.

It works in three steps: get the template, fill it in, then check and import.
1. Get the template
Download CSV Template saves a spreadsheet with four columns to fill in:

























ColumnWhat goes in itSample IDThe sample’s id (like exp-123), or just its number.Sample ImageThe sample image’s filename.Blank ImageA blank’s id, or a photo filename (an unregistered photo here becomes a blank).OrientationWhich way the strip’s open side faces: U, D, L, or R.
Fill one row per sample in any spreadsheet program, then save it.
2. Check it
Choose CSV loads your file. Validate CSV checks it without changing anything and shows a preview — how many rows are ready, how many are blocked, and which photos it would register as new blanks. A row is blocked (and skipped) when its sample or photo can’t be found, or the photo is already assigned somewhere else.
3. Import
Commit with Import Assignments (every row clean) or Import Valid Rows (skip the blocked ones). If any row names a photo that isn’t a blank yet, the app asks you to confirm registering those first.
Import only fills in fresh samples — it skips any sample that already has a photo, a blank, or results. So it’s a safe first pass, never a way to overwrite work you’ve already done.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/images/ass.title: Assign Images
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/images/ass.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ImagesAssignImagesProcessingQueueCSV BulkAssignment


Before the app can read colors from a sample, it needs two images: the sample image (the printed strip on the lightbox) and a blank image (the same lit lightbox with nothing on it). The blank image lets the app correct for uneven illumination.
For that to work, the app aligns the blank image with the sample image point by point — so the camera must not move, and the lighting must not change, between the blank and the samples in that session.
Capture one consistent session

Fix the camera and lightbox in place before capturing the blank image. If either moves, begin a new session with a new blank.
Keep exposure, focus, camera orientation, and lighting unchanged throughout the session. Disable automatic changes where your camera workflow allows it.
Let the lightbox reach a stable state before capturing the blank and samples.
Keep the complete strip and enough surrounding lightbox visible for extraction; do not clip the strip at the frame edge.
Preserve a reliable association between each image and its physical sample ID until assignment is complete.

The current Image Inbox imports .cr2, .dng, .tif, and .tiff files. Put
supported files in Calibration\Inbox before using Import from Inbox. If
you are unsure which installation is active, Open Inbox Folder opens the
exact folder used by this Calibration app.


                  
                  Capture procedure draft 
                  
                

Add the validated camera mode, exposure method, focus procedure, lightbox warm-up guidance, framing example, and session naming convention here after the final physical workflow is documented.



You capture everything on the lightbox outside the app; this screen connects those images to your samples. Open the Images tab and stay on the Assign Images subtab. It has three panes, left to right.

Image Inbox (center)
Where images enter the app. Put supported files in Calibration\Inbox, then
click Import from Inbox. Open Inbox Folder opens that location in File
Explorer. The top-bar Refresh Data action only refreshes the displayed
state; it does not import waiting files. Nothing on this screen can use an
image until you import it.
Imported images are grouped into Unassigned, Assigned, and Ignored. Each usable image has a rotate button and an × button to ignore it. Rotating an assigned image clears that sample’s open-side direction so it can be set again. Once a sample is measured, its image cannot be rotated until the result is rejected or reset.
Click a photo to select it. Below the grid, Selected Image names your pick, with two actions:

← Register as Blank turns the selected image into a lightbox reference (see the left pane).
Assign Image to Sample → attaches it to the selected sample as its sample image.

Registered Blanks (left)
Your list of registered blank images. Add one by selecting an image and clicking ← Register as Blank, or by dragging an image onto this pane.
Use one blank for every sample captured in the same unchanged session. Click a blank, then Assign Blank to Sample → to attach it to the selected sample. Click the small × on a blank card to unregister it.
Assign Images and Blanks (right)
Samples are split into Ready For Processing and Needs Assignment. Click a sample to make it the target for the → buttons in the other panes. Each card shows its strip diagram and filament list, plus an image slot and a blank slot. Click the small × on either slot to remove that assignment.
Every card also has a four-arrow control for the strip’s open-side direction. Choose the arrow that points toward the open side in the sample image so the app reads the swatches in the correct order. A sample is not ready until it has a sample image, blank image, and open-side direction. Ready samples show a ready badge.
You can also drag an image from the inbox directly onto a sample card’s empty image or blank slot.

Before processing
For every sample, confirm that the physical strip, sample record, sample image, blank image, and open-side direction all agree. When each sample shows ready, continue to Processing Queue.
Doing more at once
Prisma keeps managed copies of imported images. Two Image Inbox actions operate on that managed set:

Clean Up Unused removes imported images that no sample uses from active custody and moves their source files to Removed Images inside the inbox.
CSV Bulk Assignment assigns sample images, blank images, and orientations
to many samples at once. See CSV Assignment Import.

To see how the blank is actually used when the app reads a strip, see Extraction.
