prisma-calibration/how-to-use/images/pro.title: Manual Processing
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/images/pro.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ProcessingQueueManualProcessingModeling


When the app can’t find a strip on its own, you show it where the strip is by clicking the four corners. This happens most with very see-through filaments that blend into the lightbox. Open it with Manual Process on any sample in Failed or Flagged for Manual Processing (see Processing Queue).

The window shows the sample’s photo. Click the strip’s four corners in this order: top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left. Placed corners can be dragged to nudge them.
The app reads the strip inside those corners and uses the sample’s open-side direction to order the swatches.
Then:

Extract & Process reads the strip from your corners and shows a preview. Nothing is saved yet.
Reset Corners clears them so you can start over.

While ordinary manual extraction is working, let it finish; it does not expose
a cancel action. A Cancel button can appear when this same corner-placement
window is opened from the separate maintenance re-extraction workflow, whose
candidate-generation job supports cancellation.
Once the preview looks right:

Accept re-runs the extraction from the same corners and commits the result. In a batch, it moves you to the next sample.
Retry discards the preview so you can replace the corners.

The committed manual result still goes to Post-Processing Review like any other extraction. It does not become the trusted measurement until you give it the final Accept there (see Processing Queue).
To fix many at once, Manual Process All opens the same window as a queue that walks through every flagged sample in turn.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/images/pro.title: Processing Queue
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/images/pro.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}AssignImagesProcessingQueueModelingManualProcessing


This is where the app reads the colors out of your samples, and where you approve the results. Process All works through the ready samples one at a time; then you check each result and accept the good ones. Only an accepted result becomes the sample’s trusted measurement — the one the models are allowed to learn from.
Open the Images tab and switch to the Processing Queue subtab. A sample appears here once it is ready: it has a sample image, blank image, and open-side direction (see Assign Images).

The screen has two panes. The left, Pre-Processing Queue, is work still to do. The right, Post-Processing Review, is finished results waiting for your yes-or-no.
Extract — the left pane
Samples ready to measure sit under Ready to Process. Each card shows the sample’s strip layout, sample image, blank image, and open-side direction — a last chance to spot a mismatched assignment before processing.
The one button you need is Process All, which steps through every sample that was ready when you started: for each one, it finds the strip in the photo, straightens it, corrects the lighting with the blank, and reads each swatch’s color. A progress panel names the sample being worked on and counts processed, flagged, failed, and remaining. (For what happens inside, see Extraction.)
Each card also has its own actions: Process (measure just this one), Flag (set it aside for hand placement — see below), and Reassign (detach the photo and send the sample back to Assign Images).
Only one extraction runs at a time. Start another while one is going — or while the models are being built — and the app asks you to wait. That’s expected, not an error.
Approve — the right pane
Every finished result lands in Post-Processing Review, and counts for nothing until you act on it. Each card shows the sample’s photo and blank, the strip the app cut out of the photo, and a mock strip built from the colors it read — with the measured thicknesses labeled — so you can compare at a glance:

Accept — keep this result as the sample’s trusted measurement. This is the step that matters: only accepted results feed the models.
Reject — throw it away and send the sample back to be measured again.

Accept All and Reject All apply the same choice to every card at once.
What to inspect before Accept

Confirm that the extracted strip includes the complete physical strip and is not cut off or dominated by surrounding lightbox.
Confirm that the swatches run in the same order as the sample record. A reversed order usually means the open-side direction is wrong.
Compare the extracted strip with the measured-color preview for obvious boundary, glare, contamination, or swatch-placement errors.
Confirm that the sample image and blank image came from the same unchanged capture session.

Reject an extraction when the image assignment, strip boundary, orientation, or measured swatches are wrong. Do not reject a sound measurement merely because it later disagrees with the current model; use Sample Comparison to investigate that separately.
When a sample won’t extract
Sometimes the app can’t find the strip on its own — most often with very see-through filaments that blend into the lightbox. Those samples don’t get measured; they land in one of two spots in the left pane:

Failed — the app tried and couldn’t. Nothing is saved.
Flagged for Manual Processing — you or the app set it aside for hand placement.

For these, click Manual Process to place the strip’s corners by hand — see Manual Processing. Each card also offers Reassign (send it back to Assign Images to fix the photo) and Unflag (put it back in the normal queue). Each group’s header has a Manual Process All button to walk the whole group through hand placement in one sitting.
Next steps

Process All to measure the ready batch.
Send anything in Failed or Flagged through Manual Processing.
Accept the good results, Reject the bad ones.
Accepted samples are now trusted measurements — continue to Modeling.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/images/ind.title: Images
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/images/ind.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}SampleLogbookImagesModelingAssignImagesProcessingQueue


The Images tab is where the physical world enters the app. Everything before it is bookkeeping: the Sample Logbook records what you printed, but the app still knows nothing about how those strips actually behave. The photographs you took on the lightbox hold that information, and this tab turns them into numbers — one measured color for every swatch on every strip.
That happens in two steps, shown as two subtabs:

Assign Images — tell the app which sample image belongs to which sample. Each sample needs a sample image, a blank image of the empty lit lightbox, and an open-side direction so the app reads the swatches in the right order.
Processing Queue — the app finds each strip in its photo, straightens it, corrects the lighting, and reads the color of every swatch. You review what it read and Accept the results that look right.

Do them in that order: a sample can’t be measured until its photos are attached.

Why this step matters
A sample’s accepted extraction is its trusted measurement: the color of each swatch at each printed thickness. Modeling fits the calibration models from accepted measurements. The two checks on this tab — matching images to the correct physical strips and reviewing extractions before accepting them — determine which evidence reaches those fits.
Where you are in the loop
You arrive here after creating samples in the Sample Logbook and printing and photographing the strips. As you work, each sample’s status advances: unassigned → incomplete → ready (sample image, blank image, and open-side direction assigned) → processed (measured, awaiting review) → accepted. Once accepted, the sample is available to Modeling.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/maintenanc.title: Fit Models
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/maintenanc.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}StandardOperationsFitModelsRe-extractSample Images


This is the step that turns your accepted measurements into Calibration’s current working color models. Nothing you measure or curate reaches a future published library until you run it, but fitting alone does not change the library a Generator is already using.
You can start it from two places — the Fit Models button on the Modeling tab, or the Fit Models card in Maintenance. They’re the same job.

What it builds
One run attempts the three current-fit stages in a fixed order from the currently included evidence:

Color Model v1 and Color Model v2 — the two color models.
The Camera Transform — fitted when needed; Force Camera Transform fits it regardless of its current status when at least five eligible samples exist. With fewer than five, that stage is skipped for insufficient evidence even when forced.

Each model replaces its current Calibration files when that stage succeeds. If a later stage fails, an earlier successful replacement remains current. Color Model v1 has one further qualification: if some filament profiles fit and others fail, its successful profiles can become current before the workflow reports the failure and stops.
A successful run makes both color-model entries on Modeling Current. The Camera Transform is also Current if it was rebuilt or was already up to date; an insufficient-evidence skip can leave it Missing or Stale and continues to block publication. Generator still sees only its selected published library. Once all three entries are current and publication readiness passes, use Publish Models in Calibration’s top bar, then select the newly installed library through Config → Model Library in Generator.
Running it
It follows the standard rhythm — Start Workflow → Run Preflight → Fit Models (see Standard Operations). Once fitting begins, it runs to completion and does not offer a Cancel button. Fitting does not change samples, measurements, or exclusions, but a successful stage replaces Calibration’s current working models. The app does not offer a history of old working fits: if you need to keep a model set for printing or comparison, publish it before fitting again. What a fit produces depends on the evidence you included, so review that first on Modeling.


                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Keep Calibration open until Fit Models finishes. Force-closing it while a model is being saved can leave its files and status out of agreement. After an abnormal stop, check all three model statuses and Publish Models readiness before using the working set.


Like every heavy job, it runs alone where resources conflict: it will not start during a backup, restore, RAW-archive task, conflicting extraction/evidence write, another model fit, or another maintenance job. The app reports the conflict rather than queueing the fit.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/maintenanc.filePath: Prisma Calibration/How To Use/Maintenance/Re-extract Sample Images.md
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/maintenanc.title: Re-extract Sample Images
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/maintenanc.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}FitModelsRe-extractSample ImagesBackup /Restore


Re-measures samples that already have accepted measurements — for example after the app’s measuring improved, or when a batch needs redoing. It’s built to be safe: your accepted measurements are untouched until you explicitly save, and you review every new result first.
Start it from the Re-extract Sample Images card in Maintenance.


Choosing the scope

Data — Complete, Transmission Only, or Appearance Only: which half of the color data to recompute (Transmission vs Appearance). Complete redoes both.
Coordinates — Use Accepted Coordinates reuses each strip’s already-accepted corner positions; Re-detect Strip finds each strip from scratch (and forces Data to Complete — a full re-detect has to redo everything).
Samples — All Accepted, or Selected Samples with a box for ids, separated by commas or spaces (e.g. exp-055, exp-056).

The run

Run Preflight — counts the targets and warns which ones will need hand-placed corners.
Extract Images — re-measures into a fresh candidate set. Nothing accepted has changed.
Samples the app couldn’t auto-detect come first as a manual step: place their corners by hand (same idea as Manual Processing), then Review Results.

Review, then commit

Review Extracted Images lists every candidate with a before/after comparison of its strips. For each sample, choose Save (keep the new result) or Skip (keep the old one); failures offer Retry. You must decide every sample before you can commit.
Then:

Save Results — writes only the kept candidates over the old measurements, and shows the final counts.
Discard Results — throws the whole candidate set away; nothing changes.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/maintenanc.title: Standard Operations
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/maintenanc.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}MaintenanceStandardOperationsFitModels


Every Maintenance operation except Re-extract Sample Images runs through the same dialog, in the same three beats. Nothing is written until you’ve seen the preview and pressed the run button.

1 — Start Workflow
Select the operation’s card and click Start Workflow. The dialog restates what the operation does and shows its options, where it has any:

Mode — for the rebuilds and exports: Missing Only (fix only what’s absent or broken) versus Force Rebuild / Force Export (redo everything in scope). Missing Only is the usual choice.
Export Options — for Export Geometry Files: Only Geometries Used By Samples or All Geometries, plus STEP / STL checkboxes.
Fit Options — for Fit Models: a Force Camera Transform checkbox (see Fit Models).

2 — Run Preflight
Run Preflight inspects your data and reports what the operation would do — a summary, warnings, and any blockers — without changing anything. If preflight finds a blocker, the run button stays disabled.
3 — Run
The run button is named for the job — Run Audit, Run Maintenance, Export Files, or Fit Models. Progress streams into the dialog. Operations that can stop safely show Cancel; after you click it, the button changes to Cancelling… and the dialog remains open until the current safe unit finishes. Operations labeled Runs to completion do not offer Cancel. A Result section then shows the outcome and where the report was saved. (Reports collect in the Activity Log.)
Use the offered Cancel action rather than killing Calibration. Safe-point cancellation preserves completed units and stops between units; it is not a rollback of the whole run. A hard process stop has weaker guarantees and can interrupt a multi-file preview/visual replacement between files. After an abnormal stop, restart through the launcher, rerun the relevant audit or rebuild, and inspect its report before trusting the affected derived files.
The one extra gate: running Export Geometry Files in overwrite mode asks you to type a confirmation phrase first, since it replaces existing files.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/maintenanc.title: Maintenance
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/maintenanc.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}TutorialsMaintenanceBackup /RestoreStandardOperationsFitModelsRe-extractSample Images


The top bar’s Maintenance button opens a dialog of housekeeping operations — checks, rebuilds, exports, and Fit Models. Operations appear as cards grouped by category; click one to select it, and Start Workflow appears on the right. Each card says whether it is Read-only or writes something. A grayed-out card is unavailable, with the reason shown.

Only one maintenance job runs at a time — and none while a backup or restore is running. Start a second and the app tells you what’s already going.
The operations

Audit — four read-only checks (Audit Library Integrity, Audit Missing Artifacts, Audit Orphaned Artifacts, Audit Source Image Custody). They report problems — missing files, stray files, photo custody gaps — without touching anything.
Images — Rebuild Image Previews and Rebuild Extraction Images Only regenerate the app’s derived images if they’re missing or broken; Re-extract Sample Images re-measures samples, with review — see Re-extract Sample Images.
Calibration Models — Fit Models builds the color models. See Fit Models.
Geometry Artifacts — Regenerate STEPs/STLs rebuilds the app’s internally managed geometry files; Export Geometry Files writes user-facing print files (the same workflow opened from the Geometries toolbar).
System Maintenance — SQLite Integrity Check (read-only database health check) and Quarantine Orphaned Artifacts (sets aside files nothing references — not deleted, moved into Calibration’s app-managed maintenance quarantine, where you can inspect or recover them through the reported path).

Everything except Re-extract runs through the same three-step rhythm — see Standard Operations.
The Activity Log
The dialog header’s Activity Log button lists standard-operation reports — Name, Type, Status, File Name — newest first. A standard job blocked before execution, or whose worker raises before returning its report, has no row. Re-extract Sample Images instead keeps generation/apply reports with its staged candidate set, not in this list. Clear Log deletes only the Activity Log’s report files — never your samples, photos, backups, candidate sets, or data.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/modeling/c.title: Curating Samples
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/modeling/c.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ModelingOverviewCuratingSamplesFilamentCoverageSampleComparison


The Samples subtab of Modeling decides, strip by strip, what the models learn. It shows one row per sample with an accepted extraction: Sample, Strip, Filaments, Fit State, and Extracted Appearance. Samples that have not reached accepted extraction are counted on Overview instead of appearing here.

Exclude and Include
Click a row to open its comparison drawer. Under Sample Exclusion, use Exclude Sample or Include Sample to change whether the whole sample counts in the next fit. The measurement is not deleted; it is only withheld.
If only one swatch is suspect, use the controls under Swatch Exclusion in the same drawer. The sample’s Sample Record provides the same per-swatch control. Changing either kind of exclusion marks affected models Stale; run Fit Models after you finish curating.
Finding the rows you care about

The Filter dropdown narrows the list: All, Included, Excluded, Filament Excluded, Has Excluded Swatches, Stale, and Missing Model.
Filaments… opens a picker; chosen filaments appear as chips and the list shows only samples containing them. Clear removes them. Use it to review every strip a suspect filament touched.
Click the Sample, Filaments, or Fit State column heading to sort; the controls row counts how many rows are showing.

Stale and Missing Model are global model-state filters, not judgments about individual samples. When any current model has the chosen state, the filter shows all otherwise matching accepted-extraction rows; when none does, it shows no rows.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/modeling/f.title: Filament Coverage
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/modeling/f.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}CuratingSamplesFilamentCoveragePublishModels


The Filaments subtab of Modeling answers a different question than the other two: does each filament have enough included evidence to be modeled well? Read it as a gap-finder.

One row per filament: Filament, Brand, Samples, Fit Samples, Incl. Swatches, Excl. Swatches, and Health. Every column is sortable.
Health sums up the row:

Good — at least eight swatches are currently included. This is a coarse evidence-count check, not a guarantee that the evidence spans every useful thickness or role.
Sparse — fewer than eight swatches are currently included.
Excluded only — it appears in samples, but every one is excluded, so it contributes nothing.
Excluded — the filament carries the permanent exclude flag from Filaments.
Stale — at least one current model needs rebuilding. This state applies globally and takes precedence over the row’s ordinary evidence-count health unless the filament itself is Excluded.

The detail view
Click a row for the filament’s coverage detail: Summary, Coverage (included/excluded sample and swatch counts), Model State, and Samples. Include in Fits / Exclude from Fits changes the filament’s exclusion setting, just as it does under Filaments. Show In Samples jumps to the Samples subtab pre-filtered to this filament so you can act on what you found.

For Sparse, first check whether useful samples or swatches were excluded. If the included evidence is genuinely thin, print and measure more strips. Excluded only means the existing samples cannot contribute until a sample or the filament itself is included again.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/modeling/m.title: Modeling Overview
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/modeling/m.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ModelingModelingOverviewCuratingSamples


The Overview subtab of Modeling summarizes the evidence and model state before you run Fit Models.

Current Evidence
Four cards summarize what the next build would learn from:

Evidence Samples — included samples over accepted-extraction samples (e.g. 41 / 55). The first number counts accepted-extraction samples that are eligible and have at least one included swatch. The second counts every sample with an accepted extraction, including samples excluded at the sample, swatch, or filament level. Samples without an accepted extraction are reported separately under Needs Attention and are not part of this denominator.
Swatches — included swatches over total.
Excluded Samples — how many you’ve switched off.
Excluded Swatches — how many single swatches are sidelined.

Needs Attention
This list combines two different kinds of attention:

A Stale or Missing model means the model needs fitting. This is a reason to run Fit Models, not a blocker you must clear beforehand.
Samples blocked by excluded filaments cannot contribute while one of their filaments has Exclude from model fits selected.
Samples without accepted extraction counts every sample record that does not yet have an accepted measurement, including unassigned and incomplete samples as well as results waiting in the Processing Queue. Those samples do not contribute to the current fit.

Review the list to confirm that the included evidence is intentional, then run Fit Models (Fit Models). The empty-state message is No immediate blockers, but the list does not need to be empty merely because a model is stale or missing.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/modeling/p.title: Publish Models
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/modeling/p.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}FilamentCoveragePublishModels


Publish Models in the top bar copies Calibration’s current models into a library that Generator can use. Later changes in Calibration do not change a published library.
Run Fit Models first, then check the results on Modeling. You need current copies of Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and The Camera Transform before you can publish.
Check readiness
Open Publish Models. Publication Readiness checks the filament list and all three models. If it reports Publication blocked, read the reason beside the affected item. A missing or stale model needs fitting; missing or changed model files also need attention before publication can proceed.
After correcting a problem, use Refresh in this dialog to check again. The publishing buttons become available when the checks pass and the required library details are filled in.
Name the library
Under Library Details, enter:

Library name — the name users will see in Generator.
Version — the version you are publishing, such as 1.0.
Publisher or author — your name or the name of the group supplying the library.
Description and Release notes — optional descriptions of the library and what changed.

Library lineage ID is optional. Leave it blank for a new, separate library. For a compatible update to a library you have already published, reuse the Lineage ID shown in its earlier publication result. Keep that ID with your library’s records. It tells Generator that the releases belong to the same library; using the same name alone does not do that. Each publication still receives its own release ID.
Choose where it goes

Publish to Generator installs a new library in this Prisma Suite’s Generator/Model Libraries folder. It is installed without becoming active. In Generator, open Config → Model Library, select it, and choose Activate and Restart Prisma when you are ready. Finish your current work before restarting.
Export Library Package writes a ZIP in Calibration/Output/Published Models. Use Open Published Models Folder to find it. To use it in another Generator installation, open Config → Model Library there and choose Install Library…, then activate the installed library when ready.

Keep the publication dialog open until the operation finishes. The result shows the library name and version, together with its Library ID or the exported package path.
What is included
The library contains the filament list and the files Generator needs for all three models. It does not include Calibration’s database, sample records, photographs, measurements, or private notes. Keep a Calibration backup too if you want to preserve the evidence used to fit the models.
Changing filament exclusions or fitting again affects future publications. A library you already published stays as it was.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/modeling/s.title: Sample Comparison
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/modeling/s.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}CuratingSamplesSampleComparisonFilamentCoverage


Click any row on the Samples subtab to open a side-by-side comparison for that sample: what was measured, next to what each model predicts for the same strip. The drawer also contains the sample and swatch exclusion controls.

The drawer shows Transmission Domain and Appearance Domain side by side. Each domain contains:

Measured Transmission or Measured Appearance — the accepted measurement.
Predicted Transmission (Color Model V2) / Predicted Appearance (Color Model V2) — the Color Model v2 prediction.
Predicted Transmission (Color Model V1) / Predicted Appearance (Color Model V1) — the Color Model v1 prediction.
Prediction Error — an OKLab error graph comparing each prediction with the measurement, swatch by swatch.

Color Corrections: On/Off changes the displayed predictions without changing the measurements. Both domains remain visible; see Transmission vs Appearance for what they mean.
Reading it

If both predictions broadly track the measurement, the sample is behaving consistently with the current models.
If one swatch is clearly inconsistent with its neighbors, inspect the extraction and physical strip before excluding only that swatch under Swatch Exclusion.
If the whole strip disagrees, verify its geometry, filament assignments, sample image, blank image, and open-side direction before using Exclude Sample.

Treat the comparison as evidence, not an automatic pass/fail score. A high prediction error may identify a bad sample, but it may also reveal useful evidence that the current models do not yet represent well.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/modeling/i.title: Modeling
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/modeling/i.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ImagesModelingModelingOverviewCuratingSamplesFilamentCoveragePublishModels


Everything upstream produced measurements; this tab is where you decide which measurements the color models learn from, then fit Calibration’s current models. A separate publication step copies those models into a Generator library.


The header — model status and Fit Models
The header shows the status of each current working model — Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and Camera Transform — as:

Current — a fit is saved, and none of the measurements or fitting choices it used have been marked as changed. Newly accepted samples do not automatically make an existing fit stale; run Fit Models to include them. Publish Models checks the saved model files before creating a library.
Stale — a measurement or fitting choice used by the model has changed since it was built. A Fit Models needed banner appears. Run the fit again after you finish making changes.
Missing — never built yet.

Fit Models fits Color Model v1 and Color Model v2 from the currently included evidence. It also fits the Camera Transform when needed, or whenever Force Camera Transform is selected. See Fit Models. What the models are is covered in Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and The Camera Transform.
Two ways to keep data out

Here (and on the Sample Record): exclude one sample or one swatch from the next fit. These controls are reversible and suit one suspect strip or swatch.
On Filaments: Exclude from model fits removes a filament wholesale until the setting is cleared. Use it for a retired or mis-measured filament. A Generator library published afterward leaves that filament out; previously published libraries do not change.

The subtabs

Overview — is the evidence healthy? Your pre-build checklist.
Samples — include or exclude each sample; compare measurements to the models.
Filaments — does each filament have enough data to be modeled well?

The usual loop: read the Overview, spot-check and curate Samples, check coverage on Filaments, then Fit Models. A stale or missing model is a reason to fit; it is not something you must clear first.
Publish the exact current generation
Fit Models and Publish Models are deliberately different operations:

Fitting replaces Calibration’s working models. They may need fitting again as you add or change measurements.
Publishing creates a new Generator library from the current Color Model v1, Color Model v2, Camera Transform, and filament list. It never modifies a previously published copy.

Press Publish Models in the app’s top bar. The dialog checks all four required components and blocks publication if a model is missing, stale, invalid, changed on disk, or inconsistent with the others. When it reports Ready to publish, enter a required Library name, Version, and Publisher or author; description and release notes are optional.
Choose one action:

Publish to Generator validates and installs a new library in this Suite’s Generator\Model Libraries. It is installed inactive so the running Generator cannot change underneath an open session. Open Config → Model Library in Generator and choose Activate and Restart Prisma when ready.
Export Library Package writes a validated ZIP under Calibration\Output\Published Models. Send that unchanged ZIP to another Generator, or distribute it as a model-library update; the receiving user opens Config → Model Library in Generator and chooses Install Library….

Both actions include the same filament list and the files Generator needs for the three models. The published library does not include Calibration’s database, sample records, raw photographs, per-sample predictions, or notes.
For a later compatible update to the same library, reuse its Library lineage ID. Leave that field blank to create a separate library. See Publish Models for the full publishing steps.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/sample-log.title: Creating New Samples
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/sample-log.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}SampleLogbookCreating NewSamplesSampleRecord


+ New Samples on the Sample Logbook creates records for the physical strips you will print. Each sample combines one geometry with one filament assignment for every material role.

Before you start
The required filaments must exist under Filaments. The required strip designs must exist under Geometries. To use a bundle, it must have a Mapped status under Manage Bundles.
Choose a source
Under Select Geometry Source, choose:

Single Geometry — create samples from one strip design.
Geometry Bundle — create samples from every geometry in a mapped bundle.

A bundle does not create one combined print. It creates a separate sample record for each member geometry.
Assign filaments
For a single geometry, assign a filament to each LR role. For a bundle, assign filaments to its shared slots, such as Shared Filament A. One shared assignment fills every geometry role mapped to that slot, even when those roles have different LR numbers or one is fixed and another is variable.
Each role or shared slot has two modes:

Single — use one filament for every sample in this set.
Multi — create a separate set for each selected filament.

Only one role or shared slot can be Multi. Select at least two filaments for it; all other roles remain Single and require one filament each.
Know how many samples will be created

























Source and assignmentResultOne geometry, all roles Single1 sampleOne geometry, one role Multi with N filamentsN samplesBundle with G geometries, all shared slots SingleG samplesBundle with G geometries, one shared slot Multi with N filamentsG × N samples
For example, a three-geometry bundle with four filaments selected for one shared slot creates 12 samples.

Review and create
Selected Geometry Preview shows the source. Sample Summary and Sample Preview show the exact number of records, their new sample IDs, geometry, and role assignments. Check these before continuing. Optional Notes apply to every sample in the set.
Click Create. The records appear in the Sample Logbook as unassigned.
Print and identify the strips
Export the geometry files and match every LR body or file to the same role shown in the sample preview. See Export Sample Geometry. Print at full size.
Keep each physical strip associated with its sample ID. This is especially important for Geometry Bundle and Multi runs, where many similar strips are created at once.


                  
                  Physical sample custody draft 
                  
                

Before printing, prepare one labeled location for every sample ID: a tray position, bag, envelope, or other container that cannot be confused with its neighbors. Move each strip directly into its labeled location after printing. Keep the label with the strip through photography and review, and do not mark the swatches or any area used for extraction.


Once the strips are printed and photographed on the lightbox, continue to Images.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/sample-log.title: Sample Record
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/sample-log.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}Creating NewSamplesSampleRecordImages


Click any sample in the Sample Logbook to open its record — everything the app knows about that strip, in one drawer. It opens read-only, with the sample’s ID and status in the header and an Edit button; click Edit to change anything, which swaps in Save, Discard, and Delete.

The sections

Filaments — which filament fills each layer. Changeable in Edit mode.
Images — the assigned photo and blank; in Edit mode, Unassign source and Unassign blank detach either.
Strip — a preview of the calibration strip.
Sample Geometry — which geometry this sample uses (changeable in Edit mode), with a Copy Path button that copies the geometry’s folder location.
Notes — free text.
Model Fit — see below.

The expand button in the header widens the drawer to show the sample’s measured results: the extracted strip image beside the colors the app read from it.

Changing the strip changes the measurement. If you change a measured sample’s geometry or filaments, the app clears its measurement — the old numbers described the old strip. Check that the record and photograph describe the same physical strip, then process it again. If the strip itself has changed, take a new photograph.

Model Fit — keeping a measurement out of the models
Two controls decide what this sample contributes the next time you run Fit Models:

Exclude this sample from model fits — withholds the whole sample from model fitting. The measurement stays; it just does not count. Reversible any time.
Per-swatch toggles — in the expanded view, each measured swatch has its own Included / Excluded toggle for withholding one swatch without losing the rest of the strip.

The Sample Comparison drawer under Modeling provides the same sample and per-swatch exclusion controls beside the model comparisons.
Delete removes the sample entirely. Prefer excluding — it keeps the data without letting it influence anything.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/sample-log.title: Sample Logbook
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/sample-log.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}GeometriesSampleLogbookImagesCreating NewSamplesSampleRecord


The Sample Logbook (the Logbook tab in the app) lists every sample: one sample geometry filled with specific filaments. Each record tracks one physical calibration strip from creation to accepted measurement.

The list
One row per sample: ID, Strip, Filament, Brand, Image, Blank, and Status. ID, Filament, Brand, and Status are sortable. The line above the table counts your samples and how many are measured. A red chip in the Image or Blank cell means that image file cannot be found — re-attach it on the Images tab.
Status tells you where each sample is:

unassigned — just created; no photos yet.
incomplete — has some of its sample image, blank image, or open-side direction, but not all three.
ready — has a sample image, blank image, and open-side direction; waiting in the Processing Queue.
processed — measured, waiting for your Accept in the Processing Queue.
accepted — a trusted measurement; it can feed the models.
failed / flagged — automatic measurement didn’t work or was set aside; see Manual Processing.

What you do here

+ New Samples creates samples from a geometry — see Creating New Samples.
Click a row to open that sample’s record — its filaments, photos, notes, and measurement controls. See Sample Record.

The usual path: create samples here, print the strips, then attach their photos on the Images tab.

prisma-calibration/how-to-use/index.title: How To Use
prisma-calibration/how-to-use/index.content:
The calibration app measures how your filaments pass light, so the generator can reproduce their colors in a print. You photograph printed filament strips on a lightbox, the app reads the color out of each photo, and once you’ve checked the results it builds the color models the generator prints from.
The steps run in order. You set up the library — your filaments and sample geometries — once. Everything after that you repeat for each new set of strips.
The workflow


.htu-diagram svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-diagram a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-diagram a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-diagram a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}Set up onceRepeat for each batch of stripsFilamentsGeometriesSampleLogbookImagesModelingGuides and toolsTutorialsMaintenanceBackup /Restore


Every box is a page. The top row is the workflow, left to right: set up Filaments and Geometries once, then run Sample Logbook → Images → Modeling for each batch of strips. Maintenance and Backup / Restore live in the top bar and work from any tab.

Filaments — add each filament you want to test.
Geometries — design the calibration strips you will print.
Sample Logbook — fill a geometry’s material roles with filaments to create samples.
Images — give each sample its lightbox photos, then pull the colors out.
Modeling — check the measurements, then build the color models.

Steps 1 and 2 are one-time setup. Steps 3–5 are the loop you run for every batch of strips.
One heads-up: the app’s own tab strip is arranged for day-to-day use — Logbook first, then Images, Filaments, Geometries, Modeling — so the two setup tabs sit in the middle of the strip, not at the left.
Top-bar tools
These top-bar buttons work from any tab:

Refresh Data — reload the app’s current data when a view looks out of
date. It does not import files that are waiting in the Image Inbox; use
Import from Inbox on the Images page for that.
Maintenance — housekeeping jobs, and the button that builds the models.
Publish Models — copy the current models into a library for Generator, or export a library ZIP to use elsewhere.
Backup / Restore — save a copy of your work, or bring one back. See Backups.

Getting set up

Getting Started — installing and launching the app, and a first run end to end.
Tutorials — draft walkthroughs.

Good to know
Operations that would interfere with each other cannot run together. For example, fitting must wait while measurements are being changed, and maintenance must wait for a backup or restore. If an operation is blocked, the app tells you why.
Nothing you measure reaches a print until you run Fit Models, publish the models, and activate that library in Generator. To understand what a measurement is or how the models work, see How It Works.

prisma-calibration/index.title: Prisma Calibration
prisma-calibration/index.content:
Prisma Calibration measures how 3D-printing filaments transmit light. It turns controlled photographs of printed calibration samples into working color models, then can publish a model library for the Prisma Lithophane Generator. Each published library stays as it was when you published it.
Why calibration is needed
The color of a backlit print depends on the filament, its thickness, and the other filament layers around it. A filament’s name or displayed color is not enough to predict these effects. The generator needs measurements from real printed samples.
Calibration builds a reusable library of these measurements. You add to it when you introduce new filaments or need better coverage; you do not repeat the full calibration process for every lithophane.
What the app does
The calibration workflow has five main stages:

Define your filaments and the sample strips you will print.
Print the samples and photograph them on a lightbox.
Assign and process the photographs to measure each swatch.
Review the measurements and fit Calibration’s current working models.
When that exact model set is ready to use, publish it as a new Generator library.

The app manages the samples, photographs, measurements, model-fitting process, and publication step. Printing and photography happen outside the app. Calibration never edits a model library after Generator has installed it.
Where to begin

Getting Started — prepare the app and complete the calibration workflow for the first time.
How To Use — instructions for the tasks and screens in the app.
How It Works — explanations of sample measurement, color models, and the camera transform.

prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.title: Installing Prisma Generator
prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.content:
Prisma Generator is a portable local application with packaged releases for Windows x86-64 and Linux x86-64. A packaged macOS release is coming soon. Prisma does not use a conventional installer: download an archive for your platform, extract the whole folder, and keep that folder together.
Not every beta publishes every platform at the same time. Start with Prisma’s GitHub Releases page, read the newest release notes, and use the most recent release that explicitly provides a packaged asset for your platform. A source archive is not a substitute for the packaged application unless you intend to run Prisma as a developer.
The wiki describes the current application, which may include features added since the latest packaged beta. Use the release notes to check what your download includes.
Choose a download

Prisma Generator is for making lithophanes with published model libraries. It includes Prisma Standard Models. Launch it with Prisma Generator.exe on Windows or Prisma Generator on Linux.
Prisma Suite includes Prisma Generator and Prisma Calibration, which you can use to build and publish your own model libraries. Its two launchers are Prisma Generator.exe and Prisma Calibration.exe on Windows, or Prisma Generator and Prisma Calibration on Linux.

You can install model-library updates later in either version. You only need to download Prisma Suite if you intend to create your own model library that includes calibration data for filaments that are not in the pre-installed library. I recommend trying Prisma Generator with the existing model library before attempting to calibrate your own filaments.
Extract it on Windows

Download the current Windows x86-64 ZIP from Prisma’s GitHub Releases page. Choose either the standalone Generator or Suite archive.
In File Explorer, right-click the ZIP and choose Extract All. Do not run Prisma from inside the ZIP preview.
Move the extracted Prisma folder to a normal writable location, such as Documents. Do not put the live folder in Program Files, a cloud-synchronized folder, or a network share.
Keep the entire folder together. The executables, bundled software, settings, images, exports, libraries, and Calibration data use paths inside this one portable folder.

Extract it on Linux

Download the newest Linux x86-64 .tar.gz offered on Prisma’s GitHub Releases page. The newest overall release may be Windows-only, so follow any platform note in its release description.
Extract it with your archive manager or run tar -xzf followed by the downloaded archive’s path. Do not try to run Prisma from inside the archive.
Keep the extracted folder in a normal writable location, not a cloud-synchronized folder or network share.
Open a terminal in the extracted Prisma or Prisma Suite folder and follow the launcher instructions on Launching Prisma.

The current Linux packages target x86-64 systems with glibc 2.38 or newer. They are built and smoke-tested under Ubuntu 24.04 on WSL2; native desktop integration has not yet been verified on a separate Linux machine.
Neither packaged platform requires Python, PyCharm, VS Code, a CAD package, an FFmpeg installation, an operating-system HEIC codec, or manual dependency setup. The packages include the software needed to run Prisma and open supported images.
Install it on macOS (coming soon)
A packaged macOS release is planned. Installation instructions and the supported Mac architectures will be added after the release build has been compiled and smoke-tested on the target hardware.
Windows warning
Prisma is not currently code-signed, so Windows SmartScreen may call it an unrecognized app. Only use a ZIP obtained from Prisma’s official GitHub Releases page. If you trust that download, choose More info and then Run anyway.
Extracting a newer Prisma release does not update an older live folder in place. Unless a future release includes a documented migration procedure, keep each extracted version separate and maintain independent copies of important data.

prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.title: Launching Prisma Generator
prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.content:
Open the extracted Prisma folder and start the Generator launcher.
On Windows, double-click:

Prisma Generator.exe in the Generator-only download.
Prisma Generator.exe in the Suite.

On Linux, open a terminal in the extracted folder and run:
# Generator-only package
./"Prisma Generator"
 
# Suite package
./"Prisma Generator"
A console or terminal window will open and run a server that makes Prisma Generator accessible only on your computer. Prisma Generator should then open automatically in your system’s default browser. The launcher normally uses http://127.0.0.1:8010. If that port is busy, it chooses another local port automatically and prints the actual address in the console. If your browser does not open automatically, manually navigate to the address stated in the terminal window. Starting the same app again will not run a second server for the same Workspace; it opens the already-running Generator in your browser.
Keep the console or terminal open while you use Prisma Generator. Closing it will stop the local server and make the Generator unavailable. Explicitly saved Palettes, Settings Profiles, Saved Runs, source images, and exports remain available. The Solve Timeline and Solve Queue are cleared when Prisma starts again; unfinished queued work does not resume automatically. Recent temporary Autosaves can support exact recovery after restart, but they are retention-limited. Use Workspace → Save to preserve related work, or save individual runs for portable archives.
The first launch of a new Generator Workspace shows a welcome prompt offering First-Time Setup. Choose Start First-Time Setup to walk through Printer Configuration, the active Extrusion Width, the Model Library, Active Filaments, theme selection, saving work and resetting the workspace, and Help & Guides, or choose Not Now to dismiss the prompt. Complete the setup before making your first lithophane.
The folders Prisma creates
On first launch, Generator creates these folders beside the executable:

























FolderWhat belongs thereGenerator/ImagesOriginal source artwork. Add one or several images through the app or copy supported images here. Prisma never replaces these originals.Generator/ExportsCompleted 3MF/STL exports, one folder per export.Generator/Model LibrariesValidated, installed published libraries. Manage these through Config → Model Library in Generator.Generator/WorkspaceApp-managed settings, saved palettes and runs, disposable prepared-image and solve caches, and logs. Do not rearrange individual files inside it.
Generator keeps its normal state inside the extracted Prisma folder, not in a separate per-user application-data location such as %LOCALAPPDATA%. You may move or copy the entire Prisma folder while the app is closed. Do not manually combine one installation’s Workspace or Model Libraries with another.
If the browser does not open
Read the address printed after Address: in the console and enter it in your browser. If Prisma reports a startup error, leave the window open long enough to read the message. The application accepts desktop-launcher connections only from the local computer (127.0.0.1); it is not a hosted website or a server for other devices.

prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.title: Supported Filaments
prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.content:
Prisma Generator can use any calibrated filament included and marked available in the active model library. The included model library contains many filaments, but each calibration is specific to that exact filament product.
A matte version of a filament can have different optical properties from the standard version, even when both come from the same manufacturer. A filament with the same color and finish from another manufacturer may behave very differently.
If the exact calibrated filament is unavailable, a substitute is only a plausible candidate when both its apparent color and transmission distance (TD) are very close to the calibrated product. Even then, substitution is an experiment rather than a supported match. Manufacturer data and third-party resources such as 3D Filament Profiles and FilamentColors can help screen candidates, but reported TD and color values vary and do not replace Prisma calibration.
For predictable, high-quality results, use the exact calibrated products or create a custom model library with Prisma Calibration for the filaments you own.

prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.title: Walkthrough
prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.content:
After First-Time Setup, Prisma Generator’s main workflow has four numbered steps: 1 Image → 2 Palette → 3 Preview → 4 Export. It is a single-user tool: browser tabs share the same workspace, so edits in one can affect the others. Long operations run in the background and report progress. You can submit more solves while one is running; Prisma keeps them in a queue and works through them one at a time.
Choose the app appearance
Use Theme: System on the right side of the top bar, beside Workspace, to choose System, Light, or Dark. System is the default and follows your operating-system appearance, including changes made while Generator is open. An explicit Light or Dark choice stays in effect until you change it. The choice is saved in this browser and is synchronized between open Generator tabs; it is not part of a Settings Profile or saved run.
Walk one image through
1 — Pick a source image
On step 1 Image, choose a photo from the Image Library, or use Add Image to add one or more photos from your computer. JPEG, PNG, TIFF, BMP, WebP, HEIC/HEIF/HIF, and AVIF photos are supported. Phone photos such as HEIC and HDR gain-map JPEGs may briefly show Preparing… while Prisma creates a disposable SDR working copy; your original remains untouched. The placeholder reads Select an image until you pick one; the preview and framing controls fill in once you do.
2 — Build a palette
On step 2 Palette, the beginner path is Auto-Suggest: pick the filaments the suggester may draw from under Select Filaments for Auto-Suggest, choose the exact Palette colors count and the number of Suggestions, then use Suggest Palettes to stage alternatives. By default, suggestions land in Suggested Palettes, each with a Suggest dE figure (lower is a closer numerical fit). Use Add to Deck on the palettes you want to solve. Preferences can send suggestions directly to the deck instead. Select one deck card for a single solve, or use Ctrl/Command, Shift, or a selection rectangle to select 2–10 cards for a batch. The top-bar Solve action uses those highlighted cards. See Palette.
3 — Solve and review
Select a palette in the deck and press Solve in the top bar. Solving preserves your current workspace; open step 3 Preview to review results. Solve Pitch is selected in whole multiples of the active Extrusion Width. If either physical image dimension does not divide into whole Solve Pitch cells, Prisma asks you to review a whole-cell size before continuing. Follow progress in Solve Queue or the smaller Solve progress window. When it finishes, select its Solve Timeline card: the Viewer shows the predicted lit appearance, and Inspector’s Current view shows the recorded setup and color-error figure (RMSE %). A lower RMSE is a closer numerical match, but it does not guarantee a more pleasing result. View Mode offers White Cap, Color Regions, Top Surface, and Explorer; Advanced adds Thickness Maps and lists the currently unavailable Highpass view. Use Ctrl/Command-click or Shift-click in the Timeline to compare several results together. The blocky look is deliberate: the preview honors the true solve resolution and never fakes detail the print will not have. See Preview for review and comparison.
4 — Export print files
On step 4 Export, pick the finished run under Select Run, review its captured setup in Export Options, and press Export Meshes. Choose Single .3MF (the default) or Separate .STLs under Output format. Each finished record appears under Generated Exports → Session exports with its Generated Files and Print Instructions. Use the copy button for the instructions, the folder button to open the saved files, or Download ZIP copy to collect a separate packaged copy. See Export.
From here

Supported Filaments — how exact filament calibration affects substitutions and which products are included.
How To Use — the full walkthrough of every screen and control.
Solve Queue — follow progress and manage waiting solves.
Palette and Export — the two ends of the workflow in depth.
Settings — the controls behind the defaults (solve mode, resolution, preprocessing, color regions, and white cap).
How It Works — the model and the math under the whole thing.
Prisma Calibration — where personal model libraries are built and published.

prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.title: Getting Started
prisma-lithophane-generator/getting-star.content:
Prisma Generator turns a source photo into a printable color lithophane: a stack of filament layers that reproduces the image when it is backlit. Start with the requirements below, then follow the linked pages through installation, first-time setup, filament selection, and your first exported print files.
What you need

A source image — any photo you want to turn into a lithophane. Prisma Generator supports PNG, JPEG, TIFF, BMP, WebP, HEIC/HEIF/HIF, and AVIF.
A model library that includes the filaments you intend to use. Packaged downloads include a model library with many common filaments. If the included library does not contain the filaments you want, use Prisma Calibration to create and publish a custom model library.
A multicolor 3D printer. During First-Time Setup, describe its printable area, material-system capacity, nozzles, and supported Extrusion Widths so Prisma can keep the image and generated geometry within those limits.
At least one AMS/MMU/CFS/ACE-style material system. The active Printer Profile tells Prisma how many filaments fit at once. Prisma can plan additional colors through mid-print swaps, but a palette that fits in one load is the simpler baseline.
OrcaSlicer. Prisma’s exported print-file workflow is designed and tested with OrcaSlicer. Other slicers may work but have not been tested.
The filaments from your model library that you want to print with. Exact product matches provide the most predictable color. See Supported Filaments before substituting a different filament.
Sufficient system memory for the image size and Solve Pitch you choose. Larger lithophanes and finer solve grids require more memory and take longer to solve and export.
Prisma Generator — the packaged application does not require Python, an IDE, or manual dependency installation.

Start here

Install Prisma Generator for your operating system.
Launch Prisma Generator and open its local interface.
Complete the in-app First-Time Setup to configure your printer, active Extrusion Width, Model Library, and Active Filaments.
Review the exact products available in Supported Filaments.
Follow the Walkthrough to take one image from selection to printable files.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Choosing a Color Model
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Before Prisma can solve an image it has to answer one question, over and over: given this stack of filament layers at these thicknesses, what color comes out when it is backlit? The selected color model supplies those predictions throughout a run. Recipe choices, previews, and cap construction all use the same model.
Why it is a separate piece
There is more than one way to predict a stack’s color, and Prisma ships two. Both models predict the appearance of a physical filament stack, so either can be used for recipe search, previews, accuracy checks, and the white cap. You choose the model once — the Appearance Model setting — and that choice flows through the whole solve.
The two models

Color Model v1 starts from calibrated per-filament transmission curves and composes a stack by multiplying those transmissions. Its Color LUT also applies the active Model Library’s calibrated pair corrections to two-color candidates. The base multiplication is order-independent. This is The Transmission Model.
Color Model v2 — the default — is the interaction-aware Photo-stack v2 model, built from photographs of real printed stacks. It models the ordered physical stack and cannot be reduced to per-filament profiles; its model and correction data come from Generator’s active Model Library. This is The photo-stack v2 model.

They use different methods to predict the same physical result.
What asks it, and what it answers
For a physical stack — a white base, the ordered color layers, and a white cap, each with a thickness — the model predicts its backlit color. Prisma compares those predictions in OKLab. The Appearance Model setting has four main uses:

Recipe lookup — filling The Color LUT with the predicted color of thousands of candidate stacks.
Previews — turning the solved layers into the predicted backlit image shown on screen.
Diagnostics — predicting the solved result and measuring its color distance from the solve target, to report where the print lands and where it had to compromise.
Luminance-cap response — in Luminance mode, sampling the white filament’s behavior to build the cap that carries the image’s tone (see Solve Modes and White Cap).

Staying current
Prisma records the selected model and calibration data so that
a cached Color LUT is reused only with the same Appearance Model and Model
Library data. Changing those inputs causes Prisma to build a new table rather
than silently reusing predictions made under a different model.
Generator keeps using the same library until you choose another one in Config → Model Library and press Activate and Restart Prisma. It checks the selected library when it starts again. A library contains Color Model v1, Color Model v2, and the Camera Transform together, so changing libraries can change the predictions even when the Appearance Model setting stays the same.
That restart boundary matters for older work. It clears the process’s in-memory solve state rather than relabeling it as current under the new library. Loading a whole saved run restores the solved arrays that were archived with that run; loading only its settings or solving again uses the library active in the new process. Prisma does not silently rewrite a saved run when a different library is selected.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: The Transmission Model
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Every color decision rests on one prediction: given a stack of filament layers at chosen thicknesses, what color comes out when light passes through? The transmission model is the simpler of Prisma’s two answers — the Appearance Model labeled Color Model v1 in Settings.
Light leaves the backlight white, then passes through a white base, one or more colored layers, and a white cap. Each layer absorbs part of the light; the model predicts the color that survives the full stack.
One filament, many colors
A filament does not have a single color — it has a family of colors indexed by thickness. A thin layer barely tints the light; piled on, it reads deep and saturated, closing toward black. Prisma learns this curve for each filament by measuring printed swatches, not from a physical absorption law. The measured transmission at a handful of thicknesses — the knots — is fitted, one curve per red, green, and blue channel, with a monotone cubic spline (PCHIP), so transmission can be read off at any thickness in between. Zero thickness returns perfectly clear (transmission 1). Past the thickest measured swatch the curve has no data, so there it falls back to a Beer-Lambert exponential extrapolated from the last two measurements — the only place a physical formula enters.
Stacking is multiplication
To get a full stack’s color you do not simulate light bouncing through layers — you multiply what each layer transmits, one channel at a time:
T_\text{total} = T_\text{base} \cdot \prod_i T_{\text{color},i} \cdot T_\text{cap} \quad (\text{per channel})
The base trims the light, each color trims it further, the cap trims it last. Because multiplication commutes, stacking order does not change this basic prediction. Prisma still records a print order for the physical layers and preserves it during export.
Where filaments interact
Real filaments are not perfectly independent: stack two and they interact in ways a plain per-layer multiply cannot capture. Color Model v1 corrects for that with pair corrections — small empirical per-channel multipliers measured for specific two-filament combinations. They enter when The Color LUT is built, adjusting two-color candidates. Generator always applies the active Model Library’s corrections; there is no user-facing Color corrections switch. Photo-stack v2 carries its own different correction data.
That alternative is Color Model v2 — the Photo-stack v2 model — which predicts an ordered whole stack using a model fitted from photographs of real prints. It is the newer, context-aware default; Color Model v1 remains available and uses the active library’s per-filament profiles and pair-correction data. Both are reached through the Choosing a Color Model.
Why it matters
Prisma uses these predictions to build The Color LUT before the main recipe search. The solver then compares stored candidate colors with its targets in OKLab; colors no allowed stack can reach are steered onto reachable ones first by Gamut mapping.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: The Photo-Stack v2 Model
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Prisma has two ways to predict the color a backlit filament stack will show. The simpler one, The Transmission Model, treats each layer independently and multiplies their transmissions — a good first approximation, but real filaments are not that well-behaved. The photo-stack model is the context-aware alternative: it predicts a whole stack at once, accounting for how each layer’s contribution depends on what surrounds it. A blue layer reads differently depending on what sits above it, what sits below it, how much white caps it, and which other colors share the stack. That neighbor-dependence is the point, and it is why this model cannot be reduced to one curve per filament.
It is the default. The advanced Appearance Model setting offers Color Model v1 (the transmission model) and Color Model v2 (this model); a solve uses Color Model v1 only when you select it. Either way the model is reached through the Choosing a Color Model.
Where it comes from
You do not build this model by hand. It is the product of a calibration fit: Prisma Calibration photographs real printed stacks under backlight, measures the colors they produce, and fits the model and its correction data. Publish Models then packages the current model families as a complete Model Library, which can be published to Generator or exported for another installation.
Generator uses the published library selected through Config → Model Library. Refitting or editing models in Calibration cannot change a library already installed in Generator. To use newer data, publish a new library, install it, and activate it. Generator checks that the library is complete before using it.
What it computes during a solve
The model answers one question repeatedly: for this exact stack of layers at these thicknesses, what color comes out the back? It builds the answer in stages.
The first stage works in optical density — the negative log of transmission — where stacking layers is addition rather than multiplication. It sums each layer’s optical density and adds extra terms for the effects a plain multiply misses: white behind the colors darkening them more when color is present, the front white cap behaving differently from the base, and two distinct colors interacting. Converting that total back to color, through a floor that bounds how dark the stack can read, gives the base prediction. Strip the extra terms and the floor and this stage is the multiply model; everything added is the context-awareness.
The remaining stages refine that prediction in OKLab, each pulling it toward measured evidence: keeping lower color layers from washing out under what is stacked above them; for single-color stacks, reconciling the white cap against the base and leaning on direct measured sandwiches of that one color; and for two-color stacks, pulling the result toward the physically supported one-color endpoints it sits between.
The correction layer
On top of the staged prediction sits a correction layer — a final bounded adjustment learned from the calibration photos. It shifts the prediction toward patterns in the remaining measured error. Generator applies this layer as part of Color Model v2; there is no user-facing Color corrections switch. Color Model v1 uses its own pair-correction data instead.
These predicted colors fill the lookup table the solver searches (The Color LUT) and are compared in OKLab on the way to choosing layers in The Solve.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Color Model
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ColorModelThe Color LUT


The color model is Prisma’s calibrated account of how filaments behave when stacked and backlit: given a stack of specific filaments at specific thicknesses, it predicts the color that stack transmits. The solver’s color choices rest on these predictions, so the model’s accuracy sets the ceiling on how faithfully a print can reproduce an image. The filaments a run may draw from are its Palette, and their calibration comes from the active Model Library.
The question the model answers
A lithophane is a layered stack — a white base, zero or more colored layers, and a white cap — lit from behind. The model answers one question: given this stack, these filaments at these thicknesses, what color emerges? Prisma evaluates many allowed candidates while building The Color LUT, then reuses those predictions during recipe search. The same model also predicts completed solves for previews and diagnostics.
Two models behind one boundary
Prisma began with the transmission model, shown as Color Model v1 in Settings. Each filament has a transmission curve per color channel, measured at a handful of thicknesses from calibration swatches and interpolated smoothly between them; the base prediction for a stack is the per-channel product of its layers’ curves. The model also applies the active library’s calibrated two-color pair corrections when its candidate table is built. See The Transmission Model.
Real filaments interact in ways a pure product cannot express: white context changes how colored layers read, different colors influence one another, and layer order can matter. Prisma’s newer default, shown as Color Model v2, is the Photo-stack v2 model. It is fitted from photographs of printed stacks and carries terms for white context, color interaction, cap attenuation, and ordering, followed by the active library’s residual correction layer. See The photo-stack v2 model.
Both models answer the same question about a physical stack and return the same kind of predicted color. The advanced Appearance Model setting chooses which one supplies a run. Prisma also records which model and Model Library produced those predictions so results from different choices are not mixed. See Choosing a Color Model.
What this feeds
Evaluating the model one stack at a time is expensive, so Prisma samples the allowed palette, layer, and cap combinations and bakes the answers into a lookup table the solver can read quickly; that table is built next, in The Color LUT. The active Model Library’s Camera Transform converts model predictions into display colors for previews and maps source-image colors back into the model’s domain for Target Colors.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Export
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}White CapExportSTL / 3MF


Export is the final stage. By now the generator has solved the image into a material plan and capped the color with white. Export turns that completed result into a 3D model a slicer such as OrcaSlicer can open and print. Each export produces the chosen geometry package—individual STL files or a single 3MF—together with the information needed to review and print it.
From height maps to solid geometry
The solve describes the lithophane as a stack of materials: a flat white base beneath everything, the committed color recipes, and a white cap on top. Export turns those material layers into solid model objects and checks that they are suitable for slicing. Each color material and the cap rests on whatever lies beneath it, so the running floor rises in the solved print order. That order matters—especially for Color Model v2 (Photo-stack v2), whose prediction depends on layer context—and export preserves it. The physical image area comes from the solve-grid dimensions and pitch. When Border is enabled, its configured width extends the total exported footprint outward on every side.
A run with swaps (Runs with Swaps) adds two things. The white fill that tops each filament band up to its flat ceiling becomes real geometry — folded into the same white material as the cap, never a separate filament or file. And the stacking order stops being cosmetic: a mid-print swap is valid only if its band ends at one flat height everywhere, so the material order must match the solved swap plan exactly. Export enforces this — the order is checked against the plan, an audit confirms every band starts at its constant floor and every color stays inside its band, and a mismatch is refused rather than shipped.
Why the meshing must be careful
Naively triangulating a blocky height map produces a mesh that looks closed but is not reliably so. Where two raised regions meet at only a single corner or edge — a pinch contact — a slicer tends to weld the touching points and report a non-manifold solid, which can break slicing.
The generator therefore uses a rectilinear mesher designed for this kind of stepped field. It resolves each shared corner consistently, keeps touch-only contacts from being re-welded into pinches, and closes and orients each material shell before packaging it. When one body still fails a strict welded-mesh check, export can partition it into several same-material bodies. Any remaining failure is reported in the manifest rather than being silently called watertight.
Field-derived vs exact geometry
How the white cap surface is built is a choice — the Cap mesh type setting — and it is where the field-derived vs solve-grid distinction lives.
Exact raster builds every material, colors and cap alike, straight from the solve-grid height maps. It is faithful to the solve grid but inherits its blockiness, and Field density does not apply.
The default, Field-derived, rebuilds only the white cap from a sampled surface. At 1x it uses the solve grid’s spacing; higher densities use a finer grid. Field density offers 1x, 2x, 4x (default), 8x, and 16x. This lets the cap carry smoother tonal relief than the solve resolution alone would allow—which matters most for the cap’s fine detail (see White Cap)—while the colored geometry stays locked to the grid where its color decisions were made. Higher Field density changes the cap’s geometric resolution, not the solved color recipes.
The field-derived cap keeps white coverage over the colors while allowing a finer upper surface. Exact raster follows the stepped solve grid. In either case, white fill between swap bands uses the same filament as the cap, and one material may be divided into several mesh objects.
STL versus 3MF
Both formats describe the same geometry; they differ in how material is recorded. An STL carries only triangles, with no notion of material, so the STL export writes one file per object — white base, each color material, the cap, the border — into a shared folder, to be loaded together and assigned a filament by hand. A 3MF is a container that can record a material assignment per object: the 3MF export packs every object into one file and tags each with a filament slot, so the model opens with materials already assigned. The assignment is per object, not per print layer — every object is one filament — and objects printed in the same physical material, such as a shared white base and cap, collapse onto a single slot, so the slot count matches the real number of materials loaded. This is what lets a multicolor lithophane open ready to slice.
Alongside the geometry, export writes a manifest recording the content and total dimensions, every object’s material assignment and construction role, and its mesh-quality/build reports.
The swap-banded materials feeding this stage come from Runs with Swaps.
Illustration

Export turns each solved material map into a solid shell, preserves the true print order, and packages the same geometry as either STL objects or a material-aware 3MF.
