prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: How a Solve Works
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
A solve is the journey from a photograph to a completed material plan. You pick a source image and a palette of filaments, press Solve, and Prisma decides — at every point in the image — which filaments to stack and how thick each layer should be, so that when the finished panel is backlit it reproduces the picture. Export later turns that solved plan into printable files. This page walks the entire arc at a glance; each stage links down to the page that explains it properly.
The principle underneath is the one the whole system rests on: backlit filament behaves as a subtractive color filter, and thicker colored layers transmit less light, reading darker and more saturated. A solve is the search for the stack, at each location, whose transmitted color lands nearest the target while still being something a printer can build.
The arc, stage by stage
1. Condition the image and compute its targets. The source photo is first framed and graded, then passed through whichever Preprocessing modules are enabled to reduce noise or simplify hard-to-print detail. Prisma next converts the image into the Appearance Model’s color domain and maps out-of-gamut targets onto colors the chosen palette can reach. What comes out is a field of target colors — the goal the solve aims at. See Preprocessing and Target Colors.
2. Precompute what the palette can reach. The palette’s calibrated Appearance Model predicts the backlit color of the candidate stacks allowed by the run’s palette, layer, cap, and color-count limits. Those predictions are gathered into a lookup structure — the Color LUT. Because the main candidate search can read predicted colors from the table instead of repeatedly running the optical model, the solve can score many recipes cheaply. See The Transmission Model and The Color LUT.
3. Solve a recipe per color region. The solve does not choose each pixel independently — that would yield a speckled, unbuildable field. Instead it partitions the image into contiguous regions of similar target color and picks one filament recipe per region, balancing color fidelity against clean geometry: a recipe is penalized both for missing its region’s color and for leaving a tall height step against its neighbors, since a sharp height jump prints as a visible seam. Local refinements may then restore worthwhile detail inside a broader region. The result becomes the color portion of the run’s material plan.
4. Add the white cap. A white cap is built over the colored stacks. It sets overall brightness and diffuses the backlight, and it reinforces the structural shell every viewing surface needs. The Solve Mode setting governs how it is built: in Color mode the cap realizes the thickness chosen against the full target color, including lightness; in Luminance mode it adds a separate step based on the source image’s brightness, carrying tone and fine relief like a classic lithophane. See White Cap.
5. Include the swap plan when the palette exceeds the printer. If all colors fit, nothing extra is needed. Otherwise, before the final color recipes and cap are built, a scout solve measures how the image uses the palette. Prisma divides the colors among flat, white-filled filament bands that can be loaded in sequence. The final solve respects those bands and records the result in the material plan. See Runs with Swaps.
6. Export the print files. After the solve is complete, Export reads its material plan, builds the selected mesh representation, and writes an STL or 3MF model the slicer can open.
What the solve stores
The completed run keeps the settings used for the solve and the resolved material at every location. From that result, Prisma produces the per-filament thickness maps and diagnostics used for preview and inspection. Export uses the same completed plan, so later changes in the workspace do not alter the run.
Where to go next
The stages above are conceptual signposts; follow any of them into its own page for the detail. The color decisions themselves live in The Solve; the optics that make them possible in The Transmission Model.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Image Adjustments
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}SourceImageImageAdjustmentsPreprocessing


Image Adjustments are the alterations to a source image that modify it before it enters the lithophane generation pipeline. The appearance of the adjusted source image is what the pipeline will try to replicate in the finished, backlit lithophane. A source image is adjusted in two ways: its framing and its grading. The frame specifies what portion of the image is used, how it is oriented, and what size it will be when printed. The grade is the set of tonal and color transformations applied to the frame.
Adjusting a source image is purely about how the finished product should look. This is distinct from Preprocessing, where the image may instead be modified to suit the lithophane generation process itself, or to make the printed result more amenable to printing.
Adjustments are non-destructive
Image adjustments do not modify the source image file. Each setting is stored as a parameter. Prisma previews the adjustments while you work, then prepares the framed and adjusted image from the original when you request palette suggestions or a solve. Export uses the completed run’s stored result rather than rebuilding the image.
The frame
Beyond selecting which portion of the source image is used, the frame fixes how pixels on screen relate to the lithophane as a physical object. The frame’s dimensions are the physical dimensions of the image content. When Border is enabled, its Width extends the exported footprint outward on every side. A lithophane should not be rescaled in a slicer: scaling the model alters the layer thicknesses, and it is those thicknesses that produce the image, so a rescaled print no longer reproduces it.
The frame’s dimensions, together with the solve pitch — the physical spacing between the points the pipeline solves for — also fix the print-scale raster: the version of the image the pipeline actually operates on, and the one shown in the preview. Working at print scale keeps the pipeline from solving for detail finer than the printer can render. That raster can look slightly blocky, but the blockiness is an honest depiction of how the image will resolve once printed.
The grade
The grade first decodes sRGB bytes to linear RGB and keeps unclamped working values until the end. In Color mode its fixed sequence is:

Exposure, as RGB × 2^Exposure.
Contrast, using a symmetric curve on encoded sRGB channels, then returning to linear RGB. Positive values separate interior tones with a smooth approach to black and white; negative values draw them toward middle gray. Exact black, encoded middle gray, and white stay anchored at this step. This is an Affinity-like response, not an exact vendor reproduction or a hue-preserving transform.
Highlights and shadows, using smooth, monotone curves in perceptual luminance. Shadows reshape the dark half and Highlights the light half, with black, middle gray, and white held in place. Darkening scales color toward black; brightening blends color scaling with movement toward white, limited by available channel headroom.
Temperature and Tint, applied as Bradford-LMS channel gains from a smooth joint response. Positive Temperature moves toward amber/yellow; positive Tint toward magenta. The response is Affinity-informed, with modestly extended strength, not a Kelvin calibration or an exact vendor reproduction. Gains are calculated once per settings change, with no forced luminance normalization.
Saturation, by interpolating away from or toward Rec.709 luminance with factor 1 + 0.75 × Saturation. The symmetric slider range retains 25% to 175% of the linear-RGB color difference from gray, with 0 unchanged. Full grayscale is selected separately with B/W.

Contrast leaves working channels outside the display range unchanged, retaining Exposure’s headroom. Negative contrast does not recover over-white exposure values; reduce Exposure to bring them into range. The tone curves use a bounded copy of the working color to calculate their change, then add that change back to the original working values. Neither operation is global gamut compression or recovery of detail missing from the source.
In B/W mode, Prisma applies Exposure, converts to Rec.709 grayscale, then applies Contrast and Highlights/Shadows. Contrast therefore acts on the grayscale image, independent of its original color. Temperature, Tint, and Saturation are bypassed, although their stored values are preserved for a later return to Color mode.
The result is clamped once, encoded with the exact sRGB transfer function, and rounded to eight bits per channel. This adjusted image passes through Preprocessing and then into The Solve.
Existing nonzero Contrast settings retain their numeric values but render with the new curve. The original source and historical saved-run result images are not rewritten. Tonal anchors describe the isolated contrast step, not image-average brightness or the result of later color adjustments.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Palette
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PaletteThe Color LUTRuns withSwaps


A palette is the set of filaments chosen for a print. The Color Model can predict any stack of filaments, but a given lithophane draws only from its palette, plus the fixed white used for the base and the cap. The palette is the working set the rest of the pipeline is restricted to: The Color LUT enumerates only stacks the palette allows, and every solved recipe uses only its filaments.
What a palette holds
A palette is a small list of colored filaments together with the white assigned to the base and cap. The active printer reserves its configured base/cap slot or slots, so the simultaneous color capacity is the remaining slot count. When every color fits, it remains available throughout the print. A larger palette is marked May require filament swaps while it is being assembled; a full solve automatically plans Runs with Swaps when the palette exceeds that capacity. Restricting the prediction table and solve to the selected working set keeps the search tractable and the preview honest about what the print will actually use.
Palette suggestion
Choosing filaments by hand is hard, because the best palette for an image depends on how its colors combine when stacked, not only on which colors appear in it. Prisma can suggest a palette automatically from the source image.
The suggester works in the perceptual color space the solve uses. It first summarizes the image as a set of weighted color clusters — representative colors, each weighted by how much of the image it covers — so common colors count for more than rare ones. For each candidate filament it precomputes the colors that filament can produce alone, at every thickness and a sampled spread of caps. It then scores whole palettes: every combination of the allowed size is evaluated against the weighted clusters, and the best few are kept — only when the number of combinations grows very large does it fall back to a seeded greedy search refined by local swaps. Because stacked filaments make colors that neither makes alone — a cyan over a yellow yields greens — each palette’s reachable set includes sampled two-filament pairs, so a pair that unlocks a needed mixed color is credited for it. The finalists are then rescored once more with sparsely sampled three-filament stacks, so a color reachable only by mixing three filaments is credited before the final ranking.
The user chooses the exact number of palette colors and how many suggestions to create. Prisma searches palettes of that size and returns a ranked shortlist rather than choosing one automatically. Each candidate carries estimated coverage and color error; the ranking also accounts for severe local misses instead of considering only the average. An experimental option in Preferences → Palette applies that ranking to a denser set of sampled stacks for small palettes. The same Color and Luminance distinction used by the solve applies here: a Color suggestion aims directly at the photo’s colors, while a Luminance suggestion emphasizes vivid regions and largely leaves brightness structure to the white cap. By default, results first appear in the session-only Suggested Palettes area. Use Add to Deck to keep a suggestion in the Palette Deck, then select its card for a solve. Preferences → Palette can send new suggestions directly to the Deck instead.
Illustration

This illustration shows why broad color reach is not the same as useful coverage; its dots are not measured palette results. A palette tailored to the source image can place more reachable stack colors near the colors the image actually uses.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Preprocessing Modules
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
The five preprocessing modules, and what each one actually does to the image. Their fixed order is described on Preprocessing; the settings-drawer presets and fields are covered in Preprocessing Module Settings. All five are disabled in the Basic/default settings.
Noise Reduction
An edge-preserving smoother. Each pixel is replaced by a weighted average of its neighborhood, where a neighbor’s weight falls off with two distances at once: how far away it is, and how different its color is. Nearby, similar-colored pixels blend; pixels across a strong color edge contribute little. Grain and sensor noise — small, low-contrast fluctuations — average away while stronger boundaries are largely preserved.
The three fields map directly onto the mechanism: Filter radius sets the physical neighborhood size, Edge blending sets how readily differing neighboring colors are blended, and Spatial reach sets how quickly influence falls with physical distance. Filter radius and Spatial reach are expressed in millimeters so their physical meaning remains stable when Solve Pitch changes. A radius below Solve Pitch leaves the image unchanged; larger radii are rounded to whole solve-grid cells. The filter does not depend on the selected palette.
Print-Scale Smoothing
An edge-preserving filter with a fixed physical reach. Smoothing radius is measured in millimeters and stays unchanged when Solve Pitch or nozzle size changes. Only neighboring pixel centers within that radius are included; a radius below Solve Pitch leaves the image unchanged.
Smoothing radius ranges from 0.2 to 2 mm, with 0.1 mm adjustments. Higher values smooth larger details. Edge blending increases from Less to More, allowing more different neighboring colors to mix. Passes repeats the filter, strengthening smoothing and allowing indirect influence beyond the single-pass radius.
Flat-Area Smoothing
A total-variation smoother: it seeks an image that stays close to the source while minimizing the total amount of change from pixel to pixel. Minimizing that quantity has a characteristic effect — gradual texture and gentle gradients collapse into flat patches, while genuine edges, which are worth their cost, remain. At stronger settings the result reads as deliberately graphic, closer to a screen print than a photograph.
Strength is shown on a 0–100 scale. The scale rises more quickly at the high end: equal steps multiply the smoothing strength rather than adding a fixed amount. Low, Medium, and High presets use 15, 50, and 80. Zero is the minimum enabled strength; turn the module off to stop smoothing. Mode picks what gets flattened: Lightness smooths lightness rather than chroma; Light. & Chroma smooths lightness and color together. The Graphic preset uses High strength with Light. & Chroma. Prisma repeats the calculation up to 100 times and may stop sooner when the image stops changing.
Palette Tone Fit
The first palette-aware module. Prisma estimates the palette’s printable dark-to-light range from sampled stacks; a photograph usually spans more. Rather than letting the out-of-range tones clip, this module remaps the image’s lightness into that range with a smooth three-anchor curve: the image’s shadow and highlight anchors — set as percentiles of its lightness distribution via Shadow anchor and Highlight anchor — map onto the estimated black and white, with a midpoint whose placement Midtone curve bends lighter or darker. Beyond the anchors the mapping continues linearly and clamps at those limits.
The fit changes lightness rather than chroma. Very saturated colors can still shift when the adjusted color falls outside the image’s RGB range and must be clipped. Strength blends between the original and the remapped lightness, from no effect at 0 to the full fit at 100. With a palette whose tonal range collapses to one value, the module does nothing. The preview needs a selected palette to show the fit.
Palette Saturation Fit
A palette’s reachable saturation is not one number: it varies with hue and with lightness — a palette can be rich in reds and starved in cyans, and richer in the midtones than in the shadows. This module reads the palette’s map of maximum reachable saturation across hue and lightness, and for each pixel looks up the bound at that pixel’s own hue and lightness, interpolating around the hue wheel and across the lightness range. The bound is biased high to avoid compressing colors that are already within useful reach; anything still beyond the palette’s true reach is handled later by gamut mapping.
Below Compression start — a fraction of that local limit — colors pass through unchanged. Above it, saturation is reduced without exceeding the palette’s limit or increasing the original saturation. Softness controls both the breadth of the transition and how much saturation is kept: lower values pull affected colors farther inward, while higher values keep them closer to the limit. At Compression start 100, colors beyond the limit are clipped to it and Softness has no effect. Only saturation is changed in perceptual color space, so an over-vivid color moves inward rather than shifting toward another hue. A palette with no usable saturation information leaves the image untouched.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ImageAdjustmentsPreprocessingTargetColorsNoiseReductionPrint-ScaleSmoothingFlat-AreaSmoothingPaletteTone FitPaletteSaturation Fit


Preprocessing is an optional step before solving. It occurs after Image Adjustments and before the image is reduced to a set of Target Colors. Its modules modify the image to make it better suited for conversion into a lithophane: they either simplify fine color variation, or adjust the image’s tone and color to better match the chosen palette. Whether preprocessing should be used at all — and with what settings — depends on the source image and on user preference. By default, no modules are enabled.
The mismatch it resolves
A stack of translucent filament, backlit, can reproduce only a limited range of color and brightness, and detail only down to the size of a printed feature. A photograph routinely exceeds all three: colors more saturated than any stack can make, a contrast range wider than a panel can transmit, and sensor noise and fine texture that can become visible speckle. Preprocessing brings the image closer to what the print can carry before the solver chooses recipes.
Preprocessing modules
Five modules are available, in two groups.
Reducing spatial detail the print cannot carry:

Noise Reduction — removes small image noise so color regions come out less fragmented.
Print-Scale Smoothing — smooths features within a physical radius, yielding larger, simpler color regions.
Flat-Area Smoothing — flattens gradual texture into broad areas, a more graphic look at stronger settings.

Fitting tone and color to the palette:

Palette Tone Fit — compresses the image’s tonal range into the range the palette can reproduce.
Palette Saturation Fit — softly pulls colors the palette cannot reach inward, preserving hue.

How each module actually transforms the image is explained in Preprocessing Modules.
The preprocessing chain
Any number of modules may be enabled at once. When several are, they run in the fixed order shown in Settings: Noise Reduction, Print-Scale Smoothing, Flat-Area Smoothing, Palette Tone Fit, then Palette Saturation Fit, regardless of the order in which they were enabled. Each receives the previous module’s result. Preprocessing never modifies the source image; its result is passed to Target Colors.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Runs with Swaps/index.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Runs with Swaps
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PaletteRuns withSwapsThe Color LUT


A normal run keeps every colored filament loaded from the first color layer to the last. When the palette exceeds the active printer’s color slots, Prisma instead divides those filaments among a sequence of fixed-height bands. Add the listed pauses in the slicer so the printer stops at each band boundary and the next set of colors can be loaded.
Planning happens automatically during the solve. There is no user-facing planning choice and no alternate swap method. Swap runs currently support at most 10 colored filaments, excluding the base and cap, and Palette Saturation Fit must be off. The thickness budget must allow at least one color layer per band.
Why the bands must be flat
A slicer pause occurs at one Z height across the entire panel. The lower set of filaments therefore has to finish at the same height everywhere before any slot can be reassigned.
The colored stacks do not naturally end on a flat plane. Prisma fills the unused height inside each band with the same white used for the cap. Every point then reaches the band’s fixed ceiling, making the next set of colors physically printable above it.
That white fill is also the central compromise. It reduces the light passing through the color stack and can change its color balance. The bands consume part of Max Thickness as well, leaving less freedom for the cap and color recipes. A swap run is therefore more constrained than an otherwise identical run with every color continuously available; it cannot improve the underlying optical search space, even when the larger palette makes the final result better than a smaller no-swap palette.
The scout solve
Prisma cannot choose useful band heights from filament names alone. It first performs a reduced-resolution scout solve with the full palette and no bands. The scout estimates how much of each filament the image wants and where those thicknesses occur.
The palette is already in the canonical dark-first print order. Prisma considers valid ways to assign those filaments to the available color slots across the required number of bands. Each candidate band’s height is estimated from almost all of its active scout usage and quantized to whole printed layers. The chosen plan minimizes total band height first and predicted white fill second. If the planned bands exceed the available thickness, their heights are reduced to fit before the final solve.
This is why filaments that are heavily used in different parts of the image may share a compact band, while filaments that need to stack thickly in the same places tend to require more height.
The final constrained solve
The scout does not become the printed result. Once the band plan is fixed, Prisma builds new color lookup tables whose recipes obey those bands and already include the required white fill. The full-resolution solve then runs against those tables.
Including the fill during the final solve matters: the solver evaluates the color that the physically printable, white-filled stack will transmit. It does not solve an unconstrained image and patch the bands in afterward.
The completed run stores the band assignments, their exact layer counts, and the resulting pause heights. That plan is part of the run just like its palette and cap settings.
From bands to Print Instructions
Each pause height is the white-base thickness plus the completed band heights below it. When Prisma generates print files, the resulting export record presents Print Instructions derived from the stored plan:

the initial filament assigned to each slot;
the Z height for every slicer pause;
which filament to unload and load in each affected slot; and
which slots remain unchanged.

Export presents and validates the plan; it does not optimize it again. The selected run keeps the printer and slot capacity used for its solve even if the current drawer changes later. To print on a different material-system configuration, solve again with that configuration and generate a new export.
The practical workflow and its trade-offs are covered in Runs with Swaps under How To Use. The stored bands then flow into Export like any other solved geometry.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Settings/Color Solver.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Settings: Color Solver
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Color Solver settings control the appearance model and recipe matching, the initial color regions, and the later corrections to those initial decisions. The drawer presents three core controls followed by Color Matching, Region Planning, and Region Refinement.
Core controls and Color Matching
The Appearance Model supplies predicted colors for candidate stacks and is also used by palette suggestions, previews, diagnostics, and the white-cap response. Max colors/region limits how many distinct colored filaments one recipe may contain, reducing or expanding the choices before matching begins. Adapt image to palette optionally changes the target colors according to the selected materials: White adaptation moves them relative to the predicted base/cap white, while Color adaptation adjusts colors across the image toward those available from printable palette recipes. The two strengths are independent, and the palette and available recipes themselves do not change.
OOG handling changes unreachable target colors before recipe matching. Closest color moves them toward the nearest part of the palette’s reachable color range; recipe selection follows afterward. Preserve hue reduces saturation, and adjusts lightness only when necessary, so the target moves without rotating to another hue. Mismatch tolerance decides when that change is required. Chroma bias then changes the relative importance of brightness and color accuracy during matching; it does not alter the source image. A value of 0 is balanced, positive values favor color, and negative values favor tone. Each increase of 1 doubles the color weighting; each decrease of 1 halves it.
Region Planning
The same image can be partitioned three ways before recipes are chosen:

Follow edges permits unequal, irregular regions. Strong image structure tends to become a region boundary, while locally similar areas can stay together over a larger span.
Compact produces compact, approximately even regions whose borders can still bend around image edges. It offers a more regular patchwork than Follow edges without becoming independent of the picture.
Fixed grid assigns uniform square planning cells. It is predictable and structurally simple, but an image edge has no influence on where a cell ends.

Region size sets the intended physical width of these initial regions. Prisma raises it when necessary to meet the printer’s minimum line length and Extrusion Width. Planning scale builds the initial map on a coarser image and expands it back to the solve grid, trading edge accuracy for broader regions and faster planning.
Region Refinement
When Protect neutral areas is enabled, Prisma revisits neighboring weakly colored regions whose source colors are already nearly identical. It discourages recipes from creating larger color differences than the source supports. It also penalizes excess saturation, so a falsely colorful recipe cannot spread just because it gives neighboring regions the same color. Any replacement must stay close to the region’s original best match. Low, Medium, and High change how much source color is included in this protection. Neutral chroma cutoff gives direct control; a value that differs from the presets is labeled Custom.
This correction chooses from the recipes already considered for each region. If none are suitably muted, it can choose the best available compromise but cannot create a missing recipe.
Regions are initial commitments, not permanent walls. Local corrections can replace small areas inside a region when another recipe improves the target match enough; printability checks then grow useful corrections into printable shapes or return them to the surrounding region.
Boundary mutation
Boundary mutation operates after the initial region recipes and local corrections. Each solve point along a recipe boundary tests the recipes directly beside it, above, below, left, or right. If a neighboring recipe reduces that point’s predicted color error, the point becomes part of a possible boundary change.
Changes are accepted as connected patches along a boundary rather than isolated points. Min color gain requires a patch’s average improvement to clear the chosen threshold, so weak changes are rejected even when an individual point appears better.
One pass can move a recipe boundary by one solve point. Passes limits how often Prisma repeats this step against the changed map, allowing a contour to advance farther while stopping early when nothing else improves. Mutation never invents a new stack: every accepted point borrows a recipe already present directly beside it.
For the drawer controls and day-to-day guidance, see Color Solver Settings.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Settings/Essentials.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Settings: Essentials
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
The Essentials settings establish the print’s physical limits. They determine the grid the image is sampled onto, how thickness becomes printed layers, and how much space remains for color and the white cap.
Solve Pitch and the working grid
Solve Pitch is the physical spacing between neighboring solve points. Prisma expresses it as a whole multiple of the active Extrusion Width, with one Extrusion Width as the minimum. Together with the framed print dimensions, it determines the width and height of the working image. A smaller pitch creates more points and can preserve finer image structure, but gives the solver more work at each step. Image sampling and solving use the same grid.
In Color Solver’s Region Planning, Region size is independent of Solve Pitch. Pitch says how far apart solve points are; Region size says how large an area should normally share an initial recipe decision. Prisma keeps that area large enough to meet the active printer’s minimum feature size.
The vertical budget
Max Thickness is a ceiling shared by the white base, colored layers, boundary cap, and detail cap. Increasing it can make more color recipes available and leave more room for the cap. A thicker color stack leaves less room above it; a thicker required cap narrows the color-plus-cap combinations that fit.
Base Thickness is spent first and uniformly. Cap Thickness then requests a physical amount of continuous white coverage above every color stack. Prisma resolves that request to the closest whole-layer thickness at the current Layer Height, favoring the thicker choice for an exact tie. The remaining height is available for color and additional cap relief. The white base is constant across the panel.
Layer Height sets the thickness steps
The solver expresses printable thicknesses as whole layers. Layer Height therefore defines the vertical step size of every recipe and cap decision, not only an export preference. A smaller value offers more possible optical thicknesses within the same budget; a larger value makes the set coarser. Slicing at a different layer height changes the physical recipe and invalidates the predicted color.
White materials and Solve Mode
The selected Base/Cap filament supplies calibrated optical behavior to the Color Model. White is not treated as a neutral mathematical constant: its measured transmission influences every predicted stack and the Luminance-mode cap response.
Solve Mode chooses how Prisma uses the colored recipes and white cap to reproduce the image. Color and Luminance share the same initial color targets and sequence of steps, but allow different combinations of color and cap thickness and divide the image’s light-and-dark variation between the colored layers and cap differently. See Solve Modes for the full mechanism.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Settings/Preprocessing.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Settings: Preprocessing
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Preprocessing settings alter the print-scale image before Target Colors are built. They do not change the source file, and they do not repair a solve afterward. Their purpose is to remove image variation the print cannot carry or to move the image toward the selected palette before recipes are chosen.
Two kinds of intervention
Noise Reduction, Print-Scale Smoothing, and Flat-Area Smoothing change spatial variation. Noise Reduction uses color and distance to average small fluctuations while retaining strong edges. Print-Scale Smoothing uses an exact physical radius in millimeters, independent of nozzle size and Solve Pitch. Flat-Area Smoothing instead minimizes gradual pixel-to-pixel variation, producing broad patches at stronger settings.
Palette Tone Fit and Palette Saturation Fit are palette-aware. Tone Fit remaps image lightness into the palette’s estimated printable dark-to-light range rather than directly changing chroma. Saturation Fit applies a soft knee at the palette’s hue- and lightness-dependent saturation boundary, pulling over-vivid colors inward while preserving hue and lightness.
How each module works and what its individual fields do are covered in Preprocessing Modules.
Fixed order, independent enablement
Modules are independently enabled, but their execution order is fixed:
Noise Reduction → Print-Scale Smoothing → Flat-Area Smoothing → Palette Tone Fit → Palette Saturation Fit
This order first removes unwanted spatial variation, then fits the surviving image to the palette. Each preset sets the individual fields for one module. Advanced reveals those fields; editing them changes the label to Custom when they no longer match a preset. It does not change the module’s place in the chain.
Resample kernel
The Resample kernel acts before the module chain when the framed image is sampled onto the solve grid. Lanczos retains more fine contrast and therefore gives the modules a sharper image. Area averages source pixels over each destination point when reducing an image, producing a softer result with fewer sampling artifacts. Once the print-scale image exists, all enabled modules operate on that same grid.
For when to enable each module and practical starting values, see Preprocessing Module Settings.
Comparing the modules

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Settings/White Cap.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Settings: White Cap
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
White Cap settings divide the available white thickness between a continuous surface and localized additional relief. Cap thickness affects the predicted appearance and shares the same thickness limit as the colored recipes.
Cap thickness
Cap Thickness, configured in Essentials, is a requested physical dimension. Prisma resolves it to the closest whole number of layers at the current Layer Height, chooses the thicker result when the request is exactly halfway between two layer counts, and enforces at least one white layer above every color stack. This printable thickness belongs to the continuous boundary cap.
Boundary Cap
In Color mode, Upper surface style chooses how the upper surface is shaped:

Image Aware begins with the cap thickness that gives each point its best predicted appearance, then allows smoothing within Appearance budget. It keeps enough continuous white coverage above the colors and leaves more localized correction to the detail cap.
Smooth prioritizes a clean, continuous upper surface. Smoothing radius sets the physical neighborhood over which the upper surface is smoothed; image and recipe edges reduce that smoothing locally. The underside still follows the color stacks exactly.

Luminance mode uses the Smooth boundary cap because that surface carries broad light-and-dark variation from the image. The drawer therefore hides Upper surface style and its Image-Aware-only Appearance budget in Luminance mode. The Settings Profile retains the Color surface choice while it is hidden, including when saved with a solve; returning to Color uses that stored choice. Smoothing radius remains active in either mode.
Detail Cap
Max detail layers sets the maximum number of whole white layers Prisma may add above the boundary cap; it is a limit, not a requested thickness. At each point Prisma keeps an added layer only when the Appearance Model predicts an improvement, and later printability checks may remove or enlarge features. A value of zero leaves no additional layers to place. The continuous boundary cap remains.
In Luminance mode, Shading balance divides the image’s light-and-dark variation between the smooth boundary cap and the detail cap. Moving toward Smooth lets the broad surface carry more of that variation; moving toward Detail leaves more for localized relief.
The complete cap construction, including Color and Luminance differences, is described in White Cap. For operational guidance, see White Cap Settings.
The thickness budget

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Settings/index.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Settings: How They Work
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Some settings establish the print’s physical limits, some transform the image before solving, and others alter how recipes, regions, and the white cap are constructed. The Settings drawer explains what to choose; these pages explain what each group changes and why its tradeoffs appear in the result.
The pages follow the four sections below Profile in the drawer:

Settings: Essentials — the physical grid, thickness budget, printed layers, white materials, and Solve Mode.
Settings: Preprocessing — resampling, the fixed module chain, and the distinction between spatial simplification and palette fitting.
Settings: Color Solver — the core model controls, Color Matching, Region Planning, and Region Refinement.
Settings: White Cap — Boundary Cap, Detail Cap, smoothing, and Luminance-mode Shading balance.

When settings take effect
Each solve keeps a copy of the settings it started with. Changes in the drawer apply to the next solve and cannot alter a solve already in progress or a result already stored. Settings profiles save and restore your choices.
A profile also remembers values for disabled features and for the other solve mode. Those values become useful again when you enable the feature or change modes; their presence in a saved profile does not mean they affected a particular result. The run’s details show the settings that apply to that run.
Every solve uses the Camera Transform and checks color regions and white-cap features for printability. The detail cap is also considered on every solve, within its layer limit. Settings change how these steps work, but do not turn the checks off.
For the operational controls, profile workflow, and recommended starting values, see Settings.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Target Colors/Camera Transform.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Camera Transform
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
The Camera Transform is the calibrated bridge between two ways of describing a color: the linear RGB value a filament stack produces in the active library’s model domain, and the display sRGB appearance of that backlit stack. Prisma crosses between the two to show a predicted print on screen and to translate a source image into targets the model can match. The transform ties both crossings to the calibration photographs used to fit the library.
Two directions
The transform is defined in the forward direction: given a model-domain stack prediction, it produces the display color that prediction appears as. This is what turns a solve into the on-screen backlit preview.
Its inverse runs the other way: given a display color, it estimates the model-domain value that would appear as that color. This is what Translating Image Colors uses to carry each source pixel into the model’s coordinates, so targets and predictions can be compared in the same terms. Prisma prepares the inverse in advance so it can translate an image efficiently.
How it is calibrated
The transform is fitted from calibration data — printed swatches photographed under the backlight — so it captures the response of that capture setup rather than an idealized camera. It combines a flexible color correction with smooth per-channel adjustments. Calibration stores one current working transform. Generator sees it only after the required model families and filament catalog are published together as a new immutable library, and keeps using its selected library until you explicitly activate another one.
Because source targets enter through the inverse and displayed predictions leave through the forward transform, its calibration affects both matching and preview fidelity. It is the link between model-domain reasoning and what a viewer sees.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/Target Colors/Gamut mapping.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Gamut Mapping
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
With a given set of filaments, only so many colors can be made by stacking them and shining light through. That reachable set is the palette’s gamut, and a source image may ask for colors outside it — a saturated neon, a deep electric blue, or a vivid orange that no sampled stack of these backlit filaments can closely match. Gamut mapping runs before recipe selection: it flags targets that are too far from the recipe table, then moves them according to the selected strategy when that strategy finds a better target. A flagged target may remain unchanged when the default hull route finds that it is already inside the continuous hull; final recipe lookup still chooses its nearest sampled stack.
Doing this first makes the compromise deliberate. Without gamut handling, recipe lookup would still choose its best sampled candidate for a distant target, but the selected trade-off would emerge only at lookup time. Gamut handling makes the intended trade-off explicit before that search.
Where the boundary is
The reachable set is not abstract: it is sampled by The Color LUT, a bounded catalog of candidate filament stacks and the color each one produces. A target counts as reachable when some catalog color lies within a small tolerance of it; a target farther than that from every sampled color is flagged as out of gamut. The catalog’s outer surface — the convex hull of those colors in OKLab — provides the boundary used by the default mode below. The print’s white is predicted separately by the Choosing a Color Model.
Two ways to compromise
The OOG handling setting picks the strategy, and the two differ in what they protect:

Closest color (the default) moves an outside target toward the gamut’s outer surface in three-dimensional OKLab. Prisma approaches that surface in a limited number of steps, so the result is an approximation of the closest reachable color. All three axes can move. A flagged target that already sits inside the hull is left in place — pushing it outward to the boundary would invent a more saturated color — and the solver’s own nearest-color matching handles it instead.
Preserve hue pulls the color inward along a ray toward gray, scaling its vividness down by a single factor — the hue never shifts. Lightness holds too, except when the target is darker or lighter than the sampled range, in which case it moves only as far as needed to enter that range. It never makes a target worse: if no point along the ray comes within tolerance, the target is replaced only if the best point found still improves it. This protects hue and, as far as possible, lightness at the cost of muting strongly saturated regions.

Both modes build the same out-of-gamut flag: a target is flagged when no discrete printable recipe-table color lies within the allowed tolerance, measured as plain color difference (the Chroma bias setting does not bend this test). That tolerance is the Mismatch tolerance setting. The modes differ in how they attempt to improve a flagged target, and the hull route additionally requires geometric hull violation before it moves the target.
Adapting the image to the palette
Separately, Adapt image to palette can transform the target colors according to the selected materials. It is off by default, and its two strengths are independent.
White adaptation maps ideal source white toward the model’s prediction for the thinnest printable white-only stack. It briefly round-trips the targets through linear RGB for per-channel scaling, then returns them to OKLab before the first gamut-mapping pass. 0× leaves this part unchanged, 1× applies the modeled white adjustment, and larger values apply it more strongly.
Color adaptation fits one global chromatic transform between the image’s target-color distribution and the empirical colors of all legal recipes for the current palette. It moves the target points rather than changing the palette, recipe catalog, or OKLab itself. The transform preserves target lightness before gamut handling, is applied after the ordinary gamut-mapping pass, and is followed by another pass through the selected out-of-gamut strategy. 0× leaves this part unchanged; larger multipliers move farther along the fitted transformation.
These adaptations deliberately change what Prisma asks the solver to reproduce. They can make an image more internally coherent with a difficult palette even when its literal error against the original source increases. Gamut mapping still runs just before the layers are solved — see The Solve.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Translating Image Colors
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
The colors in a source photo are not the colors the solver should aim for. They have to be translated first. This page covers that translation and why it exists.
Two color domains
Everything Prisma knows about its filaments comes from calibrated samples, including printed stacks photographed under a backlight. The active model therefore predicts colors in its own model domain rather than in ordinary screen color. The solve compares targets and predictions only after both are expressed in that shared domain.
A source photo enters Prisma as display sRGB, the standard screen-oriented encoding used by the Generator. Taken at face value its numbers would point the solver at the wrong targets, because the filament model does not predict display sRGB. The two domains do not coincide.
Pulling the photo in
After Prisma loads, frames, resamples, and adjusts the source—and, for a solve, after any enabled preprocessing modules run—it translates every pixel from display sRGB into the model domain. It uses a 33×33×33 color table, interpolating between its entries to reverse the calibrated Camera Transform. Where the Camera Transform carries a model-domain color out to its photographed display appearance, this translation runs that mapping backward to carry a display color in. Prisma can then compare the image’s colors with the filament model’s predictions in OKLab.
Every solve and automatic palette suggestion uses the active library’s color table. There is no setting to disable this translation.
Coming back out
The reverse direction matters for previews. The solve produces colors in the model domain, which are not meant to be displayed directly, so a preview of what the lit print will look like runs the prediction forward through the Camera Transform. Prisma applies this conversion when it creates the preview images. The selected color model supplies the prediction; the Camera Transform converts it for display.
Both directions come from one calibrated Camera Transform built by Calibration. Generator checks that the published library contains complete, matching transform data. If that data is missing or damaged, it cannot use the library. Install a valid published library or publish one again from Calibration. Both directions are explained in Camera Transform.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: OKLab
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
The solver repeatedly has to answer one question: how far is this candidate stack’s color from the target color? Distance between raw red, green, and blue values is a poor judge of that, because equal steps in RGB do not look equally different to the eye. A small numeric gap in one part of the range can be conspicuous while a larger gap elsewhere is hard to see.
OKLab is a perceptual color space built so that equal numeric distance corresponds to roughly equal perceived difference. Every color becomes a point on three axes — one lightness axis and two color-opponent axes — arranged so that the straight-line distance between two points tracks how different they look. The transform from linear RGB is fixed: a 3×3 matrix into an intermediate cone-response space, a cube-root compression, and a second 3×3 matrix out. Lightness here runs on a 0–1 scale, not the 0–100 of textbook Lab.
Why the solver lives here
Putting both sides into OKLab makes nearest-color lookup practical. Prisma converts the image’s targets into OKLab up front and stores each sampled candidate stack’s predicted color in OKLab too — that is what fills The Color LUT. Plain, unweighted Euclidean distance is the base color-difference measure and is used for gamut flags and reported quality:
\Delta E = \sqrt{(\Delta L)^2 + (\Delta a)^2 + (\Delta b)^2}
The solve’s source quality measure uses that distance between each target and the solved stack’s predicted color. The interface reports its root-mean-square as RMSE % — the RMS distance times 100 — so a raw OKLab error of 0.03 displays as about 3%. Lower means a closer color match under this metric.
The one control that bends the metric
By default the three axes count equally. The Chroma bias control changes candidate lookup: positive values reduce the influence of lightness relative to the two color axes, prioritizing chroma accuracy over tone when candidates compete; negative values do the reverse. Each increase of one doubles the relative color weighting; each decrease of one halves it. The control does not change the unweighted out-of-gamut test or the reported quality metric, so those diagnostics remain comparable across Chroma bias settings.
A caution on comparing numbers
This is the Generator’s yardstick. Do not compare its RMSE % directly with a differently named Calibration statistic unless that view explicitly says it uses the same OKLab distance and scale. Within Generator, RMSE % provides a consistent way to compare color error.
The space underlies everything the solver touches: how targets first arrive (Translating Image Colors), what happens when one cannot be reached (Gamut mapping), and how recipes are scored (The Solve).

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PreprocessingTargetColorsThe Solve


After Preprocessing, the image is still an sRGB array — a description of how to render the picture on a screen. That on-screen appearance is the goal: it is what the lithophane should look like when backlit. The solver must reproduce it, but it cannot operate on screen colors directly. This stage turns each pixel into a target the solver can match, through a change of domain and a change of metric, then handles targets that exceed the active palette’s sampled reach.
The model domain
The color model is built from calibration data — printed swatches photographed under a backlight. It does not reason directly in screen colors; it predicts a linear RGB value in the active library’s model domain. For the current photo-stack model, that value is the model’s flatfield-normalized output. Older models describe a closely related transmission value. A screen sRGB value is neither one, so each pixel must be carried into the same model domain before the model can be asked to match it.
Every image goes through this conversion. It applies the inverse of the library’s calibrated Camera Transform — the mapping that turns a model-domain prediction into a displayed, backlit-looking color, run backward. After conversion, the targets and the model’s predictions use the same coordinates, so the solver can compare them consistently. See Translating Image Colors.
Perceptual distance
The solver selects recipes by minimizing color difference, and raw model-domain coordinates are a poor yardstick for that: equal numeric steps do not correspond to equal perceived change. So the targets are re-expressed in OKLab, a space constructed so that straight-line distance roughly tracks perceived difference. The model’s catalog of predicted stack colors is expressed in the same OKLab space, so color comparisons use one perceptual coordinate system. See OKLab.
Handling palette limits
A palette of real filaments can produce only a bounded set of colors — its gamut — and a vivid target may fall outside it. Before recipe selection, Prisma flags targets farther than the allowed tolerance from every sampled catalog color and applies the selected compromise. Closest color moves an outside target toward the palette’s reachable boundary, while a target already inside that boundary can remain unchanged for recipe selection. Preserve hue reduces chroma toward gray while holding hue fixed and changes lightness only when needed. Optional Adapt image to palette processing can also move the target colors according to the selected white filament and the colors of legal palette recipes. Its independent White adaptation and Color adaptation strengths control those two influences. See Gamut mapping.
The resulting model-domain colors, expressed in OKLab, form the target cloud the solver uses during recipe selection and refinement.
Illustration

Each source pixel is pulled through the inverse Camera Transform into the model domain, re-expressed in OKLab, and prepared with gamut handling and any enabled palette adaptation.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: The Color LUT
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PaletteColorModelRuns withSwapsThe Color LUTThe Solve


Before matching the photo, Prisma enumerates the candidate stacks permitted by the Palette and the run’s color-count, layer, cap, and thickness limits. It predicts the color each candidate transmits and stores the results in a lookup table. With that catalog built, the main candidate search can find nearby printable stacks without repeatedly evaluating the optical model.
The motivation is cost. A solve poses the same kind of color query at many points and regions. Building the catalog once converts those repeated requests into fast nearest-neighbor lookups. Later stages may precompute a smaller set of cap-appearance curves for selected recipes, but those results are reused rather than recalculated while building the white cap.
What an entry holds
Each entry is one printable candidate — which colored filaments are present, the thickness of each, and the thickness of the white cap — paired with the predicted color in the perceptual space the solver searches (see Color Model). The cap is stored jointly with the colored layers rather than chosen in a later pass: because the cap affects brightness, a single entry describes which filaments, at what thicknesses, under how much cap. The white base beneath is fixed, so its effect is folded identically into every entry; only the cap and colored layers vary.
Building the catalog
Prisma enumerates filament subsets — one filament, two, and small stacks up to Max colors/region. For each subset it steps through cap thicknesses, and for each cap through the colored-layer assignments that fit within the run’s layer and total-thickness budgets. Each candidate is composed through the active Color Model and expressed in perceptual color space. Color Model v1 uses the transmission model and its pair corrections; Color Model v2 uses the Photo-stack v2 model and its residual corrections. These corrections are part of the Generator’s active Appearance Model rather than a user-facing on/off setting.
Two refinements keep the catalog lean. Many distinct stacks land on nearly the same color, so Prisma retains one entry per color cell for each filament combination, preferring the stack that uses the least colored material and breaking ties toward the thinner cap, which reads brighter. The advanced Chroma bias setting also changes the trade-off between color accuracy and lightness: positive values prioritize color more strongly, while negative values favor tone.
Caching
Building the catalog can take time, so Prisma saves the finished table for
reuse. It can reuse that table while the model, palette, and physical solve
limits that determine its candidates remain the same; changing one of those
inputs causes a rebuild. A larger palette, or more colors allowed per region,
enlarges the table and can slow that first build.
How the solve uses it
The solve first queries target colors across the image to seed a practical candidate set. It then chooses among those recipes for coherent regions, considering color error, neighboring heights, and later refinements rather than accepting each point’s nearest stack independently. See The Solve.
Illustration

Prisma evaluates each printable candidate once, stores its stack and predicted color together, then answers the solve’s repeated color queries with nearest-neighbor lookups.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Solve Modes
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Prisma offers two Solve Modes, chosen under Essentials in Settings: Color (the default) and Luminance. What differs directly is how the white cap is shaped — and as a result, how the print carries brightness and fine detail. The color solver, its targets, and its recipe table are the same machinery in both modes; but because Luminance mode reserves part of the height budget for the cap, the recipe table is built over a narrower range of cap thicknesses and the chosen recipes can come out different (see below).
The fundamental difference
The white cap sets a print’s brightness, and the two modes derive its thickness from different sources.
In Color, the cap is a product of the color solve. For each region the solver chooses a cap thickness jointly with its color recipe against the full target color, including lightness, and the cap realizes those solved heights. Unlike Luminance mode, Color mode does not add a separate step based on the source image’s brightness.
In Luminance, the cap follows brightness in the prepared target colors, including any changes made by preprocessing, gamut handling, or palette adaptation. Prisma normalizes that brightness range and assigns thicker white to darker areas. The white filament’s measured response and Shading balance set the overall limit for the smooth cap. The result is split in two: a smooth boundary cap carrying the broad tone, held below a brightness-derived local ceiling so it does not consume the whole height budget, and a detail cap of extra white layers placed wherever they measurably improve the predicted result, carrying fine relief the boundary cap cannot. A print made in Luminance mode reads partly like a classic relief lithophane — tone encoded as white thickness — layered on top of color.
The two modes therefore do not necessarily produce identical recipes. Luminance mode reserves a share of the height budget for the white cap. This overall cap limit comes from the white filament’s measured response and Shading balance, before the image’s brightness sets local cap heights. The reserved thickness is included when Prisma considers recipes. It narrows the range of cap thicknesses each color stack may be paired with, so fewer color-plus-cap combinations fit under the total-thickness ceiling and the best reachable recipe can differ from the one selected in Color mode.
What switching modes changes
Choosing a Solve Mode changes how Prisma builds the cap. Selecting Luminance uses the source image’s brightness and a smooth boundary cap; selecting Color uses the cap thicknesses chosen with the color recipes. Prisma checks that the cap is printable in both modes. Because of this, several controls appear, disappear, or change meaning with the mode:

Shading balance — visible only in Luminance, and the only luminance-specific knob exposed. It sets whether the broad luminance shading is carried more by the smooth boundary cap or by fine detail-cap relief: higher values put more shading in the smooth cap, lower values reserve more for fine relief. (A 0–100 slider between Detail and Smooth, default 75.)
Upper surface style — Image Aware (default) or Smooth — is a Color-mode control; in Luminance it is hidden and forced to Smooth. See White Cap.
Max detail layers — shown in both modes: the most extra white layers the detail cap may add above the boundary cap.
Smoothing radius and Appearance Model — meaningful in both modes. Smoothing radius smooths the boundary cap’s top surface in either mode; the Appearance Model (the color model used for lookups and previews) also drives the luminance cap’s response in Luminance mode.

How the cap is constructed in each mode
In Color, the boundary cap realizes the per-region cap heights the color solve already chose. By default (Image Aware) it keeps that boundary structural and preserves the solved appearance — departing from the cap thicknesses chosen by the color solve only as far as the Appearance budget in predicted color allows — and leaves optional fine relief to the detail stage; the alternative, Smooth, instead smooths the solved heights into one continuous outer surface. The detail stage may then add whole white layers, up to Max detail layers, where they measurably improve the predicted result; zero extra layers remains valid.
In Luminance, the boundary cap follows the image’s broad luminance, clamped down to an image-derived ceiling — with Shading balance governing how much of the tone the smooth cap carries versus the detail cap — to leave budget for detail. The detail cap then searches, point by point, for how many extra white layers (up to Max detail layers) most improve the predicted color and brightness. That relief must fit within the available height and the printer’s minimum feature size. The mechanics of both caps are detailed in White Cap.
Export does not apply a second mode-specific cap solve. It reads the cap already recorded in the material plan and uses the selected mesh method to turn the recorded cap heights into a printable shape — see Export.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: The Solve
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}TargetColorsThe Color LUTThe SolveWhite Cap


The solve is where a prepared image becomes a printable plan. Given the per-point color targets from Target Colors and a palette of calibrated filaments, it decides, at every point in the image, which filaments to stack and how thick each should be, so the backlit panel reproduces the photo. Thicker colored layers transmit less light and read darker and more saturated; the solve is the search for the stack that lands nearest each target while remaining something a printer can build.
It does not decide each point independently — that would yield a speckled, unbuildable field of single-point recipe changes. Instead it runs as an ordered sequence of stages, each handing a finished result to the next, and each trading raw color accuracy against clean, printable geometry.
Solve modes
The solve runs in one of two Solve Modes, Color (the default) or Luminance. The color solver, the targets, and the recipe table are the same machinery in both, but Luminance reserves cap budget up front, so its recipe table spans a narrower range of cap thicknesses and the chosen recipes can come out different. What changes deliberately is how the white cap is shaped. In Color, the cap realizes the thickness chosen against the full target color, including lightness. In Luminance, a separate source-luminance pass carries the photo’s tone and fine detail as white relief, like a classic lithophane, on top of color. The two modes are compared in depth in Solve Modes, and the cap mechanics in White Cap.
Why staged
Two goals pull against each other. Matching color exactly wants the freedom to change the recipe at every point; printing well wants large regions of constant recipe and gradual changes in height. The staged structure resolves the tension by fixing color in coherent regions first and adding refinement and fine detail only where it earns its place, rather than satisfying both goals everywhere at once.
Throughout, the solve leans on The Color LUT: instead of recomputing a candidate stack’s transmitted color from the optical model, it reads the answer from the precomputed table. Reusing these predictions reduces the work needed to compare recipes and cap thicknesses. Larger palettes and finer solve grids can still take longer.
What each stage contributes
Compile the settings. The run’s settings are first resolved into a fixed, self-consistent plan: the resolution it will solve at, the spacing of the color regions it aims for, and the printability limits it must respect. Every later stage reads this one compiled plan, which makes a run reproducible and internally consistent.
Plan the color regions. The image is partitioned into contiguous patches of similar target color, and adjacent patches are recorded as neighbors. Each patch starts with a single recipe. Working in regions rather than points keeps the result buildable; the neighbor map later lets the solve reason about the seams between regions.
Choose and refine the recipes. This is the core decision. For each region the solve scores candidate stacks under three competing pressures: how closely the stack reproduces the region’s color, how small a height step it leaves against its neighbors, and the cost of unnecessary material. The boundary pressure penalizes the square of the height gap between neighboring regions — a sharp jump prints as a visible seam — so a slightly imperfect color that sits nearly flush with its neighbor can beat a closer color that leaves a step. Each candidate includes a cap thickness, so color and overall lightness are considered together. Local recipe corrections and boundary refinement may then recover detail or improve region edges where the benefit justifies the added complexity.
Plan filler and build the white cap. Normal runs need no extra filler. Swap runs use flat white fill to complete their reserved bands. Prisma then authors the white cap over the colored stacks, applies the selected mode’s appearance policy, and enforces the product’s printability rules. See White Cap and Runs with Swaps.
Assemble the solved run. The final stage records the completed material plan and its quality and printability diagnostics. Prisma also derives per-filament thickness maps—one view per colored filament plus the white cap—for Preview, inspection, and Export.
When the palette overflows the printer
Everything above describes one pass, and one pass is all it takes when the palette fits the printer’s loaded slots. When it does not, the solve runs twice: a quick reduced-resolution scout solve measures how the image actually uses each filament, and the colors are divided into slot-sized bands. Their heights cover most of the scout’s estimated usage and may be reduced to fit the thickness budget. Each band is topped up to a flat ceiling with white. The final solve then runs the full staged sequence against recipe tables constrained to those bands, with each candidate stack’s white fill already included in its predicted color. The reserved band heights also come out of the total thickness budget, leaving the cap correspondingly less room to spend. How the bands are chosen, and why their flatness is what makes mid-print filament swaps valid, is covered in Runs with Swaps.
What comes out
The result is a solved run that specifies the resolved material at every location, alongside quality and printability diagnostics. Per-filament thickness maps provide useful views of that result. Export later reads the completed plan to build the printable model.
Illustration

The solve moves from resolved settings to coherent color regions, refined recipes, white-cap geometry, and finally the completed material plan with its maps and diagnostics.
