prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: Thickness Map
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Once the solver has committed its regions and material recipes, Prisma can represent the result as thickness maps: one height field for each filament. Every cell holds a thickness in millimeters—how much of that filament stands at that point. Prisma uses these maps to explain the solve in Preview and to prepare its geometry for Export.
Pull the layers apart and you have one field per filament — not one per color channel, but one per actual palette filament. Where a field reads zero, that filament is absent there. Where it stands tall, that color is doing the work: thicker material transmits less light, so it reads darker and more saturated. Stacked together, these fields are the recipe for the print.
The white cap rides along
A finished lithophane needs a white skin over the colored stack, so the maps also include the total white cap and its boundary and detail components. Prisma can show the components separately or use their combined height. The cap’s thickness is not a single setting stored in these maps; it is the result of cap construction, which depends on the solve mode and the available height budget. The full account is in White Cap.
(There is no white-base field: the base is a single fixed thickness under everything, folded into the color model rather than mapped per pixel.)
Diagnostics travel beside it
Prisma also derives diagnostic views from the completed solve: a per-pixel color-error map records how far each point’s predicted color landed from its target, and an out-of-gamut mask marks targets outside the palette’s reachable set. These describe the result but are not printable material.
Why it is the hinge
Thickness maps connect the completed solve to two practical uses:

Export reads each height field and builds it into printed material at the right places and depths. See Export.
Appearance checking uses the Appearance Model captured for that run to predict what the lit stack will look like, then compares that against the target — that is how Prisma knows where it matched and where it had to compromise. The prediction comes from the Choosing a Color Model.

No user control edits a thickness map. The maps are derived when the solve is finalized — see The Solve — and flow two ways from there: toward export as geometry inputs, and back through the Appearance Model for preview and quality checks.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.filePath: Prisma Lithophane Generator/How It Works/White Cap/index.md
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.title: White Cap
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
.hiw-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.hiw-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.hiw-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.hiw-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}The SolveWhite CapExport


White Cap is the final construction step of the solve. Prisma uses the chosen color recipes and their heights to build the white surface above them. Thickness maps show the resulting color and cap heights in Preview, and Export turns them into printable geometry. See The Solve for how the color recipes are chosen.
The cap is built in two stacked tiers above the color stack. The boundary cap is the cap: a continuous white surface that covers the color stack. It is always present (with an absolute one-layer minimum and a default thickness of 0.16 mm, or two layers at the default 0.08 mm layer height), it closes over the colored material so no color edge is left exposed, and its thickness affects how bright each region reads — thicker white passes less light, so it reads darker. Its underside fits the color stack exactly; only its upper surface is shaped. The detail cap is the second tier — optional whole white layers above the boundary cap. Where the boundary cap is the structural surface, the detail stage keeps extra white only where it earns its place, subject to the image signal, predicted improvement, the configured layer ceiling, and printability. It never lowers the boundary cap; it only adds above it, and a zero-layer limit permits no extra detail relief.
From colors to heights, and the budget
Each solved color is a recipe of stacked colored layers; summed at each point they give the colored stack’s height above the white base. The top of that stack is the color ceiling. Total object height is a hard ceiling that includes the white base, so the cap may use only the thickness left above the colors. In Luminance mode, the boundary cap has a separate thickness limit to leave room for detail. Prisma converts the selected Cap Thickness to the closest printable whole-layer thickness, choosing the thicker result when two choices are equally close. This sets the minimum cap thickness, never less than one layer.
In a run with swaps, the color ceiling is different: every filament band is filled with white up to a flat, panel-wide ceiling, so the top of colors-plus-fill sits at one constant height everywhere rather than following each point’s own stack. The cap’s budget is measured from that flat ceiling, and it is a hard limit of its own — whatever the brightness arithmetic below asks for, the cap can never spend more than the height left above the bands. See Runs with Swaps.
The cap settings
A handful of settings shape the cap:

Upper surface style — Image Aware (default) or Smooth. Smooth shapes the boundary cap into one continuous outer surface that carries the tonal relief directly. Image Aware keeps the boundary cap structural, preserves the solved appearance against the active Appearance Model, and places the remaining tonal relief in the detail cap instead — bounded by the Appearance budget. This is a Color-mode choice; Luminance always uses the Smooth boundary-cap path.
Appearance budget — for the Image Aware boundary cap: the most extra predicted color error (in the model’s color space) allowed as the smoothed boundary cap departs from the cap thicknesses chosen by the color solve. Lower values preserve the solved appearance more aggressively. (Default 0.004.)
Smoothing radius — how much the boundary cap’s upper surface is smoothed. Lower values keep more tonal relief in the surface; higher values produce a cleaner, more contiguous cap. The smoothing is edge-aware — pulled back toward the unsmoothed surface near strong color or recipe edges — and the underside still fits the color stack exactly.
Max detail layers — the most whole white layers the detail cap may add above the boundary cap. It permits detail height; it does not force the detail cap to use every layer. (Default 5.)
Shading balance — used in Luminance mode (below): whether the broad luminance shading is carried more by the smooth boundary cap or by fine detail-cap relief.

Color mode vs Luminance mode
The cap is built fundamentally differently depending on the Solve Mode — covered in full in Solve Modes.
In Color, cap thickness participates in matching the full target color, including its lightness. There is no separate step based on the source image’s brightness: each point begins with the cap thickness whose predicted stack best matched that color target. With the default Image Aware boundary cap, the final target surface is split into a structural boundary tier and appearance-preserving detail relief; with Smooth, the boundary tier follows the smoothed surface instead. The detail stage may then keep extra white — up to Max detail layers — wherever it measurably improves the result.
In Luminance, brightness in the prepared target colors guides the cap, including any changes made by preprocessing, gamut handling, or palette adaptation. Prisma normalizes that brightness range to set local cap allowances. Shading balance and the measured white response set the overall boundary-cap limit, keeping the smooth tier from consuming the whole budget. The detail cap then adds white toward the fuller brightness-derived relief, point by point wherever it measurably improves the predicted result, up to Max detail layers; a printability check unique to this mode keeps that freely-added detail within budget. Together the two tiers carry the image’s tonal structure as white relief — like a classic lithophane — on top of color.
Band fill changes the brightness arithmetic in a banded print, because white inside a band dims the light just as cap white does. In Color mode the solve chose every recipe with its band’s fill already included. In Luminance mode Prisma subtracts the fill beneath each point from its requested cap thickness, then applies the cap minimum and whole-layer limits. This compensates for the fill where possible; it cannot fully compensate when the fill already exceeds the requested white thickness. Without that subtraction, the fill would darken the print further.
Covering every surface
Before the solve accepts the cap plan, boundary coverage and optional detail are checked for printability. Required boundary coverage can be grown into a printable footprint; optional detail that cannot be made printable can be suppressed.
The later mesh construction depends on Cap mesh type. Field-derived rebuilds the final white surface at the selected Field density while preserving coverage over the colors. Exact raster builds the combined white cap directly from the solve grid. Either method may divide the white geometry into several objects, but every cap object and any swap-band white fill retain the same cap-white material assignment. See Export.
The completed cap plan is stored with the solved run alongside its color plan and derived fields. In a swap run, the filament bands were already fixed before the cap was built (Runs with Swaps). How the cap surface becomes mesh, and why higher field densities can carry finer detail than the solve grid, is covered in Export.
Illustration

The color ceiling follows the top of each solved stack. Above it, the boundary cap provides continuous white coverage with a layer-quantized upper profile; localized detail layers add relief on top within the remaining height budget.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-it-works.content:
Introduction
This section explains what Prisma Generator does internally and why. You do not need these details to make a lithophane, but a rough mental model can help you use the Generator intentionally and understand why different images, palettes, and settings produce different results.
Believe your lying eyes
When you perceive an image on a screen or on a printed page, a small set of components creates the appearance of many colors. Monitors use red, green, and blue (RGB) as additive primaries. Many printers use cyan, magenta, yellow, and black (CMYK) as subtractive primaries. Neither approach reproduces every color found in the real world, and there is no single correct way to build every image from a limited set of color components.
3D printers are not normal printers
Many color-lithophane systems begin with a fixed CMYK-like filament set. Prisma instead lets the palette follow the colors in the source image and uses a calibrated color model to predict how the selected filaments appear when stacked and backlit. White remains a special material for the base, fill, and cap.
In typical color printing, the range of colors is achieved by changing the size and density of colored dots. Color lithophanes are closer to stacks of stained glass: every part of the image must be filled with plastic, and each material can change only at printed-layer boundaries. The active Extrusion Width and its minimum printable line length constrain the smallest reliable features. These limits reduce both the reachable colors and the detail the print can carry.
The complicated nature of the Prisma Generator’s pipeline and its many settings is an attempt to answer the question: “How can I reproduce any image in a color lithophane as accurately as possible given the many limitations of 3D printers?”
The pipeline
The pipeline used by Prisma Generator is my answer to that question. Instead of using CMYK, the filaments used are selected based on the colors actually found in an image. Then that image is processed in a series of stages to convert its pixels into regions of color that are actually printable.
The diagram below depicts the stages that convert an image into printable model objects and their material assignments.

The main flow runs left to right; the palette, color model, and lookup table feed the solve from below. When swaps are needed, a scout solve plans their bands before the final lookup table and solve. Select any stage to read how it works.
The stages

Image Adjustments — the framing and color grading you apply to the source photo in the first tab, before the automatic pipeline begins.
Preprocessing — an optional, configurable clean-up pass that conditions the image toward what the chosen palette can actually reproduce.
Target Colors — translating every pixel into a perceptual color space and onto the set of colors the palette can physically reach.
The Solve — the core step: choosing a filament recipe for each region of the image so the backlit result matches the targets while staying printable.
White Cap — converting the solved colors into a thickness map and adding a white layer that sets overall brightness.
Export — turning the finished layers into an STL or 3MF model the slicer can open.

Feeding the solve from the side:

Palette — the filaments chosen for a print, and how Prisma can suggest them from the image.
Color Model — the model that predicts how stacks of filaments will appear to your eye when backlit.
The Color LUT — a precomputed table of printable stacks and their predicted colors, which lets the solver compare recipes without calculating each stack from scratch.
Runs with Swaps — planning flat filament bands before the final solve when the palette contains more colors than the printer can hold at once.

How settings affect the process
The pipeline pages linked above describe this process from stage to stage. Settings: How They Work describes the same process through the current Settings drawer groups: Essentials, Preprocessing, Color Solver, and White Cap.
Each page stands on its own; start with any stage and follow the cross-links from there.

Prisma’s job ends with the generated model files and the instructions attached to that exact export. Slicing and printer-specific setup happen in your slicer.
Move the export into your slicer

On 4 Export, select the generated-export record you intend to print.
Review its Print Instructions, then use the folder button (Open export folder) under Generated Files.
Import the single 3MF file, or all of the individual STL objects, without changing their shared positions or scale. The 3MF option is the simplest way to keep a multi-object export together.
Assign the named filaments to the corresponding objects or material-system slots.

Use the Layer Height and active Extrusion Width recorded by the completed run when configuring the slicer. Do not scale the exported geometry to correct its size: change the image dimensions in Prisma, solve again, and make a new export instead.
Check the sliced print
Before sending the job to the printer, verify the overall dimensions, filament assignments, layer preview, and any planned pauses. For a swap run, follow the export’s initial loading order and every later slot change; keep the assigned white filament loaded throughout the print.
Temperatures, speeds, bed preparation, and other printer- or filament-specific choices remain the responsibility of your slicer profile and material guidance. Prisma’s preview predicts the lithophane’s appearance, but the slicer’s toolpath preview is the final check of what the printer will execute.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/c.title: Configuration
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/c.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ConfigurationImagePreferencesWorkspaces


One-time setup means choosing the published model library Prisma predicts from, telling it which of that library’s filaments you own, and describing your printer. Open Config in the upper-right corner for Model Library, Active Filaments, and Printer Configuration. The same menu opens Preferences for startup defaults, interface choices, and shortcuts.
The left panel remains the app’s working dashboard: a thumbnail of the selected image, the Palette Deck (see Palette), and the active Printer, Nozzle, and Width. Frequently adjusted solve behavior belongs in Settings.
Model Libraries
A published model library contains the filament catalog and its calibrated color and camera models together. Generator uses exactly one installed library at a time; it never mixes models or filaments from different libraries.
Open Config → Model Library. Config names the library loaded by the running Generator and indicates exceptional states such as a pending restart or a library that needs attention. The Model Libraries window marks the library currently In Use, any library selected for the next launch, and any package that failed validation. Select a valid library to see its version, publisher, filament count, compatibility, and release notes.

Install Library… accepts a published Prisma model-library ZIP and validates every required file before installing it. Installing does not switch the running Generator.
Activate and Restart Prisma selects the library and restarts Generator to use it. Save your workspace or individual runs first if you want to return to them.
Remove Library is available only for a library that is neither currently loaded nor selected for the next launch. Removing the installed copy does not delete the original ZIP you downloaded.
Open Folder opens Generator\Model Libraries. Use the app for install, activation, and removal rather than manually rearranging this folder.

If the selected library is missing or invalid, Prisma opens the manager in Library Recovery mode. You can inspect or replace libraries, but lithophane generation remains unavailable until a complete valid library is selected.
Switching libraries changes the filament catalog and its calibrated models together. Saved runs remain available for review and export, but a new solve uses the newly active library.
Active Filaments
Active Filaments is the subset of the current model library that the rest of the app offers you. You probably don’t own every calibrated filament in the library, so this filter lets you hide the ones you don’t have without changing the installed model library.
Open Config → Active Filaments. A window opens with every available filament as a card; click a card to enable or disable it. All and None set everything at once, and the counter at the top shows how many are enabled. Close the window when you’re done — changes apply immediately.
Disabling a filament just hides it — nothing is deleted, and you can re-enable it any time.
Printer Configuration
Prisma needs to know your printer’s basic facts: how big it can print, how many filament slots it has, and which Nozzle and Extrusion Width combinations it supports. These determine the maximum print size, how many colors fit without swaps, the valid Layer Height range, the Solve Pitch choices, and the physical printability limits used by the solver.
Open Config → Printer Configuration. The Printer Configuration window contains:

Printer Profile (top) — choose which profile to edit. + New adds a profile; Delete removes the selected one.
General — set Printer Name, Printable Area, and AMS Configuration. Printable Area caps the lithophane dimensions. AMS units × slots per unit is the number of filaments the printer can hold at once, which determines how many colors fit without swaps (see Palette).
Nozzle Profiles — use + Add Nozzle to add a card for each nozzle you use. Each card contains Nozzle Diameter, Layer Height Range, Extrusion Width Range, and Minimum Line Length. The lower Extrusion Width bound is the Nozzle Diameter and is shown as a derived, non-editable value; set the upper bound to the largest width that nozzle profile supports. Minimum Line Length is a whole number from 2 through 10 × Extrusion Width.

For a solve, Prisma derives minimum printable width from the active Extrusion Width. It multiplies that width by the nozzle profile’s Minimum Line Length value to get the physical minimum line length, then uses those limits to reject features that are too small to print reliably. Because the checks operate at Solve Pitch resolution, the effective limits land on whole solve cells.
Changes are saved when the window closes. Discard Changes closes it without saving the draft. Invalid values keep the window open, and a save failure also leaves the draft visible instead of pretending it was saved.
Printer configuration belongs to this Prisma installation’s Generator/Workspace/config/printers.json. It is separate from Settings Profiles. A saved run retains the resolved thresholds that describe its historical result, but any new solve—including re-solving after a load—uses the currently active Printer, Nozzle, and Extrusion Width.
Picking the active print setup
Back in the left panel, the Printer area shows Printer, Nozzle, and Width. Width is the active Extrusion Width. Open it to select a saved width, remove a saved shortcut, or use Add New to save another width within the active nozzle profile’s range. Add and Enter save the value without changing the active width. Select its row separately when you want to use it.
Set all three to match the print setup you will actually use. Changing the Printer, Nozzle, or Extrusion Width can require Prisma to adjust Layer Height or the Solve Pitch multiplier. Before applying a consequential change, the review window separates You requested, Prisma must also change, This changes, and Needs attention so you can inspect the resulting Solve Pitch, Minimum Line Length, filament capacity, image-size alignment, and affected Settings.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/e.title: Export
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/e.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PreviewExport3D Printing


The Export tab turns a finished solve into the files your slicer needs, plus the filament-change plan for the print. The tab is laid out as numbered steps, left to right.
1 — Select Run
The left column lists your completed solves — the same runs as the Preview tab’s history. Click the run you want to print. Export uses that run’s captured result, palette, and settings, so later changes in the drawer do not alter it.
2 — Export Options
Review Selected solve for the print dimensions, nozzle, Extrusion Width,
Layer Height, border, and filament names recorded with that run. Then choose
the export settings and press Export Meshes:

Output format — Single .3MF (default) bundles all the model’s objects into one file, the convenient choice for OrcaSlicer. Separate .STLs writes one file per object. Most materials produce one object, but a difficult same-material shape may be split into more than one object so the slicer can handle it safely.
Cap mesh type — how the cap’s 3D shape is built. Field-derived (default) produces a cleaner, smoother cap surface. Exact raster reproduces the solve’s blocky grid exactly.
Field density — for Field-derived export, how finely the cap surface is rebuilt, from 1x resolution to 16x resolution. Higher density can make the surface smoother, but takes longer and produces larger files. 4x resolution is the default. This does not add new color detail to the solve.

Generating takes a little while for large prints; progress shows while it runs.
An exact repeat can reuse files Prisma already generated for the same run and
export choices. Changing the GPU preference alone does not require another
copy of those files.
3 — Generated Exports
Each finished export appears under Session exports. This list includes
exports from different solves; changing Select Run does not hide them or
change the export you are reviewing. The record preserves its source solve,
Output format, Cap mesh type, and Field density. Select a record to see its
Generated Files and Print Instructions.
The files are already saved in the folder shown by Prisma. Use the folder
button (Open export folder) to work with those originals, or a file’s
download button for an additional copy. Download ZIP copy makes a packaged
copy of the selected export; it is not required before slicing.
Print Instructions
Every generated export includes filament-loading instructions. For a swap run, the panel gives the initial slot assignments, pause heights, and per-slot changes. For a run that fits in one load, it records the initial loading order without mid-print changes. The copy button (Copy print instructions) takes the selected export’s instructions with you.
Runs with swaps need a little more preparation and judgment than runs whose colors all fit at once. See Runs with Swaps for the complete workflow.
Experimental GPU exports
In Config → Preferences → Export, enable Use GPU for exports and press
Apply. It is off by default and applies to subsequent exports. It requires
Windows x64, compatible AMD drivers, and the optional GPU export components.
The Radeon RX 9070 is the tested GPU; other GPUs must pass Prisma’s checks.
GPU acceleration covers Field-derived exports and Exact raster caps. Swap-band
raster exports and unsupported operations use the CPU. If GPU generation fails,
Prisma can retry on the CPU. Completed exports can still be reused. GPU export
is a separate choice from GPU solves and palette suggestions.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/i.title: Adjustments
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/i.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ImageAdjustmentsPalette


The Adjustments panel on the Image page separates the lithophane’s framing and physical output from the picture’s color and tone. Framing contains Aspect Ratio, Dimensions, Border, and Image Framing; Appearance contains color and tonal controls. Changes appear live in the large Preview. Reset restores framing and Border using your saved Image preferences, and restores image appearance to its defaults.
Framing

Aspect Ratio — choose Source Image to preserve the source proportions, Fixed Ratio to enter the Width and Height terms of a custom ratio in two compact fields, or Free when Width and Height should be independent.
Edit Framing — enables direct manipulation in the large Preview. Drag to position the Image, use the mouse wheel to scale it, and drag just outside a corner to rotate it.
Scale — zooms the picture within the lithophane. 100% is the starting image scale; parts of the source can still fall outside the lithophane. This changes the crop, unlike View Zoom.
Rotation — fine rotation in degrees, plus one-click 90° L, 90° R, H-Flip, and V-Flip actions.
Dimensions — Width and Height set the image area’s physical size in millimeters. With Free selected they are independent; Source Image or Fixed Ratio derives the other dimension. Each axis ranges from 10 mm through the active printer’s corresponding printable-area dimension. A border adds to the full print size.
Border — the button beside Width switches between Enabled and Disabled, adding or removing a raised frame around the lithophane. Width is how far it extends outward; Thickness is its printed height. Thickness follows Max Thickness in Settings unless Custom is checked. The border prints with the cap filament.

Numeric controls open a slider when selected. Mouse-wheel changes over either
dimension slider land on values compatible with the current Solve Pitch.
Direct entry may still request a size between solve cells; Prisma asks you to
review the adjusted dimensions before solving. Resizing keeps the framing
center and image position, scale, and rotation.
Select Edit Framing over the Preview to manipulate the framing outline and
image directly. Drag inside the frame to move it. With Free selected, drag
anywhere along a side or near a corner to resize it; Source Image and Fixed
Ratio expose corners only. Move just outside a corner to rotate the image.
Select Finish Framing to lock direct Preview interaction without changing
the composition.
The Unlocked/Locked button beneath Dimensions holds Width, Height, aspect
ratio, and frame resizing fixed. Locking first checks that the size fits the
solve grid. You can still reposition, scale, and rotate the image. If a later
printer or Solve Pitch change makes the locked size unsuitable, review the
proposed resize or cancel the solve.
A border can take the full print beyond the printer area even when Width and
Height alone fit. The Larger Than Printer Area dialog shows both sizes and
offers Resize to fit. Use Current Size is offered only when the current
dimensions already fit the solve grid; choosing it does not make the print fit
your printer.
Bigger isn’t just bigger: at a larger print size the same photo spreads over more solve points, so the print can carry more detail. Check Solve image at the bottom of the Preview.
Appearance
The Appearance controls tune the picture before Prisma reproduces it:

Mode — Color or B/W. B/W removes color from the target image, but it does not automatically remove colored filaments from the active palette. Use a white-only or otherwise deliberately limited palette when you want a truly single-color print.
Exposure — overall brightness.
Contrast — positive values separate darks and lights; negative values bring interior tones toward middle gray. True black and white stay fixed, so lowering Contrast does not give blacks a faded-gray appearance. In B/W this acts on the grayscale image; in Color it acts on each color channel and can also change color intensity or hue.
Highlight / Shadow — positive values brighten the light or dark areas; negative values darken them. Black, middle gray, and white stay anchored, so lifting Shadows reveals existing dark detail without turning true black gray. Lowering Highlights reduces bright tones without flattening a whole band of brightness into one level.

These controls reshape detail already present in the image; they cannot recover detail lost to clipping in the source. Their tonal anchors apply at the Highlights/Shadows step, after Exposure and Contrast. Later color adjustments can still shift or clip the result.
If Exposure pushes highlights beyond white, reduce Exposure to bring them back into range; lowering Contrast alone does not do that. Existing saved Contrast values now use the updated smooth curve without changing their numbers. Previously rendered saved-run results and source files remain unchanged.
In Color mode there are three more:

Saturation — how vivid the colors are. The range is balanced around 0: -1 reduces color strength by 75%, and +1 increases it by 75%. The minimum still retains color; use B/W to remove color completely.
Temperature — warmer (toward amber/yellow) or cooler (toward blue).
Tint — toward magenta at positive values or green at negative values.

Temperature, Tint, and Saturation remain visible but inactive in B/W mode. Their values are preserved and take effect again if you switch back to Color mode.
Temperature and Tint work together as restrained color-balance controls. They
preserve true black but allow whites to take on a cast. Strong settings can clip
bright or saturated colors; reduce the adjustment if it removes useful detail.
A practical use: if the preview after solving shows your palette can’t reach the photo’s most saturated colors, easing Saturation down here can produce a cleaner, more even result than letting the solver clip them.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/i.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ConfigurationImagePaletteAdjustments


The Image tab is step 1: pick the photo, decide how big the print will be, and frame the part of the picture you want. Everything else in the app works from what you set here.
Image Library
The Image Library pane holds your source photos. Each thumbnail shows the file’s name, pixel dimensions, and size; click one to select it (or drag it onto the large Preview). Add Image can add one or several photos from your computer; Open Folder opens the Images folder, the refresh button re-reads it, and the expand button enlarges the pane when you have many images. You can also drag the divider above the Library to change its height.
Switching to a different photo resets the framing — crop, scale, rotation, and flips start fresh for the new image.
Prisma accepts JPEG (.jpg, .jpeg, .jpe, .jfif), PNG, TIFF, BMP, WebP, HEIC/HEIF (.heic, .heif, .hif), and AVIF. HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, and JPEG photos with a recognized auxiliary HDR gain map may briefly show Preparing… before they appear. Prisma makes a disposable, color-normalized PNG for its own work; it does not change or replace the original. For a gain-map JPEG, Prisma uses the normal SDR photo and ignores the display-only HDR gain map.
The library is the Generator/Images folder inside the portable Prisma app folder. Add Image copies photos there, and you can also place files there directly and press refresh. Successfully prepared files appear automatically. If only some files in a batch can be read, the others still appear and a warning lists each failure with a suggested action.
Loading a saved run adds it to Preview without changing the active image or
copying its photo into this folder. If you choose Use as Starting Point or
recall its image setup from Inspector, Prisma can select an identical Library
photo. If there is no exact match, the archived photo becomes a temporary active
image marked Saved run source. It can still be framed, previewed, used for
palette suggestions, and solved, but it is absent from the Library thumbnails
and count. Selecting any Library photo replaces that temporary selection.
Choosing Use as Starting Point from a run’s Preview Inspector also returns
you to this page. Prisma has applied the compatible parts of that run’s setup;
review the source, dimensions/border, framing, and
appearance here before solving. The action itself never starts a solve.
For converted sources, a saved run contains the prepared PNG used for the
solve. A run saved on this installation can also find its original Library
photo. When you import a run from a file, Prisma uses the included prepared
image rather than assuming a converted Library photo is the same original.
Ordinary JPEG, PNG, TIFF, BMP, and WebP images can be matched directly against
the included image.
Reset Workspace releases active temporary sources while preserving named saves and original Library files. Loaded workspaces can retain a missing image reference: use Workspace → Locate Image to find the same image in the Library, or choose a new editable input normally. Existing results keep their captured source identity.
Prisma uses the primary still image and honors its orientation and common sRGB, Display-P3, BT.709, and SDR BT.2020 color information. JPEGs whose only additional picture is a recognized Apple or Android HDR gain map are accepted through their SDR primary image. General multi-picture MPO, animated PNG/WebP/HEIF/AVIF, multi-page TIFF, and HDR-only PQ/HLG images are not supported; export the still image or page you want as an SDR sRGB JPEG or PNG first. RAW/DNG, videos, Live Photo video companions, GIF, JPEG 2000, and JPEG XL are also outside the supported image library.
Almost any supported photo can be solved, but that does not mean every photo will make an equally good lithophane. A sharp source with readable contrast and important details large enough to survive the print resolution is a stronger starting point.
Preview
The Preview pane shows the framed and adjusted target image that the rest of the app will use, with the physical dimensions marked. It is not yet a prediction of the printed result. If something important is cut off here, fix the framing before moving on.
Select Edit Framing over the Preview to unlock direct frame movement,
edge/corner resizing, Image scaling, and Image rotation. Finish Framing
locks those gestures and recenters the framing outline onscreen without changing the
composition or View Zoom.
View Zoom, Fit to Image, and Fit to Frame change only how much you
see onscreen. Fit to Image shows the whole source; Fit to Frame shows the
lithophane and its border. These controls do not change the print size or crop.
Adjustments
The Adjustments panel on the right is where you set the print’s size and shape and, optionally, tune the picture itself. It has two choices:

Framing — lithophane size and shape, image framing, rotation, and an optional raised border.
Appearance — brightness, contrast, color adjustments, and a black-and-white mode.

Both are covered control by control in Adjustments. Reset (top right of the panel) restores framing and Border using your saved Image preferences, and restores image appearance to its defaults.
Whole-cell image sizing
Width and Height are requested physical dimensions. A solve is made from whole
Solve Pitch cells, so some requested sizes cannot be represented exactly. For
example, 100.2 mm at a 0.4 mm Solve Pitch is 250.5 cells; Prisma resolves that
request downward to 250 cells, or 100.0 mm. This keeps the corrected framing area
inside the requested frame instead of asking the Image to cover a larger area.
When this happens, warning marks beside Width and Height identify the affected
dimensions, and the summary shows the proposed image area and solve grid.
Full print includes the border. Starting a solve opens Lithophane
Dimensions with current and proposed sizes. Cancel keeps the requested
Width and Height; Resize accepts the whole-cell size and continues the same
solve. The framing center and image position, scale, and rotation stay in place.
Locked dimensions stay fixed when framing is edited. If a later Solve Pitch
or printer change makes them unsuitable, Prisma asks you to review the size
before solving. See Adjustments
for locking dimensions and dealing with a print larger than the printer area.
The info bar
At the bottom of the Preview, four figures summarize the setup:

Source image — the source photo’s pixels.
Solve image — the whole-cell solve grid at the current Solve Pitch. This is the real detail level of the print: if it’s much smaller than the source image, fine detail in the photo won’t survive, no matter how sharp the source is.
Image only — the physical image area, without the border.
Full print — the complete physical footprint, including the border when enabled.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.title: Palette
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ImagePaletteSettingsRuns withSwaps


The Palette tab is where you choose the colored filaments available to the solve. Palette choice has a large effect on the result: Prisma can mix the colors you provide by stacking them, but it cannot make every target equally well from every set of filaments.
The white used for the base and cap is selected separately under Settings → Essentials. It appears on palette cards for context but is not one of the palette’s color filaments.
Both creation modes use the enabled Active Filaments from the currently active model library. If a filament is missing, check Configuration first; use Config → Model Library only when you mean to switch the complete published model library.
Auto-Suggest
Auto-Suggest tests combinations from the filaments you allow and suggests promising palettes for the selected image.

Under Select Filaments for Auto-Suggest, select the filaments Prisma may consider. All and None are quick starting points.
Set the limits on the right.
Choose the Solve mode you intend to use.
Press Suggest Palettes to stage suggestions.
Compare their estimated fit and use Add to Deck on the palettes you want to solve.

The active white base/cap filament remains visible in the picker with a BASE/CAP label, but it is unavailable for selection because Prisma reserves it for the white support slot. This makes the filament count explicit rather than making the reserved filament appear to be missing.
The controls are:

Palette colors — the exact number of colored filaments in every returned palette. The default range is 2–16; the separately reserved base/cap filament is not counted. Preferences can change the allowed range.
Suggestions — the maximum number of distinct alternatives to return. It defaults to 5 and accepts 1–10; Preferences can change the maximum.
Solve mode — Color evaluates palettes against the adjusted image’s colors. Luminance evaluates them for the Luminance workflow, where the white cap carries more of the light-and-dark structure.

Palette colors may exceed the active printer’s simultaneous color capacity.
The AMS diagram shows the colors that fit in the printer’s physical slots and
places the remaining colors in a separate Additional colors row. Filament
swaps may be required. Auto-Suggest cannot predict an exact swap count
because the actual grouping depends on the recipes selected during the solve.
The completed solve’s grouping plan is authoritative.
The main alternatives are named Color suggested N or Luminance suggested N
to preserve the mode that produced them. Each result shows Suggest dE. dE
means delta E, a perceptual color-difference estimate; lower indicates a closer
estimated fit to the suggestion target. It is useful for narrowing the field,
not for declaring a winner. Palettes with similar scores can distribute their
errors very differently, so solve the promising options and compare their
predicted images.
For a repeatable comparison order and guidance on what to try after choosing a promising palette, see Improving a Solve.
If the selected white is unavailable to the color model, suggestion cannot run. Filaments excluded from modeling are also ignored even if selected as candidates.
Cancel requests a stop at the next safe search boundary. The progress bar remains visible as Cancellation requested until the worker actually stops; any partial suggestions returned by the search are still shown.
Experimental GPU suggestions
In Preferences → Palette, enable Use GPU for palette suggestions and
press Apply. It is off by default. The choice affects new suggestions in
the current session without restarting; an active suggestion keeps the choice
it started with. Turning it off releases the helper after active work finishes.
This feature is tested on Windows with a Ryzen 9 9900X, 64 GB RAM, and Radeon
RX 9070. Other systems are untested. It requires the optional GPU palette
components and compatible AMD drivers. Preferences shows a short availability
status; reopen its Palette page to check again. The setting is separate from
GPU export.
GPU acceleration currently applies to Color suggestions with the Photo
Stack model. Luminance suggestions and unsupported workloads use the CPU.
If the GPU is unavailable, Prisma retries the same prepared request on the CPU
and shows a short notice. Suggestions use the same ranking process, with small
floating-point differences possible. Suggestions go to the destination selected
in Preferences, just as they do with the CPU.
Ranking and where suggestions go
Config → Preferences → Palette also includes Improve ranking for small
palettes. This experimental choice compares the finalists against a denser
set of calibrated color mixtures for ordinary three- and four-color palettes.
It may take longer, especially on the CPU. Other palette sizes keep their
usual ranking. Press Apply to use it for new suggestions; it does not
change solve settings or image adaptation.
Suggested palette destination normally sends new suggestions to
Suggested Palettes, where you choose which ones to Add to Deck. Choose
Palette Deck to put new suggestions directly in the deck. Applying that
choice hides and clears the staging area, so add any suggestions you want to
keep first. This choice takes effect after Apply without restarting Prisma.
Manual
Manual mode is for building a palette directly. Select filaments under Select Filaments for Palette; the Manual Palette panel shows the current set and whether it fits in one load. A manual palette may contain more colors than the available color slots, but that run will require swaps.
Press Add to Deck when the set is ready. Clear empties the manual palette.
Suggested Palettes and the Palette Deck
The Suggested Palettes column is a temporary staging area. By default, suggestions
arrive there first so you can compare them without filling the app’s main deck.
Suggested and deck cards use the same compact title-bar and chip layout. The
separate boxed white chip is the currently selected base/cap filament; it is
shown for context and is not counted among the colored palette filaments.
Add to Deck promotes one to the session’s Palette Deck. Clear asks for a second click within three
seconds and empties only this staging area.
The Palette Deck in the left rail contains the session’s palettes ready to use.
Click a card to select and activate it. Hold Ctrl (Command on macOS) to toggle
individual cards, Shift to select a range, or drag a rectangle from the empty
space in the deck well. These bulk gestures change selection while preserving
the palette used by the editor and preprocessing preview. The highlighted cards
are the exact palettes the next Solve uses: one card creates a single solve;
2–10 cards create a batch, in deck order. A batch may freely mix manual,
suggested, saved, and loaded palettes, including
different palette sizes and palettes that require ordinary swaps. Hover over a
card to see its filament names, base/cap filament, and suggestion score when
available.
Use a deck card’s ⋯ menu to Save Palette or Create Variant. To remove
a card, select its ×, then select the ! that replaces it to confirm.
Removing it from the deck does not delete its saved copy.
Create Variant opens Manual mode with an ordered copy of the card. Remove
one or more filaments and choose replacements, then press Add to Deck.
Prisma inserts a new unsaved card beside the source without changing
the original. This is useful for placing a promising palette and one-filament
alternatives in the same Batch Solve. Cancel returns to any Manual
palette draft that was present beforehand.
Load in the deck header opens saved palettes. Select one to add an active
copy to the deck. Deleting a saved palette from that list does not remove a
copy already in the deck; that card simply stops being marked Saved.
Clear asks for a second click
within three seconds, removes every card from the session’s deck, and clears
the active palette. It does not clear the separate Suggested Palettes
staging area.
Select one or more cards, then press Solve. With multiple cards the button
shows Solve (N) and uses the existing batch cost confirmation. With no
selected cards, Solve is disabled. Prisma freezes the
image, settings, active preprocessing, printer/nozzle printability, active
model library, and white base/cap once, so only the colored palette varies.
Completed results appear progressively in Preview. A failed item normally does
not stop later ones; a shortage of memory or disk space pauses the queue for
review. Cancel stops the current solve. To stop waiting items too, remove
them in Solve Queue.
Cancelled and failed solves remain in the Timeline for review.
Reloading the browser restores the current deck and selection from the running
Prisma session. Workspace → Save keeps the deck with the rest of your work
for a later session. Unfinished Manual palettes and staged suggestions are not
included in a saved workspace.
For a first comparison, favor palettes that fit in one load. Extra colors are
worthwhile only when the predicted improvement justifies the slower solve,
white-fill trade-offs, and manual changes required by a swap run. See
Runs with Swaps
before printing one.

For the optical reason stacked filaments can produce colors that none of them makes alone, see Palette in How It Works.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.content:

Open Config → Preferences to choose how Prisma starts, which controls it shows, and the keyboard shortcuts you use. These choices belong to the application. A Settings Profile holds the settings for making a lithophane instead.
Choose a page from the list on the left, or use Search preferences to find an option. The question-mark buttons explain individual choices.
Apply your changes
Press Apply to save. Cancel or the close button discards changes you have not applied. Restore System Defaults selects Prisma’s original choices; press Apply to save that reset.
The description on each page explains when its choices take effect. Some apply immediately, while defaults for palette counts, Preview’s starting layout, and export options are used the next time Prisma starts. Applying image defaults leaves the current image adjustments alone; Reset uses those defaults when you ask it to.
Choose what appears in Settings
The Settings page lets you show or hide individual controls and preprocessing modules. Hiding a control does not turn its setting off or remove its value from a Settings Profile. Use the control itself to change how the next solve behaves. Advanced in the Settings drawer still governs the additional controls within each section.
Preprocessing Preview also has a starting visibility choice. Its image and adjustment helpers are described in Settings.
Palette, Solve, Preview, and Export

Palette sets the starting color and suggestion counts, where suggestions go, and the available experimental ranking and GPU options. See Palette.
Solve includes GPU availability and whether the Solve Queue and Solve Progress windows open automatically or only when requested. See Solve Queue.
Preview sets its starting grouping and whether View Mode starts expanded. See Preview.
Export sets the starting format, cap mesh type, and field density, and which density choices are shown. It also offers GPU exports when the required components and hardware are available. See Exporting.

The GPU options are experimental. Prisma checks availability before you can enable them; the help beside each option describes the supported setup. Unsupported work continues on the CPU. Changing a GPU choice affects subsequent work, not a completed result.
The Windows beta includes Prisma’s GPU components and uses compatible compute libraries supplied by the installed AMD driver. You do not need Visual Studio or an AMD development SDK to run it. The Radeon RX 9070 is the currently tested card; other cards have not been qualified. If the required driver libraries or hardware support are absent, GPU options remain unavailable and CPU operation is still supported. The Linux beta currently uses CPU computation.
Keyboard shortcuts
Under Key Bindings, choose a command and record the key combination you want to use. Prisma reports combinations that conflict with the browser or operating system. If you assign a shortcut already used by another Prisma command, that earlier command becomes unassigned. Use a command’s menu to clear its shortcut or restore its default, then press Apply.
The starting shortcuts are Alt+1 for Image, Alt+2 for Palette, Alt+3 for Preview, Alt+4 for Export, Alt+Q for Settings, and Alt+W for Solve. Commands such as opening the Solve Queue or Preferences start without a shortcut and can be assigned here.
Options that are not finished
Some choices are shown while their behavior is still being developed. The Interface layout controls and custom Cache Limits do not currently change how Prisma works. Choosing a cache limit here does not preserve temporary work or increase the space available for it. Save important work through Workspace → Save or save individual runs; see Preview for the difference between session history, temporary recovery, and Saved Runs.

The Advanced button at the end of the mode bar reveals Thickness Maps and Highpass. Thickness Maps provides extra diagnostic views; Highpass is currently unavailable.
Thickness Maps
One map per colored filament in the palette shows how thick that filament is laid down across the print. The grid also includes three separate white-cap cards: Total White Cap, Boundary Cap, and Detail Cap. Each map is normalized to its own maximum, so compare the reported numbers rather than treating identical colors on different cards as equal thickness. Cards report volume when available, maximum thickness, and the number of solve pixels using that material.
Use it to see what each filament is contributing — for example, whether an expensive color is barely used, or which filament is producing an unexpected region.
Click a card to open it in a lightbox. Its header stays fixed while the image changes size; use the Min–Max Zoom slider or the mouse wheel over the lightbox.
Highpass
This option is still listed, but the current Viewer cannot display it. Use Top Surface to inspect the print’s heights instead.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}AdvancedModesImprovinga SolveExport


A disappointing preview does not necessarily mean that the solver failed. The selected palette may be a poor fit for the image, or one small part of an otherwise good solve may need a controlled nudge. The most reliable procedure is to explore broadly with palettes first, then make narrow settings changes only after choosing a promising palette.
There is no single numerical score that captures everything people notice in an image. Use Suggest dE and RMSE % as screening information, but choose by comparing the predicted images at full size.
The short version

Add several strong suggestions to the Palette Deck and select them with Shift-click or a selection rectangle.
Keep the palette with the best overall cohesion, even if another run has a slightly better score.
Identify one specific defect in that run.
Make one small settings change aimed at that defect.
Solve again and compare both runs side by side.
Keep the change only when the preview is meaningfully better.

If the whole image feels wrong, return to the palette before changing many settings. If the image is already close and only one feature is wrong, keep the palette and use the targeted adjustments below.
The ordinary starting posture
Prisma’s defaults incorporate the broadly useful settings from the production-scale comparison:

Appearance budget: 0.004 dE
Smoothing radius: 1.0 mm
Cap Thickness: 0.16 mm
Boundary mutation: enabled, with one pass
Adapt image to palette: disabled

These defaults are intended to produce a strong first solve, not to be universally optimal. In particular, adapting the image to the palette remains opt-in because it can produce a major improvement when an image needs greater internal color coherence, but it changes the image’s target colors and is not a universal win.
Optional refinement profiles
Prisma includes two alternatives in the Settings Profile dropdown:

Refinement — Balanced is the safer first comparison. It enables Print-Scale Smoothing, uses one active-Extrusion-Width step for Solve Pitch, 1.0 mm cap smoothing, a 3.5 mm thickness limit, nine detail layers, and two boundary-mutation passes.
Refinement — Strong changes the solve more aggressively. It uses the same preprocessing and cap settings, with a 3.0 mm thickness limit, four colors per region, coarser initial regions, five detail layers, and three mutation passes.

These are conditional alternatives, not higher quality levels and not automatic fallbacks. Compare Balanced first when the ordinary result is promising but unresolved; try Strong when you want a more substantial alternate interpretation. Loading either profile changes several settings and resolves Solve Pitch from the active Extrusion Width while retaining the standard 1.0 mm smoothing radius.
First, compare palettes
Palette choice usually changes the result more than a reasonable adjustment to one solver setting. Prisma’s first suggestion is a strong starting point, but the suggestion order estimates color coverage before the full solve. It cannot completely predict region boundaries, white-cap seams, or whether a coherent color cast will look better than one locally accurate but distracting color.
Use this palette pass:

In Palette → Auto-Suggest, set Suggestions to the number you want to inspect (usually the default 5) and press Suggest Palettes.
Add the promising suggestions to the Palette Deck. You may also include a manual, saved, or previously loaded palette.
Select 2–10 deck cards with Shift-click or a selection rectangle. Ctrl-click toggles individual cards.
Leave the image and settings unchanged, press Solve (N), and confirm the batch if its warning appears.
In Preview, select the finished Timeline cards with Ctrl/Command-click or Shift-click to compare them together in the Viewer. Use Zoom to inspect a problem area; the images move together.

Judge the image in this order:

Does the image read correctly as a whole?
Are broad skies, walls, skin, fabric, or other familiar surfaces internally coherent?
Is any small region so wrong that it attracts attention?
Are there conspicuous seams, false outlines, or speckled patches?
Only then, which remaining run follows the source most closely?

A lower Suggest dE or RMSE % is useful evidence, not a command. A slightly less literal palette can look better when its errors are consistent across the image.
The deck cards remain available after the comparison. Click the palette you
want to refine to select it alone, then press Solve. If you want to keep
the solved result itself across a Prisma restart, press Save on its Preview
card.
To test a nearby palette rather than rebuilding it, open the promising Palette
Deck card’s ⋯ menu and choose Create Variant. Manual mode receives an
ordered copy; replace the filament you want to test and press Add to Deck.
The source remains intact, so both cards can immediately be selected
for another batch.
Then, name the defect
Avoid changing settings merely because a run is not perfect. Describe the visible problem first and choose the smallest matching intervention.













































What you seeWhat to try firstWhat the change is doingSmooth sky, wall, skin, or fabric looks chunky or steppedConfirm Appearance budget is 0.004 dE, especially after loading an older Settings Profile; if it is, compare another paletteThe lower default protects appearance more aggressively while the boundary cap is smoothed, but palette choice remains the stronger interventionRegion edges or white-cap seams look too starkRaise Cap Thickness from 0.16 mm to about 0.24 mm at the default Layer HeightAdds roughly one printable layer of optical buffer above the colors, which can soften the apparent transitionDark or strongly colored regions look too boldTry Cap Thickness values around 0.24–0.40 mmUses more of the available height for white, selectively weakening regions that were consuming much of the color-height budgetBroad regions have an inconsistent cast, or one part of a familiar object has an alien hueCompare a run with Adapt image to palette: Enabled; then vary White adaptation and Color adaptation separatelyMoves the target colors toward the selected white filament and palette’s reachable colors, which can make the solved image more internally coherentBoundary-cap smoothing creates dark outlines around raised areasReduce Smoothing radius from 1.0 toward 0.5 mmLimits how far height differences are blended into neighboring regionsAn almost-excellent solve has one small, glaring boundary defectTry Noise Reduction: Low, one additional Boundary mutation → Passes, or a small increase in Cap ThicknessProduces a nearby solution that may escape one locally plausible but visually awkward choiceFine detail is missing and the print is constrained by its maximum thicknessTry Max detail layers: 9Gives the detail cap more vertical room; it usually adds little when thickness is not the limiting factor
These are starting points, not a recipe to apply all at once.
Why some useful changes score worse
Human vision is unusually tolerant of a coherent change in lighting or overall color cast. The same object can look normal at noon or near sunset even though its measured colors are very different. An erratic color change within one familiar object is much more distracting.
That is why Adapt image to palette can make a preview look better while its literal source-error score gets worse. It may sacrifice absolute color matching to bring outlier regions into agreement with the rest of the solved image. White adaptation controls the influence of the selected base/cap white, while Color adaptation controls the broader palette-relative transformation. Because they are independent, set either one to 0× when you want to isolate the other. Keep the feature off when the ordinary solve is already coherent; compare it when pale, neutral, or familiar regions disagree with one another.
The same principle applies when choosing palettes. Prefer the result that forms one believable image over a result that matches one isolated color perfectly but makes that region look detached from its surroundings.
Use cap thickness deliberately
Cap Thickness is more than a coverage safeguard. At the default 0.08 mm Layer Height:

0.16 mm resolves to two layers and is the ordinary default; it gently softens region boundaries and reduces the perceptual prominence of lateral white-cap coverage.
0.24–0.40 mm resolves to three to five layers and can calm dark or saturated areas that look too forceful.
0.08 mm resolves to one layer and preserves the greatest available color height when maximum contrast or saturation matters more.

Prisma converts the requested dimension to the closest whole-layer thickness at the current Layer Height, so the exact effective thickness appears in the Essentials summary. Additional cap thickness does much less to already-light regions because those regions were not using much color height in the first place. Watch the predicted image rather than assuming the whole result will become uniformly washed out.
Nudge a nearly excellent solve
When only one small feature is wrong—especially a face or another familiar shape—the solver may have made a locally reasonable choice that people notice as a defect. Large global changes are risky at this point.
Instead, create a few nearby alternatives:

use Noise Reduction: Low to make a very small change to the source entering the solve;
increase Boundary mutation → Passes by one so an existing region boundary gets another chance to move;
or slightly increase Cap Thickness to soften the color-height result.

Try these separately before combining them. Their purpose is not to improve every metric; it is to give a nearly successful solve another path around one objectionable local result.
Changes that deserve caution

Do not change many unrelated controls in one run. You will not know which change helped, and interactions can hide a new defect.
Do not keep increasing smoothing. A larger radius can help a calm area while creating a dark lateral-cap outline around a neighboring raised region.
Do not enable Adapt image to palette by default for every image. It is powerful precisely because it changes the rendering target.
Do not chase a tiny score improvement when the image looks less coherent.
Do not use strong preprocessing merely to remove normal photographic texture. Overprocessing can replace natural variation with broad artificial patches.

A repeatable comparison loop
Name runs for the question they test—for example, Sky – palette 3, Cap budget 0.004, or Palette adaptation 1×. Keep the current best run visible beside each new candidate. Inspect both the whole composition and the problem area at full size.
Stop when the remaining differences are merely different compromises. The predicted appearance does not need to reproduce noisy source pixels exactly; the goal is a coherent image without a conspicuous local failure.

This guidance comes from production-scale comparisons across varied real images, palettes of three to five colors, and expert visual review. The controlled study used no-swap palettes and a 0.4 mm nozzle with 0.4 mm solve pitch. Treat the procedures as strong starting points rather than guarantees for every image, palette, or print setup.

View Mode changes what the selected run displays in the Viewer. Predicted is the everyday view; the others show the physical print behind it. Where a view maps thickness or height, a scale bar below explains the colors, and Options provides any additional choices. White Cap, Color Ceiling, and Top Surface use an Inferno gradient, including for older loaded runs with the required height data. Use the Viewer’s Zoom and Fit controls to inspect the image. Solve Timeline thumbnails always show the predicted appearance.
Predicted
What the print should look like lit from behind — the app’s best prediction of the finished lithophane. This is the view to judge results by: compare it against your source image and decide with your eye.
White Cap
Maps of the white cap’s absolute surface height on a shared scale from 0 mm
to the run’s Max Thickness. When comparing runs, the scale ends at the largest
Max Thickness among them. Higher values move toward the bright end of the
gradient, while the empty swatch means that component is absent at that point.
Show picks which part:

Both — the full white-cap surface above the colors.
Boundary — the continuous covering cap over the color stack.
Detail — the extra relief used to bring back image detail.

All three use the same absolute height scale, so their colors can be compared
directly. These everyday White Cap views show where each component’s surface
sits; the component’s actual thickness is available in Advanced → Thickness
Maps.
Contours: On/Off overlays lines marking each printed-layer step. In Luminance mode this view shows where the image’s brightness structure is being carried by white thickness.
Color Regions
Two looks at the color stack under the cap, switched by Show:

Color Ceiling — the combined height of the base and colored material before the white cap is added.
Recipe Viewer — the print rendered from its colors alone. With Recipe readout: On, move the pointer over the image to see the filament combination at that point — useful when a color surprises you and you want to know which filaments made it. The small Recipe panel stays visible while you zoom or scroll the image.

Contours: On/Off shows recipe boundaries in Recipe Viewer when the run has
the required boundary data.
Top Surface
The final printable outer surface — the actual heights the printer will build, everything included. Contours: On/Off marks the layer steps. This is the closest thing to holding the unlit print and looking across it.
Explorer
A horizontal slice through the print: pick a Height with the slider and see which material sits at that layer everywhere in the print. It is like peeling the print down to one chosen layer — the way to answer “what is the printer putting down at 1.4 mm?”
With several runs selected, Height moves through all of them together. Each
shows its material at that same physical height, even when their Layer Heights
are different.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/p.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}SettingsPreviewExportSolveQueuePreview CardModesAdvancedModesImprovinga Solve


The Preview tab is where you inspect and compare results. You start a solve, Prisma works out the filament stack for every point, and the results land here for inspection — before you’ve spent any plastic.
For an explanation of how Prisma chooses the filament layers, see How It Works.
Starting a solve
Select one or more Palette Deck cards, then press Solve in the top bar
from any workflow page. Prisma keeps your current workspace open. One selected
card starts one solve; 2–10 selected cards show Solve (N) and start a batch
in deck order. With no selection, Solve is disabled.
Click a card to select it alone. Shift-click selects a range; Ctrl-click toggles
individual cards. Drag a selection rectangle from the empty space above or
below the deck cards, then use Ctrl-click to exclude any you do not want.
Progress appears in the Solve progress or Solve Queue window. You can
keep editing and add another solve while earlier work is running; each solve
keeps the image, palette, and settings you submitted. See Solve
Queue for progress,
cancellation, and waiting solves.
For an exact repeat, Prisma may reuse compatible completed work instead of
solving again. This can come from the current session or a compatible automatic
save after restart. Prisma can also recognize a matching solve already waiting
or running. An Already solved notice means that a matching result is
available; open Preview to review it.
Before starting, Prisma checks the current Settings, active printer, Palette,
stack geometry, and border thickness. A blocking problem tells you what must be
fixed. Prisma also checks whether the requested physical image size lands on
whole Solve Pitch cells. If it does not, Lithophane Dimensions shows the
current and proposed sizes, both with and without the border. Resize accepts
the proposed size and continues the same solve. Cancel leaves the requested
dimensions unchanged. A print larger than the printer area opens Larger Than
Printer Area; Use Current Size is available only when Prisma permits it.
A batch keeps the same image, settings, preprocessing, printer/nozzle, model
library, and white base/cap filaments, then changes only the colored palette.
It can compare deck cards of different origins and sizes. Prisma deliberately
does not choose a winner.
Viewer
Select a Solve Timeline card to see its result in the Viewer. View Mode
switches between the predicted appearance, the white cap, the color regions,
and more. Each view is described in Preview Card
Modes;
the extra views behind Advanced are in Advanced
Modes.
Use Zoom to enlarge the image from its fitted size, or hold Ctrl and turn
the mouse wheel over it. Drag an enlarged image to move around it. Fit
returns to the whole image. When several results are selected, their zoom and
movement stay together so you can compare the same area in each one. Explorer
also uses a shared height when comparing results.
Drag the divider beside Inspector to give the Viewer more room, or the divider
above Solve Timeline to change its height. In the Timeline, drag a card’s resize
handle to change card size; double-click the handle to return to automatic sizing.
One thing to know up front: the result can look blocky compared with the photo. That view shows the solve grid honestly rather than inventing image detail between solved points. A field-derived white-cap export may reconstruct a smoother physical cap surface, but it does not create new color decisions beyond the solve resolution.
Solve Timeline and Inspector
Every accepted solve becomes a card in the Solve Timeline. Show Results
For chooses the source image whose runs you want to review. Group By →
Palette keeps runs together by palette; None keeps them in order. Each
run retains its Source, Image Setup, Print Setup, Palette, and Solve Settings,
even when it was cancelled or failed before producing a result.
Select a run to open its Inspector. Current shows the full summary;
Compact concentrates on dimensions and settings differences. In Current,
Details on Image & Adjustments, Printer, Palette, or Settings
opens the attached detail drawer. Historical names
and colors remain those used by the run; a separate availability note explains
whether that part can still be applied with the resources installed now.
Solve Settings are initially compared with your startup Settings Profile.
Compare to chooses a different saved profile as the common reference for
every inspected run. Loading a different profile for the next solve does not
move this reference. Unsaved profile edits are not used in the comparison.
In Settings Details, Settings shows the captured values and Compare
shows them against the reference profile. Advanced: On reveals the finer
controls. Details show the settings that applied to the inspected run; values belonging
to disabled features or another solve mode are left out.
Click a card to select that run alone. Ctrl-click (Command-click on macOS)
adds or removes individual runs; Shift-click selects a range. Selecting two or
more results puts them together in the Viewer. Click one of those images to
show its Inspector without removing the others from the comparison. Export
selects one completed run at a time.
Use the star on a card or in Inspector to mark a promising run. Starred only
filters the Timeline for the chosen source image; starring does not save the
run. The card and Inspector also offer Save, Delete, and access to the captured
settings. Delete asks for a second click. Cancel a queued or running solve in
Solve Queue before removing its card.
Cards can show Queued, Solving, Cancelled, or Failed.
A failed card keeps its concise error and can be deleted; later batch items
continue. To keep a completed run deliberately, save it. Save is available after the solve
finishes. Clear removes the cards from the current Solve Timeline display
for the selected source image, including cards hidden by Starred only.
It asks for a second click and is unavailable while a solve or export is active.
It does not delete saved runs,
automatic saves, or print files already generated.
Review, reuse, and make a new solve
These are deliberately different operations:

Review reads the run’s captured setup and result. It does not
change the workspace and does not require the same Model Library release to
be active now.
Export or reprint uses the completed run and its saved result. It does
not recompute the result against today’s library or settings.
A section drawer’s Use… action recalls only that section. For example,
Use This Palette preserves its order, while Use These Settings also
restores the Base/Cap Filament choices captured with Settings.
Use as Starting Point reconstructs every compatible part of the run as
one editable workspace. The confirmation lists what will be applied and what
must remain unchanged. Prisma then moves to Image so you can review or
modify the setup. It never starts a solve.
Pressing Solve afterwards creates a new solve from the reconstructed state
and the resources active now.

Exact Framing requires the same source content and pixel geometry. A Palette
requires all of its filament IDs in the active Model Library. Print Setup needs
a current printer/nozzle that supports its Extrusion Width, Layer Height, and
image footprint. An incompatible part is left unchanged and reported; it does
not make the historical run unavailable for review or export.
Saving and loading solves
Press Save on a card and give it a name to create a durable Saved Run — its
source image, framing and appearance, Palette, Settings, and completed result.
Names such as Run 7 are reserved for the automatic labels Generator gives new
live cards, so choose a descriptive name instead.
Load at the top of Solve Timeline opens Saved Runs. Rows marked Saved
are explicit durable saves. Rows marked Autosave are temporary,
best-effort copies made after successful solves. Prisma keeps
only a recent set, older Autosaves can be removed automatically, and Clear
Temp Files removes them. An Autosave may survive a process restart, but it is
not a durable save; use Save when you intend to keep a run.
Select a row and use Load to return the complete run to Solve Timeline and
Preview without solving again. Your current image, settings, and Palette Deck
stay as they are. To begin new work from the loaded run, use its Inspector’s
Use as Starting Point or a section’s Use… action. Use Settings in
Saved Runs loads only the captured Settings as a session-only TEMP Settings
Profile. Save promotes an Autosave to a durable Saved Run, Rename manages
a Saved row, and Delete removes the selected Saved or Autosave record.
Download writes a portable archive, while Load from file… imports one —
useful for backup or moving a run to another computer.
Reloading the browser reconnects to the current workspace and its retained
runs. To return after restarting Prisma, save the whole workspace or save an
individual run. Autosaves are temporary even when one happens to remain
available after a restart. Use Save, Download, or export the print files
for anything you must retain.
Prisma keeps the archived source with the loaded card. If you recall its image
setup, Prisma can reuse an identical Image Library photo or show a temporary
Saved run source on the Image page. Loading alone does not select it.
Re-saving the card keeps the archive’s image even if a matching Library file
is later changed or deleted.
Experimental GPU solves
In Config → Preferences → Solve, enable Use GPU for solves and press
Apply. It is off by default and applies to newly submitted solves without
restarting Prisma. The tested setup is Windows with a Ryzen 9 9900X, 64 GB RAM,
and Radeon RX 9070; it requires the optional GPU solver components and
compatible AMD drivers. Other configurations are untested.
Some parts of a solve still use the CPU. Requests the GPU cannot handle use the
CPU, and a GPU problem can cause Prisma to retry on the CPU. Inspector records
how the run was solved; enabling GPU does not replace an existing completed
result. The setting is separate from GPU palette suggestions and exports.
When the result isn’t right
Compare the predicted view against the source and trust your eye. Start with several strong palette suggestions before tuning settings: palette choice usually changes more than one reasonable solver adjustment. Once you have a promising palette, name the specific defect, change one matching control, solve again, and compare both runs side by side.
Improving a Solve provides the full procedure and targeted starting points for chunky gradients, white-cap seams, overly bold dark regions, incoherent color casts, smoothing outlines, and isolated local defects.
