prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/r.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PaletteRuns withSwapsSettings


A run needs swaps when its palette contains more colored filaments than the active printer has color slots. Prisma plans these runs automatically; there is no separate mode or setting to choose.
Swaps increase the available palette, but they are not a free upgrade. The solve takes longer, the band structure consumes part of the thickness budget, white fill between bands can dilute color, and the print requires correctly timed filament changes. A palette that fits in one load is the more reliable baseline and will generally produce an equal or better result when it can cover the image well enough.
Before solving

Open Configuration and confirm the active printer, material-system units, and resulting simultaneous color-slot count.
Select the white filament under Settings → Essentials. The printer’s configured base/cap slot or slots remain reserved for it throughout the print.
Build a palette that exceeds the remaining color slots. In Auto-Suggest, set Palette colors above the displayed simultaneous capacity. In Manual mode, simply select the additional colors.
Keep a no-swap palette available when possible so you can compare whether the extra colors actually help.

Swap runs support at most 10 colored filaments, excluding the base and cap. Turn Palette Saturation Fit off before solving. Each band needs at least one color layer; if the thickness budget is too small, Prisma asks you to increase Max Thickness, reduce Base or Cap Thickness, or use fewer colors.
Solve and compare
Press Solve normally. Prisma first runs a lower-resolution scout to estimate how the image uses the palette, then plans the swap bands and runs the final solve. This takes longer than a run whose palette fits at once.
On Preview, compare the swap run with the no-swap baseline. Look at the predicted image, not only RMSE %. Extra colors are useful when they make a visible improvement in important parts of the image; a slightly better score alone may not justify the added constraints and print handling.
The swap plan is fixed as part of the completed run. If you change the printer’s slot capacity, solve again under the new configuration.
Generate the export

Open 4 Export and select the completed swap run.
Choose the export options and press Export Meshes.
In Generated Exports, select the new export record.
Under Print Instructions, confirm the initial slot assignments and each later unload/load instruction.
Use the copy button (Copy print instructions) to carry the plan into your slicer.

Add a slicer pause at each listed height. The exported 3MF does not add those pauses for you.
The generated files and Print Instructions all belong to that exact export. Changing the current printer, palette, or settings does not revise an existing record. Select a different completed run and generate a new export when you need a different plan.
Follow the initial loading order, slot identities, and pause heights exactly. White remains in its reserved base/cap slot or slots while the colored slots change between bands. The instructions preserve the plan stored by the selected solve; generating an export does not redesign it.
Practical guidance

Prefer the smallest palette that gives a meaningful visual improvement.
Increase Palette colors deliberately; larger searches take longer, and an oversized palette may add print handling without improving the result.
Keep the white filament loaded in every assigned base/cap slot for the entire print.
Check that each required filament is ready before slicing and printing.
Treat a swap run as a deliberate second option, not the default path for every image.

For the reason the solve uses flat filament bands and white fill, see Runs with Swaps in How It Works.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PreprocessingColorSolverWhiteCap


These control the heart of the process: how Prisma decides which filaments to stack, and how thick, across the print. The drawer presents three core controls followed by Color Matching, Region Planning, and Region Refinement.
Controls marked advanced need Advanced: On. Appearance Model, Chroma bias, Planning scale, Local corrections, and Boundary mutation must also be shown in Preferences → Settings before they appear here.
Core controls

Appearance Model (advanced) — the calibrated prediction of what color a stack of filaments makes when backlit. Color Model v2 (default) is the newer model; Color Model v1 is retained for comparison. This choice affects the solve, palette suggestions, previews, and diagnostics.
Max colors/region — how many different colored filaments may stack in a planned color region (1–7). More lets tricky colors be mixed better, but slows recipe search and can make busier stacks. Start with 3.
Adapt image to palette (off by default) — changes the colors Prisma asks the solver to reproduce according to the selected white filament and palette. White adaptation controls how strongly image whites move toward the base and cap filament; Color adaptation controls how strongly the image moves toward the palette’s reachable colors. The controls are independent: 0× disables that part, 1× applies its normal fitted adjustment, and larger values apply it more strongly. Try it when pale or familiar areas break into unrelated hues, but compare the result visually because it deliberately trades literal source-color accuracy for a more coherent palette-relative appearance.

Color Matching (advanced)

OOG handling (advanced) — what happens to photo colors your palette simply can’t make. OOG means out of gamut. Closest color (default) moves those colors toward the nearest part of the palette’s reachable range before Prisma chooses recipes. Preserve hue keeps the hue, mutes the vividness, and nudges brightness only when a color is too dark or bright to print — often gentler on skin tones and skies.
Mismatch tolerance (advanced) — how far off a color must be before it counts as unreachable and gets remapped. The difference is measured as dE (delta E), a perceptual color-difference estimate; lower is stricter.
Chroma bias (advanced) — balances Tone against Color. 0 is balanced; positive values favor hue and vividness, while negative values favor brightness. Increasing by 1 doubles the color weighting; decreasing by 1 halves it.

Region Planning
Prisma doesn’t pick a recipe per pixel — it first divides the image into small color patches (regions) and solves those. These settings set how that patchwork is drawn.

Region shape (advanced) — how regions are drawn. Follow edges (default) and Compact follow the picture’s own structure; Fixed grid uses uniform squares.
Planning scale (advanced) — plan the regions on a coarser version of the image (1× = full resolution). Higher makes broader, simpler regions and faster solves, but follows fine edges less closely.
Region size — the intended size of a color patch, in millimeters. Smaller follows the image more faithfully; larger gives simpler, cleaner prints.

Region Refinement

Protect neutral areas (disabled by default) — reduces abrupt hue shifts between nearly identical weakly colored regions, especially in cloudy skies and shaded neutral backgrounds. Enable it and choose Low, Medium, or High to progressively include more source colors; the preset changes the protection’s scope, not its strength. Advanced On exposes Neutral chroma cutoff and labels values that differ from a preset Custom. Start with Medium. High may also influence pale skin and subtly colored subjects, so compare its preview with the feature disabled before printing.
Local corrections (advanced) — lets small spots inside a region use a better-matching recipe when the improvement is strong. Preserves fine detail, at the cost of more small patches. On by default.

Boundary mutation
Boundary mutation (advanced) lets boundary points borrow a recipe from the region immediately across the border when that recipe matches the photo better. It is on by default. The change is accepted in connected boundary runs, so the result shifts a contour instead of scattering unrelated points.

Passes — the maximum number of refinement passes (1–16). Each pass can move the boundary one solve point farther; processing stops early when nothing else improves. An empty field uses the default of 1.
Min color gain — the minimum average color-error improvement a connected patch must achieve. The default is 0.010 dE.

Region shapes and boundary mutation

Follow edges forms unequal patches around image structure; Compact favors compact patches that still follow edges; Fixed grid uses uniform cells regardless of the picture.

Boundary mutation refines an existing recipe boundary; it does not introduce a new recipe. Each pass can advance a boundary by one solve point.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.title: Preprocessing Module Settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}SettingsPreprocessingColorSolver


Preprocessing changes the image before color solving starts. It can reduce noise, simplify detail that will not survive printing, or move tones and saturation toward what the selected palette can reproduce. These are creative controls as much as cleanup tools: use the preview and compare runs rather than assuming stronger is better.
Resample kernel (advanced)
How the photo is sampled onto the solve grid. Lanczos (default) keeps things sharper; Area gives a softer, smoother result when reducing a large image and can suit coarse prints. Show Resample kernel in Preferences → Settings, then turn on Advanced to see this control.
The modules
Five modules run in a fixed order, each switched on or off independently:
Noise Reduction → Print-Scale Smoothing → Flat-Area Smoothing → Palette Tone Fit → Palette Saturation Fit
All five start off on a fresh install. Use the checkbox to enable a module, then choose its preset. Turn on Advanced to see the individual fields. Editing those fields changes the preset label to Custom when the values no longer match a named preset. The first three change spatial detail. The last two change the target’s tone or saturation and need a palette.
Comparing the image
Choose Open Preview beside Preprocessing to open a floating window. Drag the divider across the image to compare Input with Preprocessed. The preview updates as you change settings; Update refreshes it again when needed. This shows the image sent to the solver, not a prediction of the printed result.
The controls beside the image are another way to edit the same modules. Use each module’s power button to switch it on or off, and click its heading to expand its sample or graph. The preset picker and sample controls change the same settings as the drawer. Closing the window keeps those changes. If a module is missing, check Preferences → Settings.
Noise Reduction
Softens fine grain and noise while trying to preserve edges. It is a useful first step when texture or sensor noise is fragmenting the solved color regions. Advanced fields:

Filter radius — how large an area each point is smoothed over.
Edge blending — move toward More to allow more smoothing across color boundaries, or toward Less to keep edges sharper. It is intentionally qualitative rather than a color-distance unit.
Spatial reach — how far the smoothing influence extends inside that area.

Filter radius and Spatial reach are set in millimeters, so a preset keeps roughly the same physical meaning when Solve Pitch changes. The filter radius must land on whole solve-grid cells. If the requested distance cannot be represented exactly, the drawer shows the distance it will actually use beside the field.
Expand Noise Reduction in the preprocessing preview to see a noisy-shape sample. The spatial diagram shows its upper-right quadrant. The bracket above the grid spans one solve cell and labels its physical width. Drag the handle below the grid for Filter radius, or the handle on the curve to its left for Spatial reach. The dashed connector ties the radius handle to the requested-radius arc, while the stepped outline shows the sampled cells. The narrow curve shows how a point’s influence falls with distance at the same physical scale as the grid. Drag its point or horizontal dashed line vertically to adjust reach. The curve becomes faint beyond the effective filter radius; excluded cells contribute nothing. The fields beside Spatial reach and Filter radius accept exact values in millimeters; press Enter or leave the field to apply a value. Dragging applies the change on release. Hold Show Original to compare the same sample before filtering. The separate gradient beside Edge blending shows progressively different colors relative to a fixed reference. The overlaid curve shows how strongly those colors contribute to smoothing. Drag the point or dashed line horizontally to adjust Edge blending directly, or type a value into its field. Thin limit lines on both graphs mark the minimum and maximum handle positions. This comparison excludes distance weighting and the filter radius.
Print-Scale Smoothing
Off by default. Smooths small color variations within a physical radius, producing larger, simpler color patches. Its radius stays fixed when nozzle size or Solve Pitch changes. Advanced fields:

Smoothing radius — 0.2–2 mm, adjusted in 0.1 mm steps. Only pixel centers within this distance contribute. A radius below Solve Pitch leaves the image unchanged.
Edge blending — move toward More to blend more different neighboring colors, or toward Less to preserve stronger edges.
Passes — how many times the smoothing is applied.

The Print-Scale Smoothing sample in the preprocessing preview uses a compact pixel grid with a draggable radius control. Its Edge blending control uses the same color gradient and curve as Noise Reduction, with a reference color taken from the sample. Drag the point or dashed line, or enter an exact value in the field. The curve responds immediately; dragging applies the setting on release.
Flat-Area Smoothing
Off by default. Collapses gradual texture into broad flat areas — at higher strengths the image takes on a painted, graphic look. Advanced fields:

Strength (0–100, Less → More) — smooth fine texture into broader, flatter areas. Higher values create a more painted or graphic appearance. Zero is minimum strength; disable the module to turn it off.
Mode — Lightness smooths lightness rather than chroma; Light. & Chroma smooths lightness and color together.

The computation has a fixed internal iteration cap. It may converge sooner; there is no user-facing iteration control.
The Flat-Area Smoothing sample in the preprocessing preview uses a shaded shape with irregular lightness and color patches. It runs the actual module so you can compare the two modes and increasing strength. Show Original reveals the unchanged source sample while held.
Palette Tone Fit
Off by default. Needs a palette. Remaps the photo’s brightness range to the palette’s estimated printable range, so shadows and highlights fit it instead of being clipped. Advanced fields:

Strength (0–100) — how fully the remap is applied (0 = none, 100 = full).
Shadow anchor — how much of the darkest part of the image is treated as “black.”
Highlight anchor — how much of the brightest part is treated as “white.”
Midtone curve (−100 to +100) — negative values bend midtones darker; positive values bend them lighter. Zero keeps the mapping between the anchors straight. Equal magnitudes move the midpoint equally in opposite directions.

The Palette Tone Fit graph in the preprocessing preview shows the mapping from input lightness to output lightness. The bars show where the image’s tones fall. Drag the shadow and highlight markers to change the anchors, or the midpoint to bend the curve. The markers follow the actual tones in the image, so a Shadow anchor of 0 sits at its darkest tone and a Highlight anchor of 100 at its lightest.
Palette Saturation Fit
Off by default. Needs a palette. Gently pulls colors that are more vivid than your palette can print back within its reach, keeping their hue and brightness. It cannot be used for a full solve that requires filament swaps. Disable this module or choose a palette that fits the printer’s available color slots. Advanced fields:

Compression start — how close to the palette’s limit a color must be before it starts getting pulled in. Lower starts earlier and affects more of the image.
Softness — lower values pull affected colors farther inward. Higher values keep more saturation and spread the transition over a wider range.

The Palette Saturation Fit graph in the preprocessing preview shows how saturation changes relative to the palette’s reach. Drag its handles to adjust Compression start and Softness. The bars show how much of the image falls at each input saturation. At Compression start 100, colors within reach stay unchanged and colors beyond it are clipped to the limit; Softness has no effect at that setting.
Comparing the modules

The first three modules simplify spatial detail in different ways. The palette-aware modules instead move tone or saturation toward what the selected palette can reproduce.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.title: White Cap Settings
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}ColorSolverWhiteCapPreview


Every lithophane has a white cap above the color stack. The cap diffuses the backlight, affects the predicted appearance, and forms the viewing surface. Its required boundary cap continuously covers the solved color stacks. An optional detail cap can add localized white relief above that boundary where the image calls for it.
Cap thickness
Cap Thickness is set in Essentials. It specifies the physical thickness you want for the continuous boundary cap above every color stack. Prisma converts that dimension to the closest printable whole-layer thickness at the current Layer Height, choosing the thicker result when two choices are equally close. The default is 0.16 mm. Every positive request still produces at least one cap layer, so every solved color stack has continuous white cover.
Boundary

Shading balance (Luminance mode only) — where light-and-dark variation is carried. Toward Smooth, more of it goes into the broader boundary-cap surface; toward Detail, more goes into localized detail relief. Suggest proposes a balance from the selected image.
Upper surface style (advanced, Color mode only) — the cap’s character. Image Aware (default) limits smoothing where it would change the predicted appearance too much. Smooth prioritizes a clean, continuous outer surface instead. Luminance mode uses Smooth and hides this control.
Appearance budget (advanced, Color mode with Image Aware only) — how much visible color change you’ll tolerate in exchange for a smoother cap. The default is 0.004 dE; lower protects the image more aggressively.
Smoothing radius — how far the cap’s top surface is smoothed, in millimeters. The default is 1.0 mm. Lower keeps more tonal relief; higher gives a cleaner surface. It remains meaningful in both boundary-cap modes, and the cap’s underside always fits the colors exactly.

Detail

Max detail layers — the maximum number of white layers the detail cap may add above the boundary cap. It is a limit, not a target: the detail cap can appear as separated bumps and ridges rather than covering the entire surface. At 0, no optional detail relief can be added.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PaletteSettingsPreviewPreprocessingColorSolverWhiteCap


Settings control how Prisma builds the lithophane — its thickness and resolution, any preprocessing applied to the image, how colors are matched, and how the white cap is built. The defaults are sensible: you can make a good print without opening this drawer at all.
The settings drawer
Press the Settings gear (top right) to slide the drawer in from the right — it works from any tab. The drawer is one continuous, scrollable layout containing Profile, Essentials, Preprocessing, Color Solver, and White Cap. On a wide window, Prisma automatically flows that layout into additional columns. The × closes it.
Advanced: Off / On (in the drawer header) hides or reveals the less-common settings. Leave it off at first — everything you need day to day is visible without it.
Some controls are also hidden by default in Preferences → Settings. Show them there before looking for them in the drawer. Hiding a control does not turn its setting off.
There’s no OK or Apply — changes take hold as you make them, and they apply to the next solve. A solve already running or finished keeps the settings it started with. Exporting an older run uses that run’s recorded settings rather than whatever is currently in the drawer.
When improving an existing preview, follow Improving a Solve: compare several palettes before tuning, identify one visible defect, and change only the control aimed at that defect.
Profiles
The bar at the top of the drawer manages settings profiles — named saves of the entire settings collection. The current profile’s name is shown, with a marker when you’ve changed something since it was saved.

Click the profile name to choose and load another profile. Load the protected built-in Basic profile to return to factory settings.
Manage opens Settings Profiles. Select a profile and choose Load, or use the star action to choose the profile Prisma loads at startup. Changing the startup profile does not load it immediately.
Save offers to overwrite a modified named profile or save the current settings under a new name. The protected Basic profile and a session-only TEMP profile loaded from a Solved Run cannot be overwritten.
Save As… stores them under a new name.

If you load another profile while the current one is modified, Prisma asks you to Save As, Discard, or Cancel first. Use Settings from Run… opens Saved Runs and loads a run’s captured settings as a TEMP profile; save it under a normal name if you want to keep it or make it the startup profile. Named profiles can be renamed in Manage. A profile must be unloaded before it can be deleted.
When Prisma recognizes an older Settings Profile, it updates the profile for the current version and keeps a backup of the previous file. A profile whose format Prisma does not recognize is not loaded.
Profiles are how you keep useful setups around — for example, a high-detail profile and a quicker draft profile — and switch between them in two clicks. When you find settings that work, save them.
Prisma ships two optional profiles derived from production-scale solve comparisons: Refinement — Balanced and Refinement — Strong. They are alternate solve recipes, not replacements for Basic and not guaranteed improvements. See Improving a Solve for their intended order and tradeoffs.
Essentials
The everyday section: the print’s size and thickness limits and the main solve-mode choice. The information button beside Essentials opens Thickness details, showing the printable cap thickness and available color layers.

Solve Mode — the biggest single choice in the app. Color aims the filament stacks directly at the image’s colors. Luminance lets white-cap thickness carry more of the image’s brightness and fine detail, with color underneath. Compare both when subtle light-and-dark structure matters; the better choice depends on the image and palette.
Solve Pitch — the size of one solve point, shown in millimeters. It changes in whole multiples of the active Extrusion Width, with one Extrusion Width as the minimum. Smaller = more detail but slower solves and exports. If changing the active nozzle or Extrusion Width would alter this or another dependent value, Prisma shows the consequences for review before applying the print-setup change.
Layer Height — must exactly match the layer height you’ll slice with. If these disagree, the printed colors won’t match the preview.
Max Thickness — the print’s total thickness budget. Thicker gives the solver more layers to work with — deeper darks and richer color — at the cost of print time.
Base Thickness — the solid white plate the print sits on.
Cap Thickness — the desired physical thickness of the continuous white boundary cap. Prisma resolves it to the closest printable whole-layer thickness at the current Layer Height.
Base/Cap — the white filament used for the solid base and the top cap. This is chosen here, not in the palette (see Palette).

Warnings below the table explain any values that need attention before solving.
The other sections
Each has its own page describing every setting and what it does to the print. The short version:

Preprocessing — resampling and optional clean-up of the photo before solving: noise reduction, smoothing toward printable detail, and reshaping tones and saturation toward what your palette can reproduce. Each optional module is a simple preset picker; all start off.
Color Solver — how colors are adapted, matched, and refined. It includes Appearance Model, Max colors/region, Adapt image to palette, Color Matching, Region Planning, and Region Refinement.
White Cap — the white layer above the colors. It controls the boundary surface and optional detail relief; in Luminance mode, Shading balance determines whether broad shading comes from smooth cap thickness or fine relief.

There is no separate swap-planning setting. When a palette needs more colors than your printer can hold at once, Prisma plans the required filament bands automatically during the solve. See Runs with Swaps for when to use them and how to carry the plan into the slicer.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/s.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PreviewSolveQueuePreview CardModes


Prisma runs one solve at a time. You can prepare another image, palette, or
settings change and press Solve while earlier work is still running. The
new solve waits its turn. Each one keeps the setup you submitted, so later edits
do not change a waiting solve.
The activity button beside Solve shows the current progress and number of
waiting solves. Click it to open or close the solve window. The small Solve
progress window shows the current run, palette, Settings Profile, stage,
progress, elapsed time, and Cancel. Its maximize button opens the full
Solve Queue; Restore down returns to the small progress window.
Waiting solves
The queue lists each solve’s Image, Palette, Profile, and Pitch. Delta
summarizes changes from the Settings Profile as it was loaded when you
submitted the solve. Hover over that value for the fuller list, or over the color
chips for filament names. Click the arrow beside Image to give long
filenames more room.
Remove cancels a waiting solve before it starts. Use the row checkboxes and
Remove selected for several, or Remove all waiting for the whole waiting
list. Removing all waiting asks for a second click. These actions leave the
current solve running.
Cancel stops the current solve; it does not cancel later waiting solves.
Prisma shows Stopping… until it has stopped. Completed results remain
available, and cancelled runs keep a Timeline card that you can review or delete.
Completed work
Enable Show completed to include finished, cancelled, and failed entries.
Clear history removes those entries from this queue window and leaves
their results in Preview. Preview
is where you inspect, compare, star, and save the results.
An ordinary failed solve keeps its error while the next waiting solve
continues. If Prisma runs out of memory or disk space, the queue pauses and
shows a dialog. Free the needed resource, then choose Retry. Cancel
closes that dialog and leaves the queue paused; Resume in Solve Queue lets
you try again later.
Window visibility and returning to work
Drag either window by its title bar. Closing it hides the window without
cancelling work. Config → Preferences → Solve → Window visibility controls
when it appears automatically. A window opened from the toolbar stays open
until you close it; a dismissed window stays hidden for that period of queued
work.
Reloading or reopening the browser reconnects to work accepted by the same
running Prisma session. Waiting solves do not survive a Prisma restart. Save
completed runs or the workspace before closing Prisma when you want to keep
them.

Open Help & Guides in the top bar to start guided instruction inside Prisma
Generator. Its menu has direct shortcuts to First-Time Setup, Prisma
Generator Basics, Settings Drawer, and Saving & Loading. Select
Guides Library… to browse the complete catalog.
Getting Started

First-Time Setup — configure Prisma Generator for your printer and learn its essential utility controls.
Prisma Generator Basics — create, compare, inspect, and export a complete tutorial lithophane.

Page Guides

Image Guide — prepare and frame the tutorial image while exploring Image controls.
Palette Guide — prepare suggested palettes and explore the Deck and Manual builder.
Settings Guide — review essential solve controls, Settings Profiles, the Color Solver, and White Cap.
Settings Drawer — explore how every stage of a lithophane solve is shaped by Settings.
Preview Guide — create two tutorial solves, then compare and inspect their results.
Export Guide — create a tutorial solve and generate its print files.

The Guides Library notes that Preview Guide creates two tutorial solves and
Export Guide creates one tutorial solve and print files.
Preview

Explore the Interface — preview how Prisma can identify controls without changing them. This catalog entry carries a Preview badge.

Save, Reuse, and Export

Saving & Loading — save and restore Palettes, Settings Profiles, and completed Solved Runs.

Before a teaching guide starts
Most teaching guides preserve your current work before preparing a temporary
tutorial workspace. Ending the guide restores your image setup, settings,
printer setup, Palette Deck, staged suggestions, retained solves and exports.
The original workspace name, unsaved changes, and unfinished Manual palette
draft are retained too.
Refreshing or reopening the page during a guide restores the previous workspace;
the guide does not resume. Recovery also survives a server restart. While the
guide is active, other Prisma windows remain read-only, and Workspace Save,
Load, Reset and Delete are unavailable. Your saved Preferences remain unchanged.
First-Time Setup works with your current configuration instead of preparing
a teaching workspace. Explore the Interface only demonstrates how guides
identify controls and restores the presentation it changed.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/w.title: Workspaces
prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/w.content:
.htu-localnav svg text{font-family:inherit;font-size:13px}.htu-localnav a rect{transition:stroke .15s ease}.htu-localnav a:hover rect{stroke:var(--secondary);stroke-width:2}.htu-localnav a:hover text{fill:var(--secondary)}PreferencesWorkspacesImage


Open Workspace in the top bar to save related work together. A saved workspace keeps the image setup, current settings and printer setup, Palette Deck and its selection, completed solve results, and export records. Unfinished Manual palettes and staged suggestions are not included.
The top bar shows Untitled until you save or load a workspace. An asterisk beside its name means there are unsaved changes.
Save and Save As
Save updates the workspace you have saved or loaded. The first Save asks for a name. Save As… creates a separate copy under a new name; it does not replace a workspace with the same name.
Finish or cancel active work before saving or changing workspaces.
Load, rename, and delete
Load… lists your saved workspaces. Select one and press Load. If the current work has changed, Prisma offers Save or Discard; close the dialog to cancel.
Each saved row also has Rename and Delete. Deleting a save removes that named copy, without clearing the work already open or deleting Library images, Saved Runs, exported print files, or Preferences.
Reset Workspace starts a fresh workspace with your startup defaults. It asks what to do with unsaved changes first. Saved workspaces and individual saves remain available.
When a saved image is missing
A workspace keeps references to ordinary Image Library files, so keep those originals too. If a saved image is missing, add the original file to the Library and choose Locate Image… from Workspace. Select the missing source if Prisma lists several, then select the matching Library image and press Locate.
Prisma checks the image contents. A new filename is fine, but an edited or re-encoded photo will not match. You can instead choose another image for a new solve. Existing results keep their original recorded source.
Keep exported files too
Export records refer to the print files already written in Generator/Exports. Saving the workspace does not copy those files into it. Keep the files or use Download ZIP copy in Export when you want a separate copy.
To keep or share one result separately, use Download in Saved Runs.

prisma-lithophane-generator/how-to-use/i.content:

A color lithophane is a thin printed panel that reveals a color image when lit from behind. You give Prisma a photo and the filaments available to you; it works out a printable stack and exports the files your slicer needs.
This section is the practical guide to the app. It explains what to do and what each choice changes. For a conceptual view of the machinery underneath, see How It Works.
The workflow in the app
The conceptual workflow and the controls are nearly the same, but a few decisions live outside the numbered tabs:





































In the appWhat you are decidingConfig in the upper-rightOpen the occasional setup windows for Model Library, Active Filaments, and Printer Configuration. The left rail keeps the active Printer, Nozzle, and Extrusion Width visible.1 ImageWhich image area to print, its physical size, and any image adjustments.2 PaletteWhich colored filaments the solve may use.Settings gearOptional solve, preprocessing, region, and white-cap behavior for the next run.Solve → 3 PreviewBuild a run, inspect the prediction, and compare it with earlier runs.4 ExportChoose a completed run and generate its 3MF or STL files. Each Generated Export keeps its own Print Instructions, including any swaps.3D PrintingMove the generated files into the slicer, prepare the printer, and light the finished panel.
Most iteration happens between Palette, Settings, and Preview. Change one meaningful thing, solve again, and compare the runs side by side.
Navigation shortcuts
The default shortcuts use Alt on Windows or Linux, or Option on macOS:





















ShortcutAction1, 2, 3, or 4Open Image, Palette, Preview, or Export.QOpen or close Settings.WStart the currently selected Solve mode when Solve is available.
The shortcuts follow the physical 1 2 3 4 and Q W key cluster. They do not run while you are typing in an input, text area, dropdown, or editable field.
Use Config → Preferences → Key Bindings to change these shortcuts or add
ones for Solve Queue, Suggest Palettes, Preprocessing Preview, and Preferences.

New here? Getting Started covers installing and launching the app and walks through a first solve.

Appearance
Use the Theme control in the right side of the top bar, beside Workspace, to choose System, Light, or Dark. System follows your operating-system appearance, including changes made while Generator is open; an explicit Light or Dark choice stays fixed. Generator saves the preference in this browser and synchronizes it between open Generator tabs. It is an interface preference only—not part of Settings Profiles, saved runs, or exports.
Setup

Configuration — tell Prisma which filaments you own and which printer setup is active.
Preferences — choose startup defaults, interface behavior, shortcuts, and optional GPU use.
Workspaces — save related work, load it later, and locate a moved source image.

Learn in the app
Use Help & Guides in the top bar for guided instruction attached directly to
the current interface. The menu provides shortcuts to several major guides;
Guides Library… opens the complete catalog. See In-App
Guides for the current
catalog and the workspace behavior to expect when a teaching guide starts.
Make a lithophane

Image — choose a photo, set the physical print size, and frame it.
Palette — choose colored filaments manually or ask Prisma to suggest them.
Settings — tune print thickness, solve behavior, preprocessing, and the white cap when needed.
Preview — build and compare predicted results.
Solve Queue — follow the current solve and manage waiting work.
Improving a Solve — compare palettes first, then use targeted settings changes for specific visible defects.
Export — generate print files for a selected completed run.

Special workflow

Runs with Swaps — use more colored filaments than the printer can hold at once and carry the resulting Print Instructions into the slicer.

After export

3D Printing — slice, print, and light the result.

Workspace → Save preserves the current image/settings, Palette Deck, retained solves and export records for later work. Save As creates another named copy; Load restores one. Unfinished palette drafts and staged suggestions are not saved. Finish or cancel active operations before saving. See Workspaces for the save, load, and missing-image controls.
Reset Workspace starts fresh with startup defaults. Modified work offers Save or Discard first; closing the dialog cancels the reset. It preserves saved workspaces, saved runs, source images, completed exports and Preferences. Reusable caches and recent automatic archives remain available.
A fresh server starts a new workspace. Reloading or reopening a browser tab against the same running server reconnects to accepted work. Browser-retained layout choices remain separate from saved workspace contents.

prisma-lithophane-generator/index.content:
Welcome to the documentation wiki for Prisma Lithophane Generator. Prisma Generator converts a photo into a 3D-printable color lithophane using a photo-specific palette instead of limiting every print to cyan, magenta, yellow, and white. A palette chosen for the particular image can reproduce its colors more accurately.
Organization
This wiki is divided into three sections, each intended to answer a different kind of question:

Getting Started — a quick-start guide that helps you install and run Prisma Generator for the first time. It includes a step-by-step walkthrough of the basics, from choosing an image to exporting printable files.
How To Use — a user guide covering Prisma Generator’s features and controls. If you are unsure what a setting does, start here.
How It Works — explanations of the concepts and processes behind Prisma Generator. This section describes the ideas without discussing code or their specific implementation.

readme.title: README
readme.content:
This folder is an Obsidian vault and the source of the published docs site. To read it locally: Open folder as vault in Obsidian → choose this Documentation/ folder → start at Prisma Lithophane Generator or Prisma Calibration. On the website, the landing page at / covers the same ground.
Prisma has two portable distribution packages on Windows and Linux. Generator-only is the streamlined option for making lithophanes from a published model library. Suite adds Calibration, which owns the private sample database and working model fits. Calibration can publish a complete immutable library for Generator, but Generator never reads Calibration’s live Workspace. A packaged macOS release is planned for public launch, but it has not yet been built or smoke-tested. The user-facing installation, launcher, folder, and backup guidance lives in each app’s Getting Started section.
Everything here uses built-in Obsidian features only (wikilinks, tags, graph view, backlinks, search) — no community plugins — so the same vault publishes as a static Quartz website without rework.
Structure
Two top-level sections, one per app, each with three sections:

Getting Started — orientation and a first run.
How It Works — the phenomena and the math, textbook register, no code identifiers.
How To Use — a plain, task-focused user guide.

The one rule these docs follow
Check behavior claims against the current application. Use source files and the interface as evidence, rather than older notes or remembered behavior. A deliberately future-facing claim must use the RELEASE-INTENT convention below. Keep the evidence for a review in docs/; the wiki itself should describe Prisma in language its users can follow.
Authoring rules (for maintainers and agents)

Never hard-wrap a wikilink or inline-code span across a line break — Obsidian won’t parse it. Don’t hard-wrap body prose at all.
Use explicit full-path links when a page name occurs in more than one section. Folder links are resolved by the copy script using their surrounding section; an ambiguous tie stops the sync. Don’t give two pages in the same folder names that differ only in case — their slugs collide.
Landing/overview diagrams are generated by scripts/gen_landing_diagrams.py and injected between LANDING-DIAGRAM markers; How To Use diagrams by scripts/gen_howto_nav_diagrams.py; per-page How It Works diagrams by scripts/gen_local_nav_diagrams.py. Edit the script tables and re-run — never hand-edit the generated blocks.
Keep screenshot capture notes in <!-- TODO: ... --> comments so they do not appear in the reading view.
Check links with scripts/check_docs_wikilinks.py (the vault should stay at 0 dangling links).

Source-only editorial annotations
Use HTML comments for notes that belong in the Markdown source but must not appear in Obsidian reading view or on the published Quartz site. Start each comment with one of these labels so its intent is unambiguous:

<!-- RELEASE-INTENT: ... --> — a deliberately future-facing statement expected to be true for a named release or launch. State what must be verified before removing the comment.
<!-- VERIFY: ... --> — a factual claim that is provisional and needs evidence or testing.
<!-- TODO: ... --> — a known placeholder or unfinished content change.
<!-- QUESTION: ... --> — a request for maintainer or agent input.
<!-- EDITORIAL: ... --> — a writing, structure, or Markdown-syntax instruction rather than literal page text.

Keep a visible qualifier such as “coming soon” when a future-facing page might be published before the planned feature or package is actually available. Do not use an invisible comment to conceal a statement that would mislead readers on the currently published site.
Publishing
scripts/sync_docs_to_quartz.py mirrors the vault into the local Quartz clone’s content/ (stripping title-duplicate leading H1s and rewriting folder-index wikilinks on the copy). scripts/publish_docs.py additionally builds and pushes the live site — only run it when the site should actually update.

index.title: Prisma Documentation
index.content:
Prisma is a color lithophane generator: photograph 3D-printed filament swatches to characterize how each filament transmits light, then decompose an image into a stack of filament layers that reproduces its colors when backlit. You can start with the included model library or use Prisma Calibration to measure your own filaments.
The two apps

Prisma Lithophane Generator — turn a photo into a backlit color lithophane and export print files for a multi-color 3D printer. The Generator-only Windows and Linux packages include a published Standard Model Library.
Prisma Calibration — measure how filaments transmit light on a lightbox, fit personal working models, and publish a model library for the Generator. Calibration is included in the Windows and Linux Suite packages.

Calibration keeps its samples, photographs, and working models separate from Generator. Generator uses one published Model Library at a time. After fitting your models in Calibration, use Publish Models to make them available to Generator or export a library for another installation. Later changes in Calibration do not alter a library you have already published.
Each app is organized into three sections:

Getting Started — orientation and a first run.
How It Works — the phenomena and the math.
How To Use — a plain, task-focused user guide.

Use the graph and search to explore.
The wiki describes the current application. Packaged beta downloads can be older and may not include every feature shown here. Check the notes for your download on Prisma’s Releases page.
